RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
AFOOAR SIX OV A MORNIN'.

When th' east wind blows keenly, An' inornin's are dark, Wod fooak—helter skelter— Peyl off to ther wark. Some's warm i' ther top-cooats, Some shiver i' rags, While clogs cutter-clatter 0 t' street leught on t' flags. Tewd Labour's id sorros. To ged a good seet 0' th' way id abides 'em, just wander deawn t' street, An' nooatis o th' pinched tab' faces yo' meet Afooar six o'clock ov a mamba'. ' On th' rooa.ds deawn to t' fact'rys Fooak drooave on i' swarms, Some wayk, jaded wimmin Hey babbles th' arms. Lapped up they blankets, • Thor ta en eawt o' bed t' depth o' cowd winter, Tiro' t' struggle for bread. Poor innocent things ! It's a sin an' a shame To use em' thad way,—but whoa con yo' blame? ileaw wod eawr Deoth-rate be if o wur used t' same, A bit afeoar six every mornin' ?

Ther's odd chaps, so mopish, Slink dreely on t' rooad ; They seem to like warkin' As weel as a toad. Tiler t' sooart' at mek misery, An' drink just like fish ; They'd spend Life in' th' aleheawse If they hed ther wish. Just watch 'em stare sheepish tort th' " pub's " whido- sill.

Ther bad thro' neet spreein' off leatherheyd swill; An' id comes like a blessin'—a pint or a gill A bit afooar six ov a mornin ! Ther's lots o' pale childer, • Like ghosts flittin' by, To see 'ern brings teardrops To th' pityin' eye. Id may be compulsion 'At fooarces 'em eawt, But often it happens Ther's reason for eleawt. An scooars o' sich like, every wark-time th' week. Gooa sadly to toil, wi' warm tears o' ther cheek; God help 'em! Ther punished, for t' weather's so bleak, 4 bit afooar six ov a mornin' ! Yo'll see odd young fella's ' At corners yo' pass, Stood towkin' soft nonsense To some bonny lass. Or. if rain be teemin,' Yo'll find 'em i' wait, Wi' big umberellas To tek heragate. For mony a bit o' sly courtin' gets done, ' Afooar th' time for labour hes fairly begun ; Just mark th' off-hand ways they hey, nobbut for fun, „. A bit afooar six ov a mornin' ! Yo'll nooatis hawf-timers 'At's getten too ripe, Wi' sitch a bowd swagger, Strut, smookin' a pipe! Yo'll see hurried mothers Rush sadly fro' th' noss, Yo'll hear odd chaps singin', An'some doin' woss. Ther's th' healthy an' poorly; ther's th' humble an th preawd, An' poor hawf-clam'd childer 'at's fit for a shreawd, 0 mingled i' t' streom ov a work-a-day creawd A bit afooar six ov a mornin' !
PEEPS INTO THE PAST.
SCRAPS FROM LOCAL RECORDS. BY "OLD MORTALITY."

The reputation of Warrington ale is of old-stand- ing. So far back as 1709 Warrington was spoken of as a place of great note for its malting trade. The trade had here been brought to " as great perfection as that at Derby," and the ale brewed from Warring- ton malt was not inferior to the most noted ales in England. One of the earliest of those who made money out of beer in Warrington was John Earle, "the earliest trustee of the Blue School," who lived before the year 1690.

The liquor trade still flourishes in the town, but another old industry has entirely vanished from the locality—that is, the making of sail cloth. It is re- corded that about the year 1769, sail cloth for the royal navy was made in Warrington and in the sur- rounding Tillages, to the value of about £70.000 a year, and that about 10,000 persons were employed in this trade and in the fabricating of coarse linens.

Arthur Young, the famous traveller and agricul- turist, passed through Warrington in 1769 in his tour through the north of England, and he gives some interesting details as to the wages paid in the sail-cloth and sacking manufactures. The sail-cloth was spun by women and girls who earned 2d. a day; the bleaching was done by men who received 10s. a week. The cloth was " wound " by women who earned 2s. 6d. a week, "warped" by men making 75., and "starched by men at 10s. 6d. a week. The last operation was the weaving in which the men received 95., the women 55., and the boys 3s. 6d. a week. In the sacking branch the wages were on much the same scale.

Too SMART FOR THE GENERAL—MarshaI Alexander Suvoroff, the greatest of Russia's modern generals, was something of a humorist in his way, and delighted in playing tricks on Iris soldiers and asking them puzzling questions. He would often disguise himself as a private soldier and wander through the bivouacs, enjoying the strange adventures that befell him. and the plain-spoken criticisims upon himself which he often heard. On one , or two occasions. however, this reckless joker met with ! his match. A trooper having brought him a message from the colonel of a dragoon regiment which had just been engaved in a skirmish, Suvoroff asked the man ! pointedly, " What is the difference between your colonel and myself ?" The question was a very awkward one toanswer, for Colonel Soltikoff was one of the hand- somest men in the Russian army, while the old marshal was hideously ugly. But the soldier, not a whit taken aback, replied. molly, "The difference is that my colonel cannot make me a sergeant, whereas your excellency can do so whenever you like." Thus caught in his own trap, Fuvoroff had no choice but to laugh and to give him the required promotion. At another time the general was prowling at night around the outposts. , looking out for a chance of playing one of his usual tricks. According to custom, he was very lightly clad, although it was a bitterly cold night in mid-winter; for the old warrior was very proud of his power of enduring cold (which was superior to that of any man in his army), and he never lost a chance of displaying it. Buddenly he came upon a sentinel, awl called out to him: "Hello, brother! now many stars are there in the sky ?" The soldier knew the marshal's voice at once, but, pretend- ing not to recognise him, he replied," Just wait a bit and I'll count 'em for you," and began deliberately, "one, two, three, four," and so on. To the sentry, wrapped in his thick frieze coat, this was a good joke enough; but the thinly clad general soon found it much colder than he liked, and when the soldier had got up to one hundred, and was still counting away as if he would never leave off, Suvoroff stopped him short, and having taken his name, made off as fast as his half-frozen feet would carry him. But the next 'morning the shrewd sentry was made a corporal for having been "too smart for the general."—Herrper's Magazine. " OH, Yes I" Cough Mixture, Chiretta Balsam. Belief in three minutes. What a number of unsettled questions there are in the world! I notice that in the early months of 1853 an "Original Essay and Historical Debating Society" was started in Warrington, and the mem- bers seem to have at once set about attempting the solution of some of the most recondite problems. On one occroion they attempted to define the very "best form of government," and on another they endeavoured to give a final answer to a question involving complex issues—" Is commerce the result of civilisation or civilisation the result of com- merce?" "Does the perusal of fiction tend te enervate the intellect ?" was one of the matters of debate, and these intrepid "original essayists" did not even shrink from a subject which has for a large number of years exercised the best Debating Society talent, namely, "Was the execution of Charles I. justifiable?"

Warrington is soon to become a shipping port, and perhaps she will again send forth vessels from her own ship-yards. Looking over some records of 1853, I see it stated that there had just been launched from the ship-building yard of the Bank Quay Company, a beautitully-modellad iron steam- boat of 170 tons. She was to be fully rigged as a schooner, and to have a pair of highly-finished oscillating engines put on board by the Vulcan Foundry Company before she left Bank Quay ship- yard.

It is a well-known fact that the right of fishing in the river Mersey near Warrington was at one time a very valuable privilege, and in 1697 we find Mr.Thoinas Patten, of Warrington, writing in the following fashion to Mr. Richard Norris. "I am informed," writes Mr. Patten, "that there is a design to bring a bill into the House of Commons against fish weares that hinder navigation in navi- gable rivers and that take and destroy fish and the fry of fish. You may well know the mischief that is done in the river Mersey at East ham, or at least have frequently heard what vast numbers of sal- mon trout are taken so as to supply all the country and market towns twenty miles round, until the country is cloyed, and when they cannot get sale of them they give them to their swine."
MR. HILLSON AND TTIE " LIVERPOOL
DAILY POST."

_ The "Star" says:—ln 1878 the" Liverpool Daily Post" was not in a very prosperous condition, and the then proprietors even talked of selling it to the licensed victuallers for a mere song. Mr. Hillson organised a syndicate, of whom he himself was one, bought the paper, and now is rewarded by drawing an income of some thousands a year from one of the most prosperous newspaper properties in the world. The one mistake Mr. Hinson made at the time was not to buy the whole concern: for some of lila partners are Unionists,and have made things a little unpleasant now and than—especially for Mr. Russell, the editor, whose most promising Parliamentary career they insisted on putting an end to. Mean- time Mr. Hillson's business as a solicitor has steadily gone on. so that he now looks for- ward to an early retirement from more active work. Though he has been one of the most active and influential of election agents for a quar- ter of a centuty, he has always kept personally in the background, has made no speeches, presided over no meetings, and sought no candidatures. But he has at last yielded, and a few months ago became the candidate for Barnstaple. In two visits he has paid to the constituency, he has succeeded in win- ning all hearts, and is an immense favourite. This is due to charming manners—the manifestation of a truly kind and sincere nature. Mr. Hillson is tall, fair-haired man with features of classic regula- rity and beauty. He is the youngest looking man almost of his time ; for though he is fifty-three years' old and is a grandfather, he could pass for forty. j Finally, Mr. Hillson is a man of great culture. He has a knowledge of the English poets only equalled by that of Mr. Russell, and there are few evenings that can be more pleasant than those spent in listen- ing to his rolling out with unfailing memory whole I volumes of Shelley. Beats, and Browning—his favourite poets.

"Summer Rambles Round Manchestr! is thetitle of a handsome volume issued by Mr. Alfred Rimmer, and published by Mr. John Heywood, of Manches- ter. "Around Manchester" must not be taken to mean in the immediate neighbourhood of Manches- ter, but covers an .area for some twenty or thirty miles distant from Manchester as a centre, and thus includes much that is choicest and beat, both in Lancashire arid Cheshire. The articles have been re-printed, with additions, froth the "Manchester Guardiano! and some .of them have previously appeared in our columns. Mr. Rimmer is an artist of no mean power, as the illustrations abundantly testify. He has a keen eye for the picturesque, and knows how to present what to some would be an Unpromising building in its best aspect. It is of great advantage that he is able to work so well, both with pen and pencil. He is a capital writer, for he is always interesting, and can crowd a num- ber of facts into a small space without giving the impression that what he furnishes is a mere cata- logue. Mr. Rimmer has walked from one end of England to the other. He is familiar with all that is beautiful in every county, and speaks net only with discrimination, but with authority. As a matter of local interest, it may be mentioned that Bank Hall is one of the. sixty or seventy illustra- tions with which the book is adorned, and it is accompanied with an appropriate sketch of the history of what forms at present the Town Hall of Warrington. The book is, of course, rich in views and descriptions of the old halls, and in its way it is not to be surpassed. It is well printed, on good toned paper, and is altogether a work worthy of preservation. The "Manchester Quarterly," published for the Man- chester Literary Club, by Mr. John Heywood, has for frontispiece an admirable portrait of the late Matthew Arnold, followed by a paper by Mr. C. E. Tyrer. Other articles are "On Crusts," by W. Y. Wild; "Features of facts and fancy in the works of George Elliott," by James T. Ford; "Some Lancashire Rhymes," by John Mortimer; "In Memoriam, Henry Lewes, musician," by John Bannister; and "An Autumn Evening," by J. A. Goodacre. "The Prose Writings of Thomas Davis, edited with an introduction by T. W. Rolleston, "is the current issue of the Camelot series, published by Mr. Walter Scott. Davis was a writer of high character, and great ability, who has done not a little to form the opinion of his countrymen and help to shape the events which have culminated in the demand for Home Rule. The subjects treated in this volume are exceedingly numerous, and, as Davis was always earnest, sincere and observant, it is a matter of course to say that the book is one of great value to students of Ireland. The first chapter is an address delivered before the Historical Society of Dublin, and it cannot but be read with' profit by all who are mak- ing a study of language with a view to either speaking or writing. The bulk of the essays are of a literary and historical character, alth•ugh a portion of them are devoted to politics. They are all admirably written. "The life if Honc.re De Balzac "is written by Mr. Frederick Wedmore for the " Great Writers" series issued by the same firm.. Mr. Wedmore has a profound belief in the genius of Balza°, for he ranks him with Goethe, Wordsworth, Dickens and Browning, but it can hardly be said that in this volume hegives the reader that evidence of the quality of Balzac which might have been ekpected. When he speaks of Balzac as a great subject, and says that his biography of him is a small book, it is simply in the sense that it does not place the man Balza° vividly before the reader, although there is plenty of clever criticism as to the works of the great author. Still, the " Life "is likely to be acceptable, issued as it is in a popular, cheap form. "The Life of John Milton," 14y Dr. Richard Garnett, appears in the same series, and is an altogether satiefac- tory production. There have been many lives or Milton, some covering much that only indirectly related to the poet's career, but the one before us may be regarded as hitting the happy mean in that it is neither too diffuse nor too condensed. There is a picture of the stirring times in which Milton moved, and just and sympathetic criticism of his genius. Both the lives eg Milton and Balzac are funished with a full index, and a complete bibliography. "The Magazine of Art " for January is an unusually stmng,number. The frontispiece is a beautiful etching of E. J. Poynter's beautiful picture "A Roman Boat Race." "Loch Torridon," by A. C. Swindon, is a powerful piece of writing, admirably illustrated by McWhirter. The following couplet in the poem is especially fine "And softer than dewfa.ll, kindlier than starlight, keener than wine; Came round us the fragrance of waters, the life and the breath of the brine." Mr. Mortimer Mempes contributes a paper on "The Art of Dry-Point." We have, too, amongst other illus- trated articles " Personal reminiscences of Jules Bastien- Lepage," "The Corporation Gallery of Glasgow," and "Old Blue and White Nankeen China." "The Womans's World" opens with "Edna Lyall at Home," a bright sketch by Frederick Dolman, which is accompanied by a portrait of the novelist, and picture of her study. Along with an article on "Mr. William Morris's Domestic Art," there is a striking portrait of Mr. Morris. A paper on" Women as pianoforte players" is I adorned with several portraits of eminent artistes. There are other articles and illustrations besides the meal article on the latest fashions, which is unusually well illustrated. " Cassell's Magazine" commences the year well, and grows brighter every year, both in text and illustration. There are four serial and complete stories, and no less than a dozen miscellaneous papers, amongst which may be mentioned" Impressions of the White House," by an Anglo-American; "Some early Spring flowers" ; "The story of a dwelling-house " • "The career of Joachim " ; ' The gatherer," an illustrated record of invention, discovery, literature, and science. "The Quiver" can hardly be said to Jag behind the "Family Magazine," for it is equally excellent as an illustrated magazine of Sunday and general reading. Amongst the contents for January we have !--" With the crew of the Shaftesbury, " Music of the early Psalters," "Stumpy, a Christmas story, "The image which fell down from Jupiter," "Scripture lessons for school and home," "A new years parable," &c. The frontispiece of " Little Folks is a charmingly coloured picture of" The pet of the fold," which is well worth framing. The two serial stories are "Master Rockafellar's Voyage," and "Nobody's House." Amongst the other contents are "Noble deeds of noble children," " That sulky boy, Jack Frost," "Our Little Folks' own pages," and "A picture wanting words," &c. Part 4 of the " Cp.binet Portrait Gallery" contains pottmits of Miss Maud Millett, the Duke of Westminster, and Mr. Lewis Morris. They are all splendid specimens of photography, by Messrs. W. and D. Downie, and each is accompanied by appropriaM descriptive letterpress. The "Cabinet Portrait Gallery is likely to be in demand by all who can thoroughly appreciate fine-art photography. We have also to hand from Messrs. Cassell and Co. part 3of the " Dore ' Gallery," and "Paradise Lost," illustrated by Dom, both in their way unique works; part 48 of " illustrated Shakespeare;" " Familiar Wild Flowers," part 47; part 13 of th'e "Story of the Heavens," by Sir R. div.head: THR SPIRITUALISTS.
div.p: THR SPIRITUALISTS.

With the spiritualist I have witnessed manifesta- tions which have simply astonished me, and at which I could net make an attempt at explaining. At one meeting, where not more than two or three people knew me, I was given the name, trade, and vanous other circumstances connected with one of my deceased parents, while here amongst us. To this might be added instances without end, but such as are familiar to those who devote a little attention to these matters. I must confess there is always a ridiculous side to these displays of occult power, more especially if one visits, as I have done several times, the vulgar descendant of the old time astrologer. The fortune teller hangs his, or her sign out unblushingly. To cast your horoscope with egg or tea cup is as common as it could possibly have been in the days of our grandmothers.

div.head: NEW vinsus THE OLD.
div.p: THE NEW vinsus THE OLD.

This city numbers amongst its inhabitants repre- sentatives from all climes, and of all the religious systems, and I must be excused if I point out one feature which has forced itself upon me more than others. While the teachings of all the more modern developments aim at forming and cementing a human brotherhood, and strive in as practical a manner as possible to show what the higner life is, all the old musty traditions as to belief, as to social life, and as to the relationship of tnaster and servant are held as tenaciously as ever by the orthodox Christians. One other feature, which is a 'sad one, is the surprising amount of superstition existing in the minds of the members of the Romith church. We have here Spanish, Italian, and Mexican, and their superstitous condition is simply pitiable. Of the condition of the poor ignorant Irishman we have seen enough, but take all these nationalities to- gether in this city, and the experience of the stay- at-home Englishman goes for nothing. Rusty horse shoes are in. great demand. But we may leave this subject; there is nothing about it good, and I cannot promise that what follows is more worthy' of attention, or can be better understood.

div.head: TIIROSOPHY.
div.p: TIIROSOPHY.

The caption at the head of this letter mere fit- tingly applies to what I am now going to say a few words about, that is Theosophy. My friends must not mistake the. lam not a Theosophist. Ido not understand it. but lam seeking to do so. One can scarcely rush into the fold of a party that tells you it has no specific faith, that it has no religion, no creed, or code of doctrines.. One of my good friends, writing me a few weeks ago referring to a conver- sation he had had respecting the polemical argu- ment held in the columns of the " Examiner " re- cently, said the atheist's position is untenable, inasmuch as it tended to destroy; indeed did des- troy, the strong desire which is in man for the life i hereafter, that s immortality. I Wish to say I grant my friend's argument so far as it touches the great majority of the human race.. I will add, the small minority may be left in their citadel of strong-mindedness. Now, this altogether leaves out the question of Biblical Christianity, and we ask ourselves the question.—Where is to be found a knowledge of the occult world? How shall the invisible be brought into touch with the visible world ? The Theosophist claims that one funda- mental truth is the basis of all the various bibles, alike in the symbolical writings of the Kabala, the Books of Hermes, the Vedas, and other sacred . . . . _

_ books of the Bast, in the Talmud, the Koran, the Christian Bible, as well as in the teachings of Pythagoras, Socrates, and the more recent philoso- phers. In" Wisdom religion" a germ of truth is to be found underlying every form of belief, worthy of the name, existing thousands of years before any of the creeds of Christendorn ' were heard of, lies ready for the searcher after Theosophic truth, an inexhaustible source of knowledge, in every groove of thought, whether on the spiritual or physical plane. In science, in art, in every intellectual pur- suit in whatever direction it may incline, Theo- sophy, as now understood, claims to embrace and pervade its study, And to render wiser and more elevated every human creature. To the student, the first truth he has to realise is re-incarnation, or spirit-evolution. It is notl meant by this trans- migration of human souls into the bodies of ani- mals, or into lower forms of human existence. It is

the sure ascent of every living thing upon this globe, from the mineral and vegetable up to man, and from man up to God, that Las to be kept in mind. We are all agreed that for many years past the tendency of intellectual thought and scientific in- quiry has been towards materialism and agnosticism. Theology has been content to repeat the phrases of those gone before. In its anxiety to retain the hell and everlasting damnation doctrine it has been compelled to retain other scientifically exploded ideas, ignoring altogether the facts as they appeared in every age, that good and true men and women who received not these shibboleths, were logically being consigned to a fate which the inner and better self of the persecuter eould not himself approve of. •

THE THEOSOPHISTS. Theosophy proposes to lead all, whatever their belief or unbelief out of their difficulties. How is it possible, it asks, to reconcile the apparent injustice of one man being born in absolute misery and want, in a position where improvement, or even the desire for improvement, is impossible ; while another, no more deserving, so far as can be seen, is surrounded by friends, luxuries, and everything that can make life desirable? How account for the condition of the crippled, blind, constitutionally unhealthy, and morally wicked, compared with those who possess beauty of form, vigorous health, honesty of purpose, and the use of all their senses, except by the theory that all are by degrees work- ing upwards, not only materially but also morally and spiritually? Why should evolution be accepted up to a certain point and then cast off abruptly? The entities occupying now the bodies of the savage and barbarous race will, in due course, re-incarnate in the bodies of men a little higher in the scale of civilisation, gathering thus, by slow degrees, the experience necessary for a more advanced develop- ment ever improving and progressing. A Theoso- phist is never indifferent to what is passing around, him; with the greatest enthusiasm he aids all pro- gressive measures. While looking with neither sorrow nor contempt on his less successful, or less honest, or less happy brother, he anxiously tries to alleviate the situation, hoping thereby to lift the inner soul to a speedier absorption by the "Absolute Power," "Supreme Unity," "Ultimate Reality," or" Divine Spirit." This absorption or reincarna- tion has dependent upon it Karma, or the law of cause and effect, which operates through the mer- it and demerit of a person's deeds in each life. Every individual is making Karma, cause and effect —either good or bad in each action and thought of his daily round, and is at the same time working out in this life the Karma brought about by the acts and desires of the last. There are here some ' self-evident propositionsovhiah are widely accepted when placed in other words. But heredity may be put forward in argument, and with which I have not space to deal, but it must be understood that the ego, the real man, the individuality, has no spiritual origin in the parentage by which it is re-embodied, but is drawn by theaffinities which its previous mode of life attracted round it, into the current that carries it, when the time comes for re-birth, to the home best fitted for the develop- ment of those tendencies. I must, although unwil- lingly, leave Karma, whose doctrine when well understood, helps to guide and assist to a higher and better mode of hfe. We have all been taught that our actions and our thoughts are most assuredly followed by a crowd of circumstances that influence for good or for evil our own future, and the future of many of our fellow-creatures. Its ethics show that active good is required of its followers as well as abstention from evil. I have had opportunities of noting that most of the active leaders in all the reform movements in this city are either Theosophists or have an intimate acquaintance with its principles. Their conduct is, so far as I see, irreproachable, and a surprising amount of eveness of temper is always apparent. When speaking of the shortcomings of others there is great charity shown. Who can say this that have mixed with the congtegations and joined in the class meetings of any of the numerous Sects? 1 am afraid tc grow weary on this subject, but should there be a desire I might go more into the matter. 810, Bay-st., San Francisco, Jan. ilnd, 1890.

CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
A SECRET FOR YEARS.
CHAPTER XLATHI. IN THE CHURCHYARD.

TIIE church clock struck eight while George Ingestre sat on the tombstone, waiting for Catherine to come out. At the last vibration, the doors opened, and the peal of the organ warned him service was over. He drew back farther into the shadow of the tower, and waited for Catherine to pass by. She came at last; her dress almost touched him; the tall, graceful figure glided by, and he followed it without fear.

She did not return by the same road she came, but went round the east side of the church, into a way less frequented than the High-street. It was a shorter and quieter path than the other, therefore she chose it, little dreaming who was grateful for its solitude beside herself. He strode up to her side, and the cry came straight from his breaking heart— "Oh, Catherine! why have you left me?"

It was too dark to- see her face, but she did not utter any cry of terror or surprise as she heard that mournful wail, and felt his hand on her shoulder, slowly, but surely, bringing her to his heart. "Catherine, Catherine! why have you left me ? " _._
Those mournful and passionate tones were not to be resisted. With a low sigh, she rested her head on his great heaving chest—his beating heart—and only said— " Thank God for this !"

"Catherine, you love me?" "I love you." And they did not speak again until she lifted her head from its rest, and placed his hand upon her shoulder; for he could scarcely stand—he was trem- bling all over. "Ay, that is right, my Catherine; rm very weak, hold me up." "Oh, Mr. Ingestre, forgive me! I have done you a great wrong." "A great wrong, my heart! Tell me what it is. I think lam going mad, but I will try to be sane. A great wrong; what is it?" "Yesterday evening a woman came all the way from London to tell me a lie about you. I believed that shameful lie, and left your house; because, think- ing it true, I could not stay in it, or ever see you again." "Ha! she told you a lie, and you believed it. How then, Catherine, eh?"

"I walked to Lowmoor, and took lodgings for the night with the dairy-woman, meaning to leave by the first train for London; and I was on the plat- form, waiting, when a gentleman came up to me in great haste. He introduced himself, and said he was your first cousin, Ingram Ingestre, and had some- thing important to communicate about your affairs. At first I would not listen; and he then said, ' I know why you leave Redfern like this—l knew it last night; and now I have come to tell you that the person whose tale drove you nom it lied grossly. Mr. Ingestre—George Ingestre—li as no wife living; he was not married to the mother of those two children. If you choose, I can bring a witness to prove it. She was not his wife; and, although against my own iu- terest, I assure you of this. And, to confound the machinations of a devil, I tell you, do not forsake George Ingestre : take pity on him. Then he went and I—ah ! I returned to Lowmoor, certain that you would look for and find me at last."
"Find you at last! Nearer—nearer to me! h hold my hand. Found you at last! Oh, Cathetrel how could you leave me? Cruel, cruel!"
His eye; were hidden on he; shpulder, and his heartbroken sobs shook his frame. Without another word, she led him back into the now deserted grave- yard, and they sat down on the nearest tomb.

It was both cold and damp, and the grass beneath her feet was like a bit of marsh, it was so wet end oozy. But what did that signify? They were to- gether, his arm fast round her, her hand in his; and cold and damp were things unfelt. To him that seat on the tombstone seemed a velvet couch, for there he could press her to his aching heart, and lean his head upon her shoulder. She did not speak again until his strong emotion bad sub- sided—until th)se terrible sobs had ceased, and his great frame no longer shook like a leaf torn by De- cember winds. Then she asked after Cleland. "I have found her, Catherine; she is safe—at least, I know where she is. And now, tell me again, my darling, what Ingram Ingestre said— tell me again; I did not hear correctly." " George, he told me of a great sin you have core- mitted. He told me that the poor dead boy—dear Ross—and his sister were not your legitimate children; and that the mother, who is living now, had said so herself.°

Here Ingestre burs,, into a loud laugh; ended it, began another, and another, until Catherine thought his wits were gone. "Ah ! the hand is clear enough in this, my Catherine !" he laughed. "Se Ingram told you that, and she, the mother, swore it? A pretty one she is! Ha, ha! have you seen her, my own ? have you seen the sweet mother of my children? Only one left now. Thank God, the other is gone! Thank God, I say, with all my heart, the other is gone ! " Here he stood erect, and lifted his hat from his head, as he repeated, solemnly, "Thank God, he never lived for this! But have you seen her—the mother ? " " Yes ; it is the woman you be; e called Mrs. ?Ammo."

alt is. She has a white face, and masses of yellowish hair. That is the woman. She is a drunkard; she tkuk to drinking a year after we—we agreed to live together as man and wife. the bora me tho children, and then I left her. I couldn't :ive with a drunkard, Catherine, who invited the raff of the streets to her bouts in my drawing-rooms. At first I tried doctors, and, finding them useless, a math house ; but the fools turned her adrift, and swore she was sane. Then. in a drunken fit, she stole a man's watch—that was in Ira!and —and was sentenced to seven years across the sea. the returned eight months ago, and you have seen her, Catherine. Very wrong of me to live with such a woman, wasn't it?" he con- tinued, with a curl of the lip; "but I couldn't well help myself, you see, when the thing was once done. But now lam going to have a wife. Catherine. for- give me! forgive me, my heart and make me a better man."
"Oh, Mr. Ingestre ! you have been a bad—a butt man, indeed!"

- "A bid man, indeed," he repeated; "but a better now—now that I hare you. See, my own—think what my lie has been; such a castaway thing, no good influence near. Only the weight of this fearful woman round my neck; the dread of the filthy crea- ture turning up again, and lookirc, my children in the lace, to tell them that she—that loathsome she was their mother. It has made me drink, and made me swear; it has made me careless of God and man. But I am not young n?w, Tlly ill life is half sprmt ; and I crave with all a man's might for something better, something worthier; and that may come to me through you, by your teaching, by your presence, by the kind love in your deep eyes. Catherine, you 'wit/ take me into your heart: you will fold me round in its great love ; you will b one with we, in this world and in the next? Catherine, you will be my wife?"

There was a short, tierce struggle in her heart, it was but natural---a desire to roveege her past suffer- ing on him now, battling with toe passionate love that rose up to meet his own. For one brief moment only; love triumphed; she put her hand on his, and

"I will be all you wish me; I will forget the seventeen years of agony I have suffered by your wrong-doing; I will forget all I have heard since; I will inquire into no other errors of the past. Only let the future be clearer—only be what you wish to be—a wiser and a better man, and I—l will never rePent that you made me your wife at last. For all th-se yells I have kept my love to you, and for very conscience' sake would neither love nor marry any other. Yes, I will be your wife, when and where you please.' "Catherine, I have the license in my pocket now. I brought it down to-day, the ring as well." "See, I have the ring on my ringer now, that you married me with before. I will have that again." She did not see the sizsm that crossed his features as he said—

Let me look—which is the finpr ? Ah, I see; made out of a goldoa moitiore. I won't have it." And he slipped it off her huger, and flung it away among the graves. " We'll have a new ring and a new wedding; and, Catherine, I'll put it on to-morrow morning, peace God, at eight o'clock, in Redfern Chorch. Will you be there P Stay; are you too tired ti, walk home with me to-night ? it is only six miles. We shall be at Redfern by twelve o'clock." No, she would not do that; she would remain at Lowmoor for the night, and be at the church by eight o'clock to meet Mr. lugestre. She would rise early, and walk. He was not satisfied; he could not bear to leave her. 'Six miles apart, and he not knowing what might come to her! lie had so much to say; would she not walk back with him those short six miles'?" No, she would not; and he was forced to be con- tent. They must part, too, at the corner of the road, for she had no wish to be seen with him at night, in a Waco wbere he was so widely known.

zen gouct_-oyt, Ca.cuerwtt,' uatil morrow morning at eight o'clock. If Ido not see you then I shall be mad. Nay, mad is but a faint expression of what I shall be. All! I cannot, cannot leave you." And as he held her hands tightly to his heart, be thought of a face he had seen that night, and a clammy sweat burst out uppn him. "I shall lose you yet," he said; "if we part to-night, something will take you from me." "Impossible. We believe and trust in each other. Nothing can come between us now. What should ?" His only answer was a groan, half checked. "Go, George, go. Goodnight—good-bye." He stooped down, and kissed her with a wild and passionate sorrow. " Yes, go?" he cried, "go ! leave me—tear your- self away, or we shall never part. To-morrow, to- morrow ! Oh, Catherine! forgive me." _
"For what?" "For loving you." .. .

She laughed ti low, silvery, happy laugh. "Forgiven!" "For being a selfish, brutal wretch—for being e daring, reckless man—tempting God's wrath; daring men's punishment." "To-morrow morning, my heart. Good-bye." And she glided from his grasp, and left him there on the gravestone, watching the darkness into which she had merged. Darkness, indeed, for him, when he knew that the dense shade before him no longer contained her—that she was, in truth, gone from him once more. Ile tried to think calmly of the future he should wed with to-morrow—of a future this very night had given a darker, deeper shadow to. "Does not the Evil One work for me ? " he cried out to his accusing conscience. "Fate bids tne— compels me to this act. To-morrow, Catherine —for. better or for worse. Heaven knows which it will be. And now for Redfern!" Half an hour after, he was riding furiously out of Lowmoor, with the same expression on his face a when he sat watching Time in his room the night before—watching the hours as if he hated, feared. and yet longed for what they were hurrying up. But George Ross was a desperate man then, 8134 grinned savagely at th-, horrible thoughts which assailed him—thoughts which must have made a fainter-hearted man quail. Some men are so far de- based as to sin with great relish : they are never more happy than when sacrificing at the altar of their evil deity. George Ingestre was not one of these men. Never, for one instant, did he forget to hate the evil thing he was committing, and himself beyond ali; but—strange inconsistency of humanity !--as little did he mean to turn away from it. "No," he cried; "with Catherine I will wed may fate, no matter what it may be ! If she can be happy and unconscious, what matters the serpent in my breast, gnawing my very heart out? Am I not a cams—a great strong, sinewy man, and can 'ear? /will!" He fiercely spurred his horse, and grinned again a agony.

CHAPTER XLIX. FLIGII r MAXALL and Mrs. Faunce, as she still called herself, remained a long time in that room, drinking raw brandy, by the wretched :ight of a tailew candle. Maasll could not have been guilty of such fray Mobil- t'• gen. e once. He was by natu is a refined mid luxurious debauchee, and, had he hid the means, wouel have pandered to his senses most extravagantly. P,ut late he had fallen considerably iii his social tacaes and requirements. Drink was the cry of is cowardlY nature—his guilty soul ; and therefore he drank furiously--anything, anyhow, and anywhere. • When Cleland crept from the room to her wret(l'ed„, bed, neither of the two were in is state to ob,erve And there she left them, to indulge in her own bitter thoughts, and reflect upon much that had fallen from Maxall's lips concerning her father. Her mind war" soon made up as to the course she should pursue. and, leaving her bed long before dawn, she set about putting her resolve in execution. And this was to leave the house as FAD= i"Sible' and return to Redfern in time to open her father's eyes to what he was about to do, and save him. And , so, in the dark December morning, Cleland left the wretched lodging-house as secretly as she had left fern, with her dog under her arm, her tiny bundle. and her half-emptied purse. kn..er the way to L—, and walked without many wrong-goings to the terminus, just as the e%' press was about to start. She had sufficient inolleir to pay her fare there, but not a penny beyond, en from the station at Ashby she would have to walk silg miles to Redferc, unless she went to Lowmoor first. and begged a lift from there in some wagon or cart going on. At five o'clock Cleland got out of the train at Ashby, sick, weary, and frightened, yet borne up by a strong purpose within. She had fasted all that day, haying nothing to buy food with, and being ax. proud to accept a biscuit offered her by a poorer pal- senger than herself. So she trudged bravely on to Lowmoor, her only companion the dog she carried with her. No fear of the lonely country road terrified her. She WIIA the squire's rl.aughter, and who in all the county woidd as atult her? No one did. Like many a poirer girl berore her. she went along lonely and unmolested. A she'r herd and his flock passed her, on the moor-path-- nothing else, until she entered the town, two hours after. Her feet were sore and blistered; she was faint' from low, fasting, and very sick at heart. The dog. too, whined miserably, unless she carried him; its weight increased her fatigue. Still, her brave heart did not fail her. She would not stop in Leo' moor, and ask for food and rest (which, as Mlse Ingestre, would have been most willingly bestowed on her by almost any), for moments were precious. and the eager, longing desire to see her father and Redfern once more was the only craving she had. A Her tall, thin figure, clad in deep mourning, her veiled face, attracted no notice as she Pess'a_ through the gaily-lighted town, and up the long street, down down which her father had ridden only an hour before. Past the church, beneath the shadow of which he was watching—past the long row of !anti° —past houses and people, out into the lonely cour',tri road again, went Cleland. only bent on hurrying ' poor limbs at their utmost speed. Ah! could she but have known what she svai hastening from—could she but have seen when 1001" ing back at the lighted windows of the 'church. /cll° was in their shadow! The girl, with her dog still under her arm, took fresh heart when Lowmoor lights had disaPPeared beliind the hill. "Five miles only," she thought; "and something is sure to pass me before long on the way. The millers will be coming back from market, for to-dal Is Tuesday." Sure enough, ten minutes after, the sound of wheelo came grating up behind her, and, turning round, slit saw two lamps in the distance. The vehicle came up, and she saw at once it vras tax-cart, with three men in it. The driver halted on perceiving her at the roadside waiting— " Hillo ! who be you, missus ? Want a lift ? " Cleland's heart bounded. She recognised the voice of the old cowkeeper at the home farm; and there was the sheep-dog. too, wagging his tail and leaping round about her. She merely answered in tile affirmative, and climbed up immediately. One of the two men who sat in the hack of the cart very civilly made room for her in front, and put, out his hand to assist her in. It was a coarse, common hand, but there was something white on the coat cuff, like silver lace. Was he a soldier? Cle wondered; and then, in moving back, the light of the lamp flashed ori another bright thing about him, hut what, she could net make out. She did not puzzle long, for the cart went ofl. and the motion soon sent her into a state .of dreamy langour, in which she could th-ink of nothing. A sharp shock awoke her fully to a sense of where she was. One of the men in the back of the cart hod leaned forward, and pulled the reins out of the old driver's hand—who, to tell the truth, was fast asleep —and jerked the horse up in a precipitate hilt, 0 listen the better for a sound faintly heard in the distance. "A horse!" said one of the men. " Ay• be is coming. Draw the cart across the road." And Cle and the old cowkeeper sat WonderinlV?, at it, all meant Meanwhile, the horseman came on a furious speed. (To be Continit,:d.)

THE OLD HORSE. We had an old, old man, Pimen Timofeitch. He was ninety years of age. He lived at his grandson's house, but did no work. His back was bent double p he walked with a stick, and found it hard to drag one leg after the other. All of Ins teeth were gone; his face was wrinkled; his lower lip trembled. When he walked and when he talked, he had no control over his lips, so that it was impossible to make out what he was saying. There were four brothers of us, and we all liked to ride horseback; but we had no gentle horses fit for us to ride. We were permitted to ride only on ' one old horse whose name was Voronek. One time our little mother gave us permission to have a ride,and we all ran with our dyadka * to the stables. The coachman saddled Voromtk for us, and the first to ride was our eldest brother. He took a long ride; he rode over to the thresh- ing-floor and around the garden, and when he came back, we shouted " Now start him up I" Our eldest brother began to kick Voron6k, and to strike him with his whip, and Vorondk galloped past us. After our eldest brother had ridden, the next oldest took his turn. He also had a long ride, and whipped Voronok till he galloped at break-neck speed. He wanted to ride even longer, but the third brother begged him to give him a chance as soon as possible. The third brother rode over to the threshing-floor and around the garden, and then along through the village, and then he came galloping clown the hill towards the stables. When he rode up to us, Voronek was winded, and ' his neck and flanks were black with sweat. When my turn came, I wanted to surprise my brothers, and show them how well I could ride, and I began to spur him on to his utmost speed; but Voronok would not stir from the stable. In spite of my redoubled blows he would not gallop, but only shied and backed. I grew angry with the horse, and pounded him with all my might with my whip and legs. I tried lashing him in the places where he was tenderest ; I broke the whip, and with the broken handle I began to pound him on the head. But still Voionok would not budge. Then. I turned round. rode up to our dyadka, and asked him for a heavier whip. Bet the dyadka said to me: "You have ridden him enough, sir; come down. Why torture the horse ?" I was vexed, and said:— " Why ? I have not ridden him at all I Look how I will make him gallop! Please give me a stronger whip! I will -warm him up !" . . Then the dyadka shook his bead, and said : "•Ah, sir! you have no mercy. Why warm him up? Just think! He is twenty years old. The horse is tired put; he is all winded ; yes, and he is so old ! Just think how old he is! The same as though it were Pimen Timofeitch. If you should mount on Timofeitch, and should whip him with all your might, say, now, would not that be a pity ?" I knew well about Pimen, and I obeyed the dyadka. I dismounted from the horse, and when I saw how he was laboring with his sweaty sides, and was puffing with his nostrils, and was switching his thin tail, then I realised how cruel we had been to the horse. But till that time I had supposed that the horse enjoyed it as much as I did. , became so sorry for Voronok that I began to caress his sweaty neck, and to ask -his forgiveness for the beating that I had given hit°. Since that time I have grown older, and I still always pity horses. and I always 'remember Voronek and Pimeu Tiea6feitch when I see any one abusing a horse. HOW WAS TAUGHT TO HIDE HORSEBACK. When I was a little boy, we four brothers had our, lessons every day except Sundays and holidays, when we were free and could play together. One time our father said : " You older children must learn to ride horseback; you Must be sent to riding-school." • I was the yotingest, and I asked : " Can't I learn too ?" . My father said: " You would tumble off." I began to tease him to let me learn too, and, I almost cried. My father said: "Very well, then, you shall take lessons too. Only see here: don't you cry if you fall. One who never falls from a horse will never learn to ride:* When Wednesday came, three ot, us were taken to the riding-school. We went up a great staircase, and from the great staircase we went up a narrow staircase. And the narrow staircase opened into a very large room. In this room there was sand in- stead of a floor; and gentlemen and ladies, as well as lads like ourselves, were riding on horseback. This was the riding-school. It was rather dark, and there was an odor of horses, and we could hear people cracking whips, and shouting to horses, and the trampling of horses' hoofs against the wooden partitions. At first I was afraid and did not dare to look around. But after- wards our dyadka called the riding-master, and said: "See here! give these lads some horses; they want to learn to ride." "Very well," replied the riding-master. Then he looked at me, and said, "This one is very small." But our dyadka said, "He has promised not to cry if he falls." The riding-master laughed and went away. 'Then three saddled horses were brought: we took off our cloaks and descended the staircase into the riding-room. The riding-master held the horse by the thong, and my brothers rode around him, At first they walked; then they trotted. At last a little pony was brought out. He was a chestnut, and his tail had been cropped. His name was Chervoncnik. The riding-master laughed, and said to me,' Well, cavalier, mount I" I was both glad and sad, but I tried to hide it so that no one would notice it. I made eeveral at- tempts to set my foot into the stirrup, but it was in vain, for I was too' small. Then the riding-master lifted me in his arms and set me on, saying, "The birin is not heavy he can't weigh more than a couple of pounds. At first he held me by the arm; but When I saw that they did'not hold my brothers, I asked him to let go of me. He asked me, "Aren't you afraid, then ?" I was very much afraid, but I said that I was not. I was all the more afraid because Chervonchik kept pricking back his ears, and I mad up my mind that he was angry with me. The riding-master said, "Well, only mind that you don't fall off !" And he let go of me. At first Chervonchil‘ walked around, and I sat up straight. But the saddle was slippery,' and I was afraid that I should slide off. "Well, now," asked my riding-master, "are you on firm?" , " Yes " said I. "Well, then, now trot !" and the riding-master clucked with his tongue. Chervonchik started off , in a gentle trot, and I began to slip. But still I said nothing, and tried not to tip over sidewise. The riding-master praised me, "At da, cavalier! Splen- did l" and this made me very glad. At this moment my riding-master was joined by one of his associates, and began to talk with him, and his attention was distracted from me. Then suddenly I became conscious that I was slip- ping a little toward one side of the saddle. I tried to regain my seat, but all in vain, I wanted to cry to the riding-master to stop the horse, but I felt that it would be shameful to do that, and I kept quiet. The riding-master was not looking at me. Cher- vonchik kept on the trot all the time, and I kept • slipping and slipping to one side. 1 looked at the riding-master and thought that be would h&lp me; but he was busily talking with his associates, and without looking at me, said some- thing about his "brave young cavalier !" By tins time I was far over on one side and very much frightened. I felt certain that I was going to tumble. But still I was ashamed to cry out. Chervonchik gave me one more little shake, and down I went to the ground. Then. Chervonchik stopped of his own accord! the riding-master looked around and saw that I was no longer on Cherven- chik's back. Saying,," Hullo there! my cavalier has fallen off !" lie hastened to me. When I told him that I was not hurt, lie laughed. and said . - "A child's body is like a cushion!" But I felt like crying. I asked him to seat me again, and he did so. Aria this tieiti, I did not fall again, In Om way.we went to the riding-iphool twice a week, and I soon learned to ride well, and was afraid of nothing. • * pedagogue. . a

An extraordinary state of affairs has arisen in c connection with St. Barnabas' School, Lovely-lane, Warrington, the result of which has been that • several scenes of a distinctly unpleasant character have taken place at the school, and in its immediate vicinity. The trouble that seems now to have come to a head has been accummulating for some time, and as there is now a good deal of talk about " further proceedings" being initiated, it is probable that the last of the affair has not yet been heard. The facts of the case seem to be, to go back to the commencement, that in December of 1888, Mr. A. Brown, who was then head master at the school, appealed to the National Union of School Teachers of which he is a member. in reference to a notiee "O quit" that he had received, the notice terminat- ing the engagement' at Christmas. At that time the school management consisted of the Vicar (the Rev. G. Allton) and Messrs. G. Allton, Holmes, Parr and Pim:point. At Christmas air.l Brown received a fresh notice, to terminate his ea_ gagement on March 25th, which was a legal one. Consequently, he vacated the position on the date named, and ultimately Mr. K. Y. Woollacott was Appointed as head master. Gradually changes took Place in the management, and various meetings re- garding the work of the school were held, but the Vicar declined to attend. Instructions were issued to the teachers, who declined to act upon them Unless they were approved by the Vicar, and on the 18th of last December they recdved notice to ter- minate their engagements in a month from that .FMe. WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
PRESENTATION TO THE MA.NAGER.

On Monday evening, Mr. A. H. Rathbone, the managing secretary of the Warrington Co-operative Society, was made the recipient of a handsome testimonial Of.the appreciation in which his services are held by the members of the Society, and of their confidence in him. At a previous quarterly meet- ing the members of the Society unanimously decided that a sum of £5O should be spent in the purchase of articles which could be presented to Mr.. Rathbone as a suitable acknowledgment of his 25 years' services to the Society. On Monday evening these articles were on view in the Hall. They consisted of an exceedingly elegant inlaid rosewood cabinet, made by Messrs. Garnett and Sons, of Warrington, a timepiece and bronze ornaments, a barometer.. And silver tea set. Mr. T. Birchall, the president of the Society, presided over the gathering, and amongst others present besides the, officers 'of the Society, were Councillor F. Monks, J.P., Mr. W. Owen, J.P., Cduncillor J. Shaw Green (auditor of the Society), and Mr. F. A. Monks. The cabinet and some of the other articles bore the following inscription :—" To be presented to Nil% A. H. Rathbone, by the mem- bers of the Warrington Equitable Industrial Co- operative Society, in commemoration of 25 years' loyal service as its manager and secretary, ,and also as an expression of their unabated confidence and earnest hope that he may long be spared to continue the services he has id the past to faithfully ren- dered." The CHAIRMAN, in making the presentation, said they were met to pay a tribute of respect and esteem to a ' man whose worth they had lohg known; who was to many of them a personal friend, and to the society an invaluable servant. (Applause.) For 25 years Mr. Rath- bone had served that Society in the most loyal and , honourable manner, and the manifest results of those 25 years loyal and faithful service were a far greater tribute to the worth of Mr. Rathbone than any utterance that , could be given that night. He remembered that many I years ago, when visiting St. Pains Cathedral, built by the great architect, Sir Christopher Wren, on look- I ing round he saw an inscription telling them, 1 if they wanted to find the monument of Sir' Christopher Wren, to " look around." , The fact was that there was no monument to Sir Christopher Wren, but the cathedral itself. So he would say with regard to their manager, that if they wanted to see the value of his services, "Look around. (Applause.) He had known Mr. Rathbone personally for more than 40 years, and he could assure them that during the whole Of that time his feeling of respect and esteem for him had increased. Thirty years ago, as some of them knew, Mr. Rathbone was one of a numher of gentlemen —they were working-men but they were gentlemen as well—(hear, hear)—who met together and founded that society. Some of them "Fvere there that night besides Mr. Rathbone and Mr. Monks. Their names were F. Monks R. Cook, T. Hall, A. 11. Rathbone, W. Jones, W. Hurst, J. McClew, J. Worrell, T. Birchall, Lingard, M. Knowles, Richard Cook, and John Hill. For several years the society had a chequered existence under diffe- rent managers, but at last the committee turned to a I quiet, unassomieg young member of their own body ,—a young working-man—and asked him to try his , hand. He seemed to be diffident of his powers, I for he never did seem to kaow the value of his own qualities, but eventually he was induced to try what he could do as manager. At the time this was done at a personal sacrifice as he could earn more money at his own trade than he was paid by the Society. Mr. Rathbone threw himself into the work heartily and very soon the Society began to move upwards, and from that day to this it had never receded once. It had gone on in a continual advancing state of prosperity, and to-day they were proud to think it was second in honest sound- ness,to no other Society in the kingdom. (Applause.) Mr. Rathbone's reputation as a business man stood very high, and they would agree with him when he said he was trusted by all their members. (Hear, hear.) It was important that such a man should be in the position of manager of a Society like that. He believed he might say without contradiction that the members of the Society formed the largest constituency in Warrington; it had a larger voting power than even the biggest of their wards. Their membership roll now contained nearly 3,000 names, and that really represented more than one-fourth of the population of the town. Their 'payments that quarter were at the rate of over £12,000 per annum. Think of the value of that to working-men's families. It really meant an addition to the incomes of their members of one month's purchase of provisions in the year. (The Society's prosperity so far had been very great, and they had no reason to doubt that its prosperity would be equally great in the -future. In making that presentation to Mr. Rathbone on behalf of the members, he would re-echo earnestly the latter part of the inscrip- tion, that their manager might long be spared to give the same loyal and faithful service to that society he had always done, and so continue the bond of affection which had existed between them ever since they kaew him. (Loud applause.) Mr. RATHRONR, on rising to acknowledge the gift, met with a very gratifying reception. He had, he said, always dein: the best he could for the Society. Twenty- five years ago it was difficult for him to undertake the duties of the position he held, but there was an individ- ual who was on that platform who gave him such en- couragement that he could not very well refuse. That person promised that both advise and assistance should always be given if required, and he could tell them that that advice and assistance had been given at such times as to give him confidence in remaining in their services. He had also always been fortunate in having a president and committee, who, he felt, trusted him. He had always submitted with confidence whatever schemes he had had to bring before the Committee, and they had always given him that power which a Com- mittee only could give. (Hear, 'hear). As the president had remarked, when he undertook' the duties, it was a sacrifice not only in a pecuniary sense, but also as in- volving difficulties and trials which few besides himself and family knew of. It was only as a duty that he un- dertook the work, and because the Committee gave him the full power of conducting the society. The results now spoke for themselves. (Applause.) He could tell them that it was a proud thought for him that the society had come to the condition it had under his con- trol, and he should just like to show the progress it had made by a few items. In 1861, the sales of the society amounted to £5,000, the capital to £6BB, and the divi- dend to £250. The dividend in those days was some- thing like Is. ed. in the £. The first year in which he undertook the office of manager was 1864, when their sales had gone down to £2,622, £3OO less than in the first year. Their capital was £509, and the dividend £157. In 1887, the sales had begun to increase and at the end of that year they amounted to £4,872, the capital to £1,058, and the dividends to £249. In 1872, the sales were £16,866, capital £3,353, and dividend £1,713; in 1877, sales £25,033, capital £7,708, dividend £2,602; in 1882, sales £61,000, capital £ll,OOO, and the dividends about the same as in 1877 ; in 1837, sales £40,450, capital £19,911, dividends £5,944 ; and in 1889 their sales had increased to £Bl,OOO. their capital to £30,000, and their dividends to £lO,OOO. (Applause.) He thought that showed very satisfactory progress in connection with the society, and they could easily understand that it was a great satis- faction to him to be able to report such progress. (Applause.) He should treasure the present they had given him as long as he lived, and he believed his family would do the same. He hoped the manner in which that presentation:had been made to him wnuld be an incentive to all in that .room to attend to duties in the belief that faithful services would not pass unappreciated. (Loud applause.) Councillor MoNes, who was received with applause,. having referred to his long friendship with Mr. Rath- bone, said that Mr. Rathbone had exercised an infinite amount of patience and tact in the management of that I society, as'indeed was always the case where they had successful management. In additicn to that, Mr. Rath- bone had brought to bear a cool head and a sound judg- ment. Good buying and good selling told better in the balance sheet than any amount of screwing inside the works, and he was in a position to know that Mr. Rath- bone had made many good purchases on behalf of the society. He had brought to bear a cool head, and it needed coolness in times of excitement and " spurt " to thoroughly examine their position and to know when the time had come to buy. Mr. Rathbone had also brought them another valuable quality, which money could not purchase, and that was a sterling uprightness of character. (Applause.) If any man was to tell him that Mr. Rathbone had been guilty of any little pecad- thloe,or had received bribes—and they knew how much of that was done in these days—or that he had received commission, he should say at once, from a knowledge of hi character extending over a long time, that the thing was impossible. No man he had ever met in the whole course Of his life was more upright, strict, and conscien- tious in the discharge of his duties than was Mr. Rath- bone. (Hear, hear.) Those were qualitie3Mr. Rathbone

div.head: 'EXAMINfER, SXFURDAY, -JANUARY 25, 1890.
div.p: THE 'EXAMINfER, SXFURDAY, -JANUARY 25, 1890.

had displayed long before he was appointed their mana- ger, and they gave him (Mr. Monks) great confidence in urging the Committee to make him managing secretary of the society. , The consciousness of doing his duty had always been to Mr. Itathbone a reWard and a satisfac- tion beyond anything they could give him. If ever the management of thatsocieiy broke away from that course of uprightness and conscientious discharge of duty in every act, from that day it would begin to sow the seeds of its own destruction, and he, therefore, hoped that the presentation would be an encouragement to every young man who might be aspiring to a similar position, to feel as Mr. Rathbone and others felt, that 25 years' faithful service would bring with it that 'recognition which was worth more than anything money could give. (Applause.) He trusted that presentation would stimu, late some young man who should step forward at some future time to take charge of the Society to carry it on with the same tact and patience, with the same sound judgnient in purchasing, and with the same strict , ititegrity in studying their interests as Mr. Rathbone had displayed, and if that was the case their continuous { success was assured. (Hear, hear.) He looked forward , to a time when it Would be possible to have the same integrity, the same judgment, and the same patience ' brought to bear in the manufacturing industry of this , country, as ce-operators had shown as distributors, and then success would attend manufacturing co-operation as it had attended their stores. Then they would see that strikes would be done away with, and there would be such a community of interests that every man would feel he was earning the results of his own labour. (Applause.) That was the ideal which originally lay at the formation of that Society, and he hoped ' its members would never lose sight of that ideal. Let them hope that the idea of co-operation of which that Society stood as the embodiment in Warrington would so grow that labour would rise to its proper dignity, and that men would be able to live in com- fort, in peace, and in quietness. (Applause.) The realisation of that ideal depended largely upon the men they selected for their managers, and he was glad to find that his earliest friend had been their successful manager, and that he was the recipient of their acknowledgment that night. He did" hope that many years would• be I spared to Mr. Rathbone to control the affairs of Society, and that bit by bit they should see developed that which should be satisfactory both from the material, moral and spiritual point of view. (Loud applause.) Mr. W. OWEN referred in complimentary terms to the; great business qualifications displayed by Mr. Rathbone, and to his great care for the interests of the Society. "The CHAIRMAN in moving a vote ef thanks to Mr. Monks, Mr. Owen, and also to Mr. Shaw Green, men- tioned that the presents Made to Mr. Rathbone had exceeded the £5O voted by the Society, by about £lO, but this extra cost Mr. Rathbone would pay from his own pocket. A member of the Society, however, proposed that the extra £lO should be contributed by the Society and this was agreed to unanimously. Councillor Slimy Oasek, in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman, alluded to the manner in which numerous members of the Society came to Mr. Rathbone for advice and guidance under all sort of difficulties and troubles. On the motion of Mr. ALEINSON hearty applause ap- plause was also given for Mrs. Ra:thbose, and the pro- ceedings then terminated.
It may also be mentioned that Mr. Rathbone has been presented with a very handsome gold watch and chain, of the value of about £35, by Councillor F. Monks.
3,000 DEATHS FROM CHOLERA.

The " Neologus" of Constantinople publishes disquiet- ing intelligence about the spread of cholera in Melopo- tamia. It states that there have been 3,000 fatal cases at Bussorah, the British Consul, Mr. Patrick Robertson, and his two children being among the victims.

div.head: THREE CASES OF CHILD MURDER.
div.p: THREE CASES OF CHILD MURDER.

The coroner's inquest on the body of a child found in a shed at Birkdale under circumstances pointing to death from starvation and exposure was concluded en Saturday. The jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder" against the mother, Hannah Woods, who was committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes. On Tuesday morning a married woman named Eleanor Sarah Jacobs, aged 24, packer' residing at 20, Payne-st., Deptford. murdered Emily Louisa Jacobs, aged four years, her illegitimate child, by striking her on the head with a bar of iron. Sarah Jacobs was subsequently charged at Greenwich Police Court with murder. She said the child asked her for a piece of bread, and that then she brought it downstairs and killed it. She was remanded. The inquest was resumed on Monday, at Guy's Hospi- tal, London, respecting; the death of William Bevan aged four months, lately living with his mother in Rocling- ham-st., New Kent-road. It was alleged that the mother first poisoned her child with laudanum and afterwards took a dose herself. The child died ten minutes after its admission to the hospital, but the mother, who had a powerful emetic administered to her, is now considered out of danger. Evidence was given showing that the woman's husband had been in prison for two years and upon his release he found his wife had been unfaithful to him, and had had the child in question. After a brief consultation, the jury returned a verdict of wilful against the woman.

div.head: GLASS BOTTLE TRADE SYNDICATE.
div.p: THE GLASS BOTTLE TRADE SYNDICATE.

The announcements in reference to the formation of a "ring" in the glass bottle trade have excited attention among all classes interested in that branch of industry. It is stated that manufacturers, representing in numbers and productive capacity of their works, a large majority of the entire glass bottle trade of the United Kingdom, are about to amalgamate for the purpose of being formed into a limited company. The provisional directors will not rely for its financial success on the power the amalgamation will necessarily place in their hands for increasing prices, but rather on the economies they suppose they will be able to effect in the saving of carriage and freight by supplying customers from the nearest available works, the buying of raw Imaterials, in new and improved methods of menu- I facture, and in the increased efficiency which will result at each of the works from the united practical management. It is also stated that an important feature will be the .application of machinery to the manufacture of bottles. The share capital will be .£1,400,000, divided into 100,000 ordinary shares,. of £lO each. The announced names of the principal directors are—Elias Lyon, of the firm of Lyon Bros., St. Helens, Lancashire ; William Bagley, Knottingley, Yorkshire; W. Breffit, Castleford ; J. J. Candlish, Durham; Barron Kilner, Wakefield; Dan Rylands, Barnsley; Thomas Turner, Dewsbury; and Thomas Wood, Portobello. Of the four glass bottle works in Lancashire, namely, Messrs. Lyon Bros., Limited, St. Helens; Messrs. Cannington, Shaw, and Co., St. lielens ; Messrs. Nuttall, St. Helens; and Messrs. Borron, of Newton- le-Willows, only two. Messrs. Lyon Bros., and Messrs. Borron, have joined the combination up to the present.
WARRINGTON LEAGUE OF THE CROSS.

There was a very pleasant gathering at St. Mary's School, Buttermarket-st., on Monday evening,when the new set of instruments lately purchased from Messrs. Silvani and Smith of London,were presented to the band members by the Chaplain. The attend- ance was large, and a miscellaneous musical pro- gramme that had been arranged was very ably carried out. Mr. Thomas Mather who acted as accom- panist to the vocalist.comrnenced the programme by playing an overture, which was very well received, and Miss Cavanagh, Mr. R. Eccles, Mr. J. Bate, and Mr. G. W. Taylor contributed songs in a manner that gave the most coMplete satisfaction. Mr. Durham, of Manchester, gave solos on the cornet which were much enjoyed and well rewarded with applause. During an interval in the programme, Father Flannigan, pre- paratory to presenting the new instruments to the members of the band, gaye.a short address. It was, he said, pretty certain that they all present were not total abstainers but they could certainly all admire the League of Cross. The League was established, not for reformed drunkards' not to win over drunkards, but to lift up their fellow townsmen, and cause them to realise what was the meaning of human nature; cause them to realise that they have a dignity to keep up as creatures of the great Creator. It was established that men might stand with their heads and eyes upwards and not be grovelling in the earth ; that they might keep before the eyes of the people their great aim and destiny in life, which was thatall through their days they should give glory to God and a helping hand to their fellows around: They ware gathered together that night to show their appreciation of the League of the Cross, which had now been established for nearly twenty years in Warrington, and had worked with no little success. He and the friends at St. Mary's wished to express their admiration•of the late president, Mr. David Houghton, the late president, Mr. John Mullings, and the Band C,ommi.tee,who had done such a great work. Alt honour to Mr. Houghton and his coadjutors who in about 18 months, had got together a sum of nearl/t2OO. After referring at some length to the work of John Howard, the prison reformer, Father Flannigan distributed the instruments to the bandsmen, wise demonstrated the capabilities of their new possessions by playing several selections.

div.head: MINERS' CONFERENCE.
div.p: MINERS' CONFERENCE.

A Conference attended by delegates representing over 100,000 colliers was held at Birmingham on Wednesday under the auspices of the National Federation of Miners. Mr. B. Pickard, M.P.,who presided, delivered an Ivldress,in which after urging the men to support the Federation' he advocated efforts being made to secure by Acts of Parliament an eight hours working day. He al4o held that in spite of the advances of wages given the coalowners were getting an advantage as compared with the men from the present prices received for coal. A resolution was carried adopting, with slight modification, the bill introduced by Mr. Cunninghame Graham in 1889, as embodying the views of the Conference on the eight hours question. The Conference sat again, on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. B. Pickard, M.P. The Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Unions Congress was warmly criticised for not having prepared an Eight Hours Bill for miners in accordance with a resolution of the Dundee Congress. It was resolved to ask the Prime Minister and the Home Secretary to receive a deputation on the eight hours question. With regard to mining royalties, the President urged that they should do their utmost to place the best possible information before the Royal Commission. The matter was referred to the Executive to take action. On the subject of the proposed new Employer's Liability Bill, a resolution was passed that no Act would be satisfactory which was permissive or which contained an insurance clause. Various suggested alterations Of the Mines Regulation Act were considered, and the Conference adjourned until next morning.
LORD HERSCHELL ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS.

• Lord Hesschell, speaking on Tuesday night at a Liberal meeting at Bedford, said that nothing was mcre remarkable than the growing education of the Conserva- tive party. An example of what he meant was to be found in the Allotments Act. In that measure the Conservatives carried oat legislation which was a declar- ation and embodiment of principles which four years ago they, regarded as revolutionary and unsound. They were also talking of assisted education, and he would not be surprised if soon they were ready, not to disestablish the Church, but to emancipate it from its endowments. Turning to Ireland, he said the questions affecting that country must be the first for consideration when the Liberals returned to power. As to the question which was often asked, "What is your scheme of Home Rule ?" he would say it was essential that the Irish should have the Dower to legislate on exclusively Irish affairs, and that they should have an Executive in touch with the people.

div.head: GALES: SAD LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: THE GALES: SAD LOSS OF LIFE.

Sunday night's gale was severe in the North of Ireland. I A man named Allen was killed by the blowing down of a wall in Belfast. Shipping has suffered in the English Channel. The steamer Greece, of the National Line, which was overdue, passed Dover for London on Monday morning with a heavy list to starboard. The gale did much damage on the Clare coast, and at Cloned, near Tullamore, on Sunday, four cows were killed by lightning. I Frank Ilanlcin, ship's watchman, was on Sunday night 1 blown into the James Watt Dock at Greenock by the force of the gale and drowned. The severe gale of Tuesday night appears to have caused considerable damage on the South coast, and in the West. The sea wall at Devonshire-terrace, Sand- gate, was undermined, as were the shipways of the marine parade and some buildings. In North Wales all the mountain ranges are enveloped in snow, and the storm still raged on Wednesday morning. • Three men were drowned on Tuesday night while attempting to land in Carmarthen Bay from the French barquentine Conffance, which had anchored in a dan- gerous position seeking refuge from the gale. The Ramsgate smack Otter lost a becond hand over- board during a heavy squall on Wednesday morning. The Anglo-American Oil Company's steamer Man- hattan, which left London for New York on January Mk, has put back to Queenstown, damaged by the gale.
TERRIFIC WEATHER IN..THE _NORTH ATLANTIC.

..... . The Cunard steamship Gallia arrived at Queenstown, from New York, on Monday night, much battered, and showing signs of having encountered fearful weather during the passage. The captain stated that the weather was the worst he had ever experienced in the North Atlantic. Last Friday night the vessel shipped some tremendous seas, and all the rails on the port side, from the stern to the bridge, as well as portions on the star- board side, were washed away. Five lifeboats were smashed on the davits, the iron bars of which were bent and twisted and in some cases snapped. Water entered the staterooms whilst the first-class passengers were asleep, creating considerable alarm. A large steamer was sighted with only one of her masts standing ; she ap- peared to be entirely at the mercy of the tremendous seas which broke upon her. The Gallia could render no assistance. It appears that the Cunard vessel was safely brought into harbour by the cool seamanship of the cap- tain and crew.

div.head: CONTINUED STORM.
div.p: CONTINUED STORM.

Further information concerning the effects of the recent gale in the North Atlantic is gradually coming to hand, but probably some days will pass before the full story of disaster wrought by the storm can be told. A large number of steamers sailing between British and American ports are much overdue, and all the vessels arriving report having experienced terrible weather. Nothing had on Thursday evening been heard of the missing National liner Erin. On several parts of the coast of the British Isles the wind again freshened to a gale on Thursday, in some cases with an accompaniment of snow. From South Wales severe thunderstorms are reported, while floods have in many places resulted from excessive rain on Wednesday night and Thursday morn- ing. On the Anglesey coast a fatal boat accident is said to have occurred. With a strong sea running, five men attempted to land from a vessel off Moelfre; but their boat capsized and two of them were drowned. STATE OF IRELAND.

div.p: THE TENANTS' ASSOCIATION.
