DEATH OF A CENTENARIAN.

The death is reported from Laragh, county Wicklow, of a woman named Porter, at the age of 103. She leaves two sons, the eldest of whom is enly eighteen years younger than his mother,who married at seventeen years of age. ILLNESS OF A CATHOLIC BISHOP.

_ The Rev. Dr. Leahy, Roman Catholic &shoo of Dro- more, is lying dangerously ill at his residence, Newry. On Saturday evening he was reported dead, but this was incorrect, and on Sunday evening his lordship, who is in his eighty-seventh year,was reported a little better.

POISONED BY LIGHTING A PIPE. Timothy Hassatt, ?mployed at a dyeworks in Cork, has just died suddenly from poisoning. It appears he lit his pipe at the works with a piece of paper saturated with a chemical, and soon after he complained of sore- ness of the mouth. His chin became black and in- flamed, and symptoms of poisoning spread over his body, resulting in speedy death. THE ARMAGH RAILWAY DISASTER.

At Armagh Quarter Sessions, on Saturday, before Judge Kisbey, the court was engaged hearing remitted actions arising out of the Armagh railway disaster. In one case, where a servant girl claimed £2OO, the jury found a verdict for £7O, which the judgesaid was about seven times too much; and in another case a schoolboy claimed £l,OOO, and was awarded £5O. The solicitor for the railway company stated that fresh claims were still coming in. SENTENCE ON A TOWN COUNCILLOR.

The correspondent"Cralw—a—;.—. of " states :—Mr O'Sullivan, town councillor, was sentenced, on Monday, to six months' imprisonment and to give securities thereafter for good behaviour, or undergo three months further imprisonment, for breaking through the police ranks and endeavouring to communicate with the Woodford prisoners on their arrival at Galway. MURDER OF A SISTER.

At Maeroon, on- Wednesday, William Kelly. a carpenter, unmarried, aged about forty-five, was committed for trial at the Cork Spring Assizes, on thecharge of murder- ing his sister, who lived with him. on December 26th On the morning of the 27th the woman was found on the floor of the house with wounds on the head. Pri- soner's explanation was that he found her in the yard, on the previous night, in that condition, and took her into the house ,where he left her. Medical evidence went to show that death resulted from one of the wounds in the head, which a fall would not, have caused unless from a great height. ALLEGED SLANDER ON D.R. TANNER. • -
Dr. Tanner, M.P., has cominenced an action for slander against Mr. Robert Pratt, J.P., for language used by the latter towards him at a meeting of the Cork Board of Guardians.

div.head: NEWS FROM THE DARK CONTINENT. [WITH SKETCH MAP.] STANLEY'S RECENT EXPLORATIONS.
div.p: NEWS FROM THE DARK CONTINENT. [WITH SKETCH MAP.] STANLEY'S RECENT EXPLORATIONS.

It is sought by the annexed sketch map to give readers some idea of the position of those areas in Africa which have been brought prominently before us during the past year, and particularly during the last few months. Two subjects of present Interest occur to us at least. The one is the re-appearance of Stanley after another long sojourn in the heirt of the continent, during which we have repeatedly beard of his death. and have been assured of the failure of Ms expedition and the destruction of all concerned therein.

This journey of Stanley has been a journey princi- pally through the lands which appear to be included in the territory of the Congo Free State. Stanley entered Africa upon this expedition from the mouth of the River Congo, and by proceeding up that river and along its tributaries he covered the greater part of the dis- tance he had to travel before reaching the opposite pout, at Zanzibar. It is easy to sympathise with some partiality of Stanley for this route. He was the first ex- plorer of the Congo. Before he tracked its course from beginning to end none of us knew anything about it be- yond a few miles from its mouth. And besides being the discoverer of the Congo, Stanley is the founder of the Congo State. As you see, it is a great irregular square of territory right in the middle of Africa. It is marked out to include the whole length of the Congo and of all the streams which run into it. And this Congo State is guaranteed its integrity, and its government is assured self-control by the principal natiqns of Europe. It will be seen that the Congo River takes a great bend to the north, and that a river is marked as en- tering the Congo from the east at almost the most northerly part of the bend. That contributory stream is the Aruwhimi, or Itura—it is called by both names—and it will be found on examination that it takes its rise quite close to one of the lakes (the Albert Nyanza) which form the head waters of the Nile. _ _ _

Now this is one of the most useful and interesting of Stanley's discoveries during this last journey. It unites at last the explorations of the Nile and the Great Lakes, and those of the Congo ' • and it assures us of a wonderful water communication from coast to coast and from north to south which is sure to be of great value in solving problems of the future for Africa. There is just one other of the recent discoveries of Stanley's that we may notice here and then we will go to another part of the map. We have marked the Albert Nyanza with the letter A placed just to the east of the lake. To the south and west of the Albert Nyanza is seen marked another irregularly shaped lake. This was called the Muta Nyiga, and was mapped out almost entirely from re- ports of the natives. Those reports are now shown to be quite wrong. There is a much smaller lake there, it is true, which Stanley has christened the Albert Edward Nyanza. The nomenclature of these African lakes does not strike us as particularly happy or tasteful. However there is the Albert Edward lake, and a little to the south- east of it is one of the great mountains of the world, the mighty snow-covered Ruanzori, the existence of which has been up to now utterly unsuspected. These are the principal items of Stanley's last discoveries which have so far reached us. We may just mention that Emin's country was the little bit of land to the north of Lake Albert, where the Nile runs out of the lake on its way north to Egypt and the Mediterranean. And then there is the country of the dwarfs where the explorer had much trouble and hardship. The dwarfs live on the banks of the Aruwhimi. MISSIONARY WORK IN UGANDA. The letter of Mr. Stanley, which was published a few days ago, shows for itself thatthegreat traveller returned to the borders of civilisation somewhat south of that great Central African kingdom, Uganda, in which the Church Missionary Society is carrying on a work that makes martyrs by the score. Uganda is situated on the west and north of the Victoria Nyanza, between that lake and Lake Albert. The most detailed geographical and historical information yet published concerning that unhappy country and the caravan route which connects it with Zanzibar is published in the book of a Blackburn man, the Rev. R. P. Ache, M.A., FR.G S., entitled" rs9o Kings ot Uganda." Mr. Ashe has visited Uganda twice. He journeyed along the line marked on the accompanying map pining Zanzibar with the southern extremity of the Victoria, and it is by this route that Mr. Stanley has returned home. THE PORTUGUESE,CLAIMS. - -

We now remove our attention to the scene of the territorial dispute with Portugal, which has only just been settled by a scarcely-veiled threat of war. Away to the south, almost the direct south, of Lake Albert Nyanza, at a distance of 300 miles, we come to northern extremity of the much larger lake, Tan- ganyika, which (straight-line measurements being given) is about 400 miles long to south. And then, striking off from the southern end of Tanganyika, and journeying in a south-easterly direction for 200 miles more, we reach the north end of Lake Nyassa, which stretches a further 350 miles still to the south, and the river Shire runs out of Tanganyika at the southern end, ar.d has a due south general course of about 250 miles more to the point where it joins the great river Zambesi. _ _

It is this region of Lake Nyassa, the river Shire. and the Upper Zambesi-1,000 miles or more south of Albert Nyauza—which Portugal is now endeavouring to annex. For. observe, whatever the Portuguese say as to the exploits of Major Pinto, they do not withdraw their claim upon those lands, not even when cowed by Lord Salisbury's ultimatum. And that is the vital question. If the lands are theirs, we cannot question their action. But we also have claims upon the country. They say ' that the Portuguese discovered the country 250 years ago. If they did so, the discovery was never utilised, and the knowledge once acquired was forgotten. We do know that our own Livingstone found out those rivers and lakes. Journeying north from the Cape, he passed through the Bechuanaland and the territory of the Makalolo tribes, both of which have made great ad- vances in civilisation under his influence and that of his father-in-law, Moffat. North of the Makololo, or Matebele Land, Livingstone explored the Upper Zam- besi, and then made his way up the Shire to Lake Nyasse. The same indomitable explorer pursued his quest up as far as Tanganyika, and was found there at last by Stanley, who was sent by J. Gordon Bennett, of New York, to seek him. Now, following the exploration by Livingstone of the river Shire and Lake Nyassa, British missionaries made their way thither, and have since then really accom- plished a very important advance in the civilisation of the people of those parts. The Scotch mission settle- ments of Blantyre on the Shire, and of Bandawe on the Lake, have achieved great things in the way of solidifi- cation of the neighbouring tribes or clans, in promoting the peaceful settlement of disputes, of counteracting slave-dealers' plots, of security to the natives in their little possessions and in life itself. There are other mission stations also. Quoting from Waller's " Title- deeds to the Nyassa Land," we read—" Dotted here and there, from the Mangrove swamps of the Kangone mcnth of the Zambesi to tha farthest extremity of Lake Nyassa, we pass the graves of naval officers, of brave ladies, of a missionary bishop, of clergymen, Foreign Office representatives, doctors, scientific men, and mechanics. All these were our countrymen; they lie in

glorious graves; their careers have been foundation stones, and already the edifice rises." Contemporaneously the African Lakes Company has been at work striving to secure a footing for legitimate commerce, or, as Waller says further, "to show the tribes and nations that there are more valuable com- modities in their land than their sons and daughters." The missionaries have a steamer on Lake Nyassa. The African Lakes Company have steamers both on the I Shire and the Lake, with twelve trading stations I established at intervals throughout the country, and worked by numerous English agents. The capital sunk in all this by the Company is estimated at £lBO,OOO. Now all this has been accomplished by legitimate and peaceful means. There has been no violence, such as that which the Portuguese have recently been using in order, apparently, to secure to themselves the fruits of , British enterprise; and there has been no conniving, by British agents, at the slave trade. The Portuguese can- not claim a like innocence. They have even been con- certed in the hateful traffic. Livingstone found the servant of the Governor of Tett4 at the head of a large slave gang. And whilst, up to a very recent date, there were no Portuguese at all in the disputed territory, their occupation of the coast has been marked by constant' feud with the native tribf s. "They have taught them to drink. Their missions 'Ave failed. Their colonisation is not even a name." The quotation is from Mr. H. Drummond, a recent traveller in Nyassaland. It is of this region that Livingstone wrote in the last years of his life when he said :—"1 Lave °pared the door, I leave it to you (his countrymen) to see that no one closes it after me." THE KHEDIVE'S BANQUET TO MR. STANLEY.

IThe Egyptian Government gave a banquet at Cairo on Monday night to Mr. Stanley and his companions, for which 140 covers were laid. Riaz Pasha was in the chair, and Prince Hussein, Sir Evelyn Baring. Messrs. Joseph Chamberlain Jesse Collings, and Kenrick, Moukhtar Pasha, the Chamberlain, and all the English and Egyptian general officers were pment. Riaz Pasha pro- posed the Khedive's health, and afterwards that of Mr. Stanley. He spoke in high terms of the ability displayed by Mr. Stanley and his officers in bringing the expedition to a successful issue. Mr. Stanley, who was greeted with loud applause, thanked the Government for the honour conferred on him, and gave a summary of his travels,and alluded to the difficulty he had felt in choosing his route, and to the hardships overcome during the ex- pedition. He then dwelt on Emin Pasha's continual indecision, and the delay caused thereby. It was with difficulty that he could be pursuaded to leave the Equa- torial Province in spite of the many inducements held out to him. Mr. Stanley also referred to the accident which befel Emin Pasha after the perils and trials had been endured, and concluded by thanking Riaz Pasha and the other guests for the splendid reception they had accorded him. MR. STANLEY IN CAIRO. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—Mr. Stanley List night at'ended the Khedive's annual ball, to which about a thousand guests were invited.

div.head: AFRICAN EXPLORATION.
div.p: AFRICAN EXPLORATION.

Direct tidings have at length been received from the caravan of Mr. F. J. Ja,ckscn one of the officers of the British East African Company, whor with his party, left the company's station of Machakos in August last for the north-eastern end of Lake Victoria Nyanza, with the purpose of opening up the country, and the possibility of assisting Mr. H. M. Stanley's expedition. Swahili messengers have now brought letters from Mr. Jackson, dated from Sotik. October 7. Sotik is described as being 30 mins. south latitude and 35 degrees east longtitude, and within twelve marches of Victoria Nyanza. All the people attached to the caravan were in excellent health. For twelve days they passed through a dense forest, which was wholly uninhabited. At Sotik there was ' abundance of ivory, and food was cheap. Finally the tribes were very friendly.

div.head: ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF THE
div.p: ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF THE
KING OF COREA.

A despatch from Tokio, Japan, reports that a eunuch attempted to kill the King of Cores by trying to stab him with a dagger. One of the Queens arrested the assassin's blow. A powerful conspiracy was revealed. The eunuch was tortured to death.

div.head: TEXAS TRAGEDY.
div.p: A TEXAS TRAGEDY.

A frightful tragedy is reported from Galvestoß, Texas. Two rival factions known as the "Jayhawkers " and " Woodpeckers' began to fire at each other in court, when a young man named Kyle Terry was killed, and many persons were wounded. The judge only saved himself by making a swift retreat from the bench.

div.head: PLOT AGAINST THE CZAR'S LIFE.
div.p: PLOT AGAINST THE CZAR'S LIFE.

According to intelligence received in Paris, a con- spiracy on a very large scale against the life of the Czar has been discovered at St. Petersburg. Numbers of offi- cers, and even of court functionaries, are said to have been implicated in the plot, and it is added that the ring- leader—the colonel of a crack regiment—has committed suicide.
THE WEALTHIEST LA.DY IN SOUTH WALES.

The whole of the late Mr. C. R. M. Talbot's immense property has been left to Miss Talbot, his eldest daughter, without trust or condition. The property amounts, it is understood, to some millions. Miss Talbot, who is sole executrix, is between forty and fifty Tears old, and is now the wealthiest lady in South Wales. She is a philanthropist of unbounded liberality.

div.head: GREAT BRITAIN AND PORTUGAL.
div.p: GREAT BRITAIN AND PORTUGAL.

BOYCOTTING BRITISH TRADE. The Commercial Association of Lisbon has resolved to do all in its power to restrict trade with Great Britain. The inhabitants of St. Übes have prevented a Portu- guese merchant from shipping goods on board a British steamer, which was, consequently, obliged to leave with- out cargo. Many commercial travellers of French, American, and German houses have arrived at Lisbon to try to dispose of articles of British manufacture.

THE LONGTO.N COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
EX f RAORDINARY EVIDENCE.

Some sensational evidence was given at the coroner's II inquiry at Longton on Tuesday, respecting the explo- sion at the Mossfield Colliery, by which a large number of lives were lost. William Fletcher, the under manager, deposed that on three days before the disaster, he asked Mr. Potts, the manager, to go down the pit to see about the gas, but that he failed to do so. The Cockshead was a dusty seam, and water was regularly used to lay the dust, until Mr. Potts objected. Mr. Pottscomplained of 1 the cost of working the mine, and on September sth called the foremen together, and said that if they could not get morg coal out for leas money, they must con- sider themselves under notice to leave. The inquiry was again adjourned.

div.head: O'SHEA. DIVORCE SUIT.
div.p: THE O'SHEA. DIVORCE SUIT.
ACTION AGALNST NEWSPAPERS

In the Divorce Court on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Butt, applications were renewed on behalf of Captain O'Shea for attachments against the "London Star," the Dublin "Freeman's Journal," and the London editor of the "New York Herald," for publishing comments on Capt. O'Shea's divorce proceedings. Mr. Justice Butt observed during the arguments that the sting of the thing was suggested to be that the suit had not been brought for divorce at all, but to serve other purposes. He would give his decision after hearing other cases. Justice Butt ultimately declined to hear the application against the "Freeman's Journal," no person having been cited by name. He adjourned this motion for amend- ment, and would reserve judgment on the other cases until he had heard this one. If there was any offence at .11 he said it was obvious that the "Freeman's Journal" was the principal offender. The motions were accord- ingly adjourned for a fortnight.

div.head: SATURDAY. JANUARY 25, 1890.
div.p: SATURDAY. JANUARY 25, 1890.

THE annual meeting of the sub- Education, scribers to the National Education Association was held, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. LYuLrn STANLEY; and the question of Free Education was the main topic of discussion. In the report, which was adopted, it was remarked that "an important feature in the history of the year, is the sudden- ness and rapidity with which Free Education has advanced from an academic opinion to a pressing question of practical politics. By the end of the year, a limited Free Education grant was given to the public elementary schools of Scotland, and many of the Boards have already determined to . supply out of the rates such portion of the foes as the grant will not cover." There are sonic poli- ticians—Liberal as well as Tory—who would prefer to keep the education question in the background; but this is impossible, seeing that the Government have already enabled School Boards to dispense with fees in Scotland, while Lord SALISBURY is practically pledged, by his Nottingham speech, to make education free in this country, if the antici- pated surplus is large enough for the purpose. This being the case, it behoves both parties to look ahead, or they may find themselves in difficulties. It would doubtless satisfy the clerical party to make education free solely by an extension of the grant, leaving schools to be managed as now by men who are not responsible to the taxpayers; but would that do for those who provide the money ? Would it be a sound and healthy way of doing business? We think not. On the axiom that " taxation without representation is tyranny" it would be a tyrannical thing to hand over the funds necessary to make schools free without at the same time making provision forrepresentative control of the

div.head: s ' :1 1
div.p: schools. Sir Hurnit,Roscos covered this point, at the meeting of the Association, by moving. "That this meetinpapproves the resolution of the Coun- cil incorporating free education in the programme of the Association, on the condition that every school receiving a grant in lieu of Tees shall be under public representative management during the ordinary school hours." This means that School Boards ought to become general: There ia a School Board in every parish in Scotland; and that is one reason why the Scotch are so much ahead of us in these matters, and why in particular , that country is taking the lead in the matter of Free Education. So far as a trial of free schools has been made across the border we have the authority of Mr. MIINDELLA for saying it has re- sulted in a large addition to the number af atten- dances, especially amongst younger children. The present fee system puts a barrier in the way of. attendance, for it not unfrequently happens that money which has been set aside for school pence- has—under sudden pressure—to be expended; in providing food. Indifferent attendance results- in indifferent education, and ends, sadly too often, in parents being brought before the magistrates.. They are tgus" punished for their poverty. We require to get rid of this as far as may be possible, and to get rid of it in a way which will be satisfac- tory to the money-finders. But is Lord SALISBURY, committed as he is to the squire and the parsonr prepared to do the right thing? We strongly suspect that his object is to play into the hands' of the denominationalists, and re-endow the sects. As Mr. STANLEY said, on Tuesday, " the policy of the Department just now was one of open war ou the Education Act of 1870 and oa School Boards ;- and of apparent willingness to return to the iur controlled despotism of the clergy in matters of i education." There is a striking illustration of the mischief of clerical management in the dispute at' St.. Barnabaa' School, Warrington. One school, teacher has to be evicted by force and another put in his place mainly because the clergyman of the parish has exercised authority in such a way as to cause a serious division amongst the school mana- gers. It is notorious that in hundreds of denomi- national schools the , clergyman is everything while the rest of the managers are merelY machines for registering his decrees. The school- master is thus compelled to dance attendance upon the parson. He must, teach in the Sunday school, or lead the choir, or play the organ—under fear of dismissal. Indeed, encouraged by the present Government, the attempt is being made to carrY. this worst form of denominationalism into Beard' Schools. Take, for instance, the following adver- tisements : EMBERTON SCHOOL BOAR.D.--WANTED, 25th March, 01: earlier, a Certificated MASTER. Member of Church ca England preferred. GADDESBY SCHOOL BOARD.—WANTED immediately, for a Small Mixed School, a First Class Certificated Misrscs.4. Must be Musical and able to play a small Organ PI- Church. t Afvertisements of this kind arp,insultina alike tor the taxpayers and the ratepayers. Board Schools, be it remembered, are not dependent in any degree Upon voluntary contributions; arid the Boards in question are no more justified in saying "Church- man preferred" than a Corporation would he ill using the phrase in advertising for a Town Clerk or a Borough Surveyor. It is time there was an end to sectarian domination; let the cobllor stick to his last. If the schoolmistress of her free will likee to "play a small organ in church," nobody has 9. 1 right to trespass upon her inclination ; but it is an impertinence and a degradation to make Sunday duty a condition of the appointment. We need Free Education, and we need universal School Boards; but we must see to it that these boons are not crippled by the fetters of sectarianism.

Mr. Gladstone IT is some years now since Lord at RANDOLPH CHURCHILL referred to Chester. Mr. GLADSTONE as "all old man in a hurry." Mr. GLADSTONE is certainly old, but the odd thing is that there are no signs of age in his- speeches, and he is certainly not in a hurry. Chi the contrary, he cautions his followers agaiest building upon the expectations of an early disso- lution, and points the cheerful moral that the longer the Tories delay the next election the worse they will be beaten. The speech at Chester, on Wednesday, covers a considerable range °f topics, but, like the roads which in the olden time all led to Rome, they all end in Home Rule' Nobody understands better than the leader of the Liberal party the art of utilising in politics the principle of conservation of energy. His mind i° wonderfully expansive, and lie delights in " fresh woods and pastures new ;" but, having determined to accomplish a given object, he will not ail° himself, except for a moment or so, to turn aside , from it. This was conspicuous when the tension of of the county franchise was before the country, and when a bitter cry arose agshrt the resistance of the House of Lords. If 30' Gemesroele had been a mere popularity-lienter, nothing would have suited his hand better than joining in the attack upon the reere,.; but he studiously closed his lips on the subje°4 and brought the country back to tile immediate issue—the extension of the franchise, and by that means he succeeded in his aim. And so with Home Role; it is the issue before the nati°ll —no other reform can be satisfactorily taken up until it is disposed of; and Mr. GLAD3TONE, Seeing this, concentrates his energies upon securing its adoption. It is interesting to note, by the wayetini the growing demand for an extension of the prinei" ple to Scotland and to Wales does not escape hire' Indeed, it is not too much to say that the agita'- tion obtains his qualified approval. After show- ing that the resistance by the Tories and DiSSEIr tient Liberals to Home Rule for Ireland had brought into prominence the question of Home Rule for Scotland, he added: "What I wish too point out is this: That either Scotland ought to : have Home Rule to manage her own affairs or else the interests of Scotland, involved in Bills essentially and exclusively Scotch, ought to be so handled that the clear and pronounced sense of the majority of the Scotch members ought to be accepted by England." But Mr. GLADSTONE went on to prove by instance after instance that the opinion of the majority of Scotch members evas disregarded, leaving to his hearers the obvious inference that it was the duty of the people of Scotland to persevere in their cleraand for a Homo Rule Parliament of their own. And. so with Wales and with England as well as Ireland to again quote the Liberal leader, "the Wants of the people grow with the advance of civilisation, and to deal with and to satisfy those wants there is urgent need of an extension of the machinery of legislation. Pressing with renewed force the argil- ments against Coercion in Ireland, Mr. GLAD." STONE showed more clearly perhaps than he has over done before that there is a %vide difference between a Coercion Act directed against crime, and a Coercion Act, such as the present, which is directed and enforced against what is regarded in this country as legitz- mate combination. The way in which people are being sent to prison in Ireland for offences which are absolutely ridiculous in the light of conunon-

T THERIS seems to be some doubt o Be, Or ;Not To Be? whether the Warrington Extension, Water, and Improvement Bill will be proceeded with during the forthcoming session Of Parliament, or abandoned with the idea of oterting afresh next year. There are difficulties in the way, as is always the ease with an important Bill; but the question to be .considered is whether the difficulties will vanish by abandoning the pre- sent measure. We think not; and we are at a loss to understand the faint-hearbatin' ess which seeing to have taken possession of many of the members Of the Warrington Town Council. It is stated that, at a recent meeting of the Committee having charge of the Bill, the advisability ,of abandoning it was gravely considered; and it is understood that no final decision on the subject km yet been taken. It is found thatthe Waterworks Company show no disposition to consider anything but a Ikery large price for their undertaking; but that inte to be expected. It is the way with mono- Posts to squeeze all they can out of the public, and give as little as possible in return. Such a eentiegency is provided for in the bill, for if the Company will not sell willingly they may be own- Polled to sell whether they are willing or not Betides, tie purchase of the Waterworks is one" only amongst other things. The "Star "says :—" When the Czar travels, a little vanguard is sent in advance, consisting of two locksmiths, two carpenters, and two masons, all of them being married men, born in the Im- perial service, and devotedly attached to their august master. Their duties are to examine walls, floors, chimneys, and fireplaces, locks and fur- niture in every room occupied by the Czar. The chimneys in particular are the objects Jai special attention, in order that no infernal machine shall be concealed in them."

The Junior Conservative Club, Piccadilly, London, would seem to be in desperate straits, for the Honorary Secretary does not hesitate to tout for members in a wholesale fashion. A prospectus and circular have been forwarded to us by a Liberal who has, a second time, been invited to become a member. By way of tempting him, he is told that " the entrance fee of Five Guineas is suspended for the present." Perhaps we shall next hear of the club being suspended; that is, if the bird-lime fails to catch anything.

--- The St. Helens jury summoned to inquire into the circumstances of the death of the woman who was drowned in the canal, on Saturday night, were justified in making a strong presentment, seeing that this is the second death that has taken place at this dangerous spot. Somebody must be held responsible for closing this death trap. It rests with the Corporation either to see to the place be- ing properly protected, or to put pressure on the London and North Western Railway Company, as owners of the canal.

On another page, we furnish our readers, this week, with a sketch map of Central and Southern Africa. It is prepared in such a way as to show the various portions which are claimed by Eng- land, Portugal, Germany and France. It will be seen that, before long, Africa will belong to every- body—except the ns/Aives. The map will be found useful to students and commercial men as it has been drawn with special reference to : Stanley's latest discoveries, some account of which is given in an accompanying sketch.

- - - With regard to the evict on of Mr. Woollacott from St. Barnabas' School, on Monday, it is to be noted that, m the protests formally lodged by him- self and by the Vicar, there is no question as to the authority of the school managers. . The point raised is, as to whether the notice should have bneli fOr con 1119'10 Or for three months. But that is a matter surely for a court of law rather than for quarrelling about in school; Mr. wz)olia_ cott ought not to have resisted ; he has not quite the claim on the school, which an Irish peasant.has on the house which he has built.

Good news at last "Two doctors of Vienna, Dr. Joliet; and Professor Weichelbaun, have suc- ceeded in discovering the influenza bacillus, after a series of experiments in the Chemical and Physi- olocioal Laboratory of the University." Having found the bacillus, how would it be to treat it to a doss of one-hundred-and-ton ton gun? It is true that it is not considered safe to fire these big guns with a full charge, lint they should be equal with a reduced charge to killing a microbe. [N.B.—There will be no "reduced charge" when John Bull is called upon to pay the bill.]

- - Mr. Hopwood, the Recorder of Liverpool, has' been scv:rely criticised for the light sentences he has imrred ; but he lms made out a good defence; and, more than that; he is practically supported by Sir Henry James, aid the Lord Chief Justice. Answering a eorrespondent,Lord Coleridge says : " Without pledging myself to details, I think that Mr. Hopwood's principles of punishment aro Cer- tainly right." There is quite enough pain and 'punishment in the world; and if there is a plan of improving criminals without being too hard upon them tha plan ought certainly to have a fair trial.

The Mayor of Sligo, and the Mayor of Wexford have been sentenced as newspaper proprietors— the one to four months' and the other to two months' imprisonment for publishing news in their respective papers. It is the work, of course, of the bungling Rem ovables, and it will be backed up by "Balfour the Brave," after which the supporters of the Government will say that there is a free press in Ireland. "Equal laws "• indeed I Why, in England permission has to be obtained from a judge before even proceedings can be instituted against a newspaper proprietor in a case of criminal libel.

It is to be hoped that the London and North- , Western Railway Company will take due notice of the expression of opinion of the jury in the case of the lad Helsby, who was killed at 'Warrington last week. It is a serious thing to have to say "probably this accident could not have occurred had the assistant been an experienced man ;" and yet it is no more than the truth. The uncle of the deceased gave his evidence frankly and fairly, and it will be a shame if he is made to suffer in any way for showing the courage of his opinion. Life must not be needlessly sacrificed in order that a Railway Company may pay large dividends. Speaking, on Monday, as Chairman of the Church Pastorali Aid Society, the Bishop of Man- chester referred to what he regarded as an unfair use of Mr, Gladstone's name in connection with' some expression of opinion as to the omployment of laymen. Dr. Moorhouse added :--" He was not a politician, but it was an open secret that he did not approve of Mr. Gladstone's policy in respect of Irish affairs. He looked upon Mr. Gladstone, how- ever, as one of the greatest and most wonderful of English statesmen, and when he saw the old lion stung by mosquitoes he could not withhold from himhis sympathy, nor could he withhold the expression of his disapproval of the proceedings of those who took his great name and dragged it in the mud." Coming from an opponent, this is a fine tribute to Mr. Gladstone's character and genius.

Cuts amt. A singularincident was witnessed by a number of the worshippers in St, Helens Parish Church. on Sunday forenoon. Whilst the Curate (Rev. E. V. Everard) was engaged reading the second lesson, a stranger, who occupied a seat in one of the galleries, was heard repeating portions allotcd to the clergy. He was asked to remain silent, and his reply was " All right, all right, all right." Immediately the sermon was concluded, the man put on .his hat, climbed over the back of the pew in which lie had been seated, and walked rapidly along the aisle. Instead of leaving by the door at that side of the church he crossed to the opposite side. Here he suddenly turned his back to the congregation and knelt—at...theAop of the steps leading to the pews, Without speaking a word he rose shortly afterwards, and left the edifice. His strange behaviour nat nr- ally excited a little commotion among those who witnessed his conduct. ACCIDENT TO Ma. W. SHAW; OF RUNCORN. About neon on Seturday, while engaged in inviting sailors to attend the services at the Mersey Mission to Seamen on Sunday, Mr. IV. Shaw, the agent, met with a serious accident. He was descending a ladder from the dock side on board the schooner Jane Pringle, when the foot of the ladder slipped on the wet deck, upon which Mr. Shaw was thrown with considerable violence. Fortunately no bones were broken, but a large wound was inflicted upon one of his legs, and it is of so serious a nature that confinement to bed is necessary for several days. Dr. McDougall is in attendance. POACHING AFFRAY AT NORTON. Between one and two o'clock on • Sunday morning the gamekeepers on the estate of Sir Richard Brooke Bart., at Norton, came in contact with a gang of about 14 poachers who were armed with heavy bludgeons. The keepers, who were greatly out-numbered, were attacked by the poachers, who made their escape without being recognised. They, however, left behind them 58 rabbits, a hare, and five nets used in snaring game. Mr. Rigby. the head keeper, was very seriously injured, and his as- sistants did not escape scathless. The, poachers are sup- posed to have come from Warrington, but no arrests have yet been made. ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now OR. J. &W. Dutton. , Sankey-It., Warriagten.—Adrt. SCALDED TO DEATH AT WIDNES. Yesterday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Bradley Hotel, on the body of Peter Beesley, agedone year and nine • months, son -of Joseph Beesley, fireman of 12, Cross-st. At noon on Tuesday while Mrs. Beesley was preparing dinner,the boy asked for a drink. She poured a quantity of very hot tea into a cup, and turned away to obtain some milk and sugar, when she heard a scream and discovered that be had taken up the cup and had a drink. His mouth and throat were much blistered, and he was in great agony. Mr. Stead, the chemist; prescribed for him and afterwards he was attended by Mr. MacLennan, but he died from the effects of the scalds on Wednesday. A verdict was returned accordingly. PETROLEUM OIL.—J. S. Garland. 51, Bridge-street. War- rltraton.—Adrt. THE CHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION. About 1,100 labourers have enrolled their names as members of the St. Helens Union. On Sunday after- noon, Mr. J. P. King attended a further meeting at Widnes with the intention of forming a similar organisa- tion here. In reply to a question lie said it was quite impossible to enter upon the undertaking that week as he was engaged on a selection of committees for the different yards in St. Helens, where he hoped the organisation would be completed that day week, and then he could devote his energies to Widnes. The men in Widnes expressed themselves ripe for the union' and one of them told him that a manager had advised the men in his yard to have nothing to do with Mr. King, but his reasons were such that the men declared themselves to be more determined than ever to join the organisation. Mr. King further said that he would not consider Widnes worthy of the name if, within a fortnight of his arrival there were not 3,000 members connected with the union.

BRUTAL ATTACK ON A WIFE. An elderly man named Wm. Gray, a labourer, at the British Alkali Works, who resided in Midwooil-St., was brought up atWiclnes Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with doing grievous bodily hard' to his wife Mary. From a statement by Inspector Heighley it appeared that the prisoner went home at half-past one, on Monday, under the influence of drink, and commenced to call his wife bad names. Be then took up from the ' table a paraffin lamp ; which he threw at her. The lamp struck the woman on the forehead and knocked her to the , ground, and while she was lying there he kicked her on ' the head, inflicting two dangerous wounds. The prisoner was wearing a heavy pair of clogs. P.C. Ratcliffe after- wards entered the house, and found the woman lying on the sofa. Her face, he said, had been' battered to a pulp and the floor was strewn with broken crockery and the remnants of the lamp. The Constable took the prisoner into custody and found wet blood on his clogs. On Tuesday morning, when the prisoner was sober, he charged him with wounding his wife, and he replied " Is that'a fact." A certificate was put in from Dr. Hutchinson stating that the woman was not able to attend court, and the prisoner was remanded for a week. ANNUAL Crcc snAzcci SALE now on. J. & W. LANCADECERE AND TIIS NEXT ELECTION. According to Ihe "Star" the most backward part of the country, from all we hear, is still Lancashire. Sir Ughtied Shuttleworth has recently Laken the work of consulting the constituencies in hand, and he is assisted by a small committee of the Liberal Members for Lancashire. There are many constit- uencies in Lancashire which certainly ought not to be begging for candidates. The Widnes Division, for instance, is a certainty, and the people there are so public-spirited, and detertnined, that they, have raised a fund to pay the election expenses of a good candidate. This is an example which we should like to see followed in other parts of the country. The amount of election expenses—the unreasonable demands for subscriptions—so long as these things last, our Parliament House will he given over to money-grubs, capitalists, and the smug bourge4sie. It is time there was a change. Akistrat CLEARANCE Sat.r • now on. J. & W. Dutton, Sankey-Id.. Warrington.- Add. RECHADirE MEETING AT SUTTON. .The annual meeting of the. Liverpool district, of the Independent Order el Rechabites, was held in the National Schools. Sutton, on Saturday afternoon. Bro. Henry Sharpies, of Manchester, the high de- puty ruler of the order, occupied the chair, and among those present were Bros. James Robertshaw of St. Helens, chief ruler of the district, John Man- ning, of LiverpOot district deputy ruler, C. C. Lloyd, the district seeretary. and representatives from Liverpool, Widnes, St. Helens, Billinge, &c. The annual balance sheet, showing a satisfactory condition of affairs, was passed. The consolidation scheme, providing for the sick funds of each tent being consolidated like the burial funds, was unani- mously adopted. The election of officers also took place, and with one or two exceptions, all were re- elected. In the evening a public meeting was held, and was presided over by the Rev. F. M. Binney, vicar of Sutton. The schoolroom was well filled The Chairman gave a hearty welcome to the repre- sentatives of the Rechabite Oraer, whose growing prosperity, he said, was worthy all .congratula- don. (Applause.)—The Rev. George Hammond (Wesleyan) followed with an address, in which he inculcated habits of abstinence, and commended the ,Rechabite movement as a glorious cause with the two aims of temperance and thrift. He wished the institution every success.--Bro. Sharpies, the high deputy ruler, also spoke, and urged the claims of the order to the support of working-men During the, evening Miss Lewis, Messrs. J. T. Elliott,' T. R. Ford, J. La.ycock, J. Twist, G. C. Miller, Wilson and others, gave an excellent entertainment.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., IN EGYPT. Arrangements had been in progress for holding a Liberal meeting in connection with Runcorn Liberal Club, on Tuesday evening last, and the.ftight lion. Joseph Stansfield, M.P., had promised to attend and speak. In consequence of Air. Brunner's enforced , absence in Egypt, the meeting was postponed, but , ilnueri apparently before having received in- forthation to tat effect, 'had despatched the follow- I ing letter, which reached EtlnVyn on Sunday :-- " Luxor, Upper Egypt, 7th Annary, WO. • My dear Handley,—l am at last obliged to give up the hope to which I have clung until the last, of being able to reach home in time for Your demonstration. The cause of my absence, the illness of my friend Mr. Ellis, will be sin- cerely regretted by all to whom he is known, and in the Northwieh Divistonhe is known to very many. Though he is reduzed to a pitiably weak condition, he is now finally clear of the fever and will, I hope, henceforward gain strength from day to day. It hats been a sad Christmas, I time for me, for in the midst of all my anxiety about Mr. Ellis there came ths pews that my secend son had been suddenly attacked by serious illness, and for days he lay at the point,of death., Now, however,—thank God for it !—he too ie Ina fair way • of recovery. Mends at home, as well as ahr,rsul. will, I know, rejoice and give thanks with me. I with 1 could be with you to join in the welcome you will give to my friend Mr. Stansfield. There is no man ananngst the Liberal leaders who is more deserving of our cordial esteem and respect than he, Mr. Stanslield is no fair weather Liberal. - Since Palmerston's days he has at all times been ready to, incur obliquy in any Mlle which he deemed to ‘iat right, and however much th: polit.l.l.l.v:Yrld may teen tnnt to time hire difrered from him, be has always held ' I ' straight en and baS fitalty brought the world round to his way of thinkiim. All honour, I say, to such, men ! I' I remember well how manfully in old days Mr. Startsfield stood up in defence of the oppressed Italians and of their much maligned leaders. Just as fearleg:ily of late years, has he taken the part of the leaders of the Irish nation in spite of the storms of abuse and vituperation showered upon them by the Tory party and the Tory press. The day, I hope, is not far distant when sitting again on the Speaker's right hand, alongside of the old chief, he may again be devoting his courage, his wisdom, and his eloqu- ence to the good old cause, and may I as your member be there and see.—Yours, faithfully, John T. Brunner.. W. Handley, Esq."

INSPECTOR O'DO..siliELL AND HIS SUPER - ANN CATION. At the meeting ot the joint Committee Of ?lagis- trates and County Councillors, on Saturday, Colonel France-Hayhurst presiding, a discussion took place with regard to Inspector O'Donnell. formerly of Runcorn. , The Chief Constable, in reply to Dr. Hodzson, said it was part of a constable's duty to subscribe 2i per cent. of his pay towards the superannuation lund, in accord- ance with the Act of Parliament. Ile did not think that a constable who voluntarily resigned had any claim on the fund. If he was recommended by the Chief Constable, under certain conditions, afterso many years' service, or after being disabled, he could obtain a grant. The Clerk read the Act as follows :—" It shall be law- ful for the justices, upon the recommendon of the Chief Constable, if they shall think fit, to order any con- stable to be superannuated and to receive out of the superannuation fund a yearly allowance subject to the following conditions:—lf heshall have served with dili- gence and fidelity over 15 years and less than 20 years, an annual sum of not more than half his pay ; if 20 years or upwards, an annual sum of not more than two- thirds his pay; provided if lie should be under 60 years of age it shall not be lawful to grant any such allowance unless upon the certificate of the Chief *Constable that he is incapacitated from infirmities of mind or body to dis- charge his duties ; also that if any constable shall be disabled from any wound or injury received in the actual execution of his duty it shall be lawful to make an allowance of not more than the whole of his pay." He (the Clerk) quite agreed with Colonel Hamersley's reading of the act. Dr. Hodgson said he took it that if a man had served fifteen years he might receive a pension of half his pay. There was a notorious case in which a constable, after serving 18i years resigned, and there did not appear to be the slightest intention to grant him any superan- nuation. Mr. Listen-11e cannot get it. Dr. Hodgson said it was evident he could not, except on the recommendation of the Chief- Constable, and be thought it would be a graceful action on Colonel Hamer- sley's part—serne members thinking this a case of extreme hardship—if some suitable superannuation were grantee. The Chairman, after the question had been discussed to some extent, ruled that the case was not now before the Committee. INSPECTOR O'DONNELL'S CASE. Mr. Tomkinson asked it there would be an opportu- nity of raising the question of the dismissal of Inspector O'Donnell, of the Runcorn Division. It was a great pity that it should be burked. The Chairman remarked that he did not see that they had that before them' nor did he see that they had any right to interfere at all between the Chief Constable and his subordinates. He understood the e.se was being brought before the notice of the Home Secretary. Under those circumstances they had better not interfere. The case was not on the agenda paper. The Chief Constable said he had no desire to " barke" the question. He was perfectly satisfied he had done what was right. A circular letter, which had been sent out, contained.a vast amount of untruthful information, and what Was More, a great deal of it was grossly libel- lous against himself. It was high time this matter was stopped. Here was an individual taking away the characters of people who had served the county—and he was not referring to himself in the slightest degree— and rendering their position almost unbearable. If this thing went on, he should ask that he might be permitted to consult the law-officers of the county for the purpose of taking criminal action for libellous slander in such Matters as were now brought up. Mr. Brundrit, as chairman of the Petty Sessional divi- PlOll me question, said the man ought to have been dis- missed years ago, and if his advice had been acted upon, there would have been none of this now. Unfortunately the Chief Constable believed the • man instead of him (the speaker), and had brought this trouble upon his ' own head. The Chief Constable wished it to be understood by every member of the Committee that he did not shirk inquiry in the slightest degree. He was perfectly certain that if they went- into the whole of the matter he would come out with cleaner hands than ever. The only un- pleasantness he ever had in Cheshire with a magistrate was through backing this man. Mr.,Tomkinson explained that he had wished to raise the question quite as much in the interests of the Chief Constable as of anybody else.

For thu. new three-horse vans to be employed in carrying on the parcels post service between Liver- pool and Manchester, twenty tenders have been received by the Liverpool postmaster, the time for receiving such expiring on Tuesday. The mail van will be of extremely light make so as to combine the maximum of speed with a minimum of weight, which, together with a full load, will generally be about a ton and a half. .The van will be drawn by three horses, and on the sides there will be in con- spicuous lettering the words " Royal Parcels Mail," with the " V.R." on the doors at the back. There will be no accommodation for passengers, so that any revival of the stage-coach era is not to be looked

for. FILTERS.-7. 8. Garland, ironmonger, Bridge-street, War- rington.—Adrt. A DISAPPOINTED WEDDING PARTY. A wedding party from Rainford met with an un- fortunate disappointment at St. Helens Parish C`hurch, on Monday afternoon. It is stated that a loving couple from the district named had arranged to consummate their "hopes of happiness" between the hours of two and three inthe afternoon, but an unfeeling and unsympathetic railway service inter- fered with the realisation of their blissful anticipa- tions. Half-past two had passed before the pro- verbial "happy couple " svith their friends had reached St. Helens station. With all haste a cab was obtained and the party was soon at the doors of the sacred edifice, but the disappointment can be better imagined than described, when they found that the clergyman engaged to officiate at the nuptial ceremony had departed to fulfil another engagement. Unwilling, but compelled, the in- tended bride and bridegroom had to return to the neighbourhood from which they lied jonrneyed: The uniting of the happy couple in the" holy bonds of wedlock " took place next morning, and congrat- ulations poured upon, them after their unhappy disappointment on the previous day. A TRAVELLING SHOW WRECKED AT ST. HELENS. An extraordinary street accident'occurred at St. Helens on Tuesday afternoon. A travelling show- man, named Green, of Preston, Was entering the town from Liverpool,and his "cavalcade "consisted of six trucks of hobby-horses and other parapher- nalia, drawn by a traction engine. As the engine was coming down the steep incline of Cropper's hill, Prescot-road, some portion of the machinery gave way and the engine swerved round against one of the dwelling houses on the side of the street. Tiappily no person sustained any injury, but the show and hobby-horses were seriously damaged. The cars were twisted and hurled about the road ; a lamppost at the spot was nearly destroyed, and three of the vehicles and their contents were scattered in a heap in the middle of the road. The street was rendered impassable, and all vehicular and tram traffic was blocked for over an hour. Ordinary vehiclea were sent round by Becleston-st. and Boundary-road, a distance of half a mile, while the tramcars, to and from Prescot, had to stop at each side of the "block," and the passengers had to walk from one eta to the other. .Another traction engine was obtained, and ultimately the disabled trucks were dragged to the fair-ground in College- lane. It iFI estimated that the loss tq the showman was about £25. FOR PRINTING of every description, try the Examiner ()dee, Warrington.

deep regret at the loss it has sustained by the death of one of its members—Mr. John Birchwood Itnison.—and the members respectfully beg to tender to Mrs. Imison and family their sympathy and condolence."—The Chairman said Mr. Timmims regretted greatly that be was unable to be present to submit this motion. Mr. 'mi- ssal had been a member of the Board for about six years and his loss was deeply regretted by every member. Ile was a capital worker, but worked in such a very MOS' tentatious and unassuming manner that people did not give him credit for all that he did. As far as the Board was concerned his placectiuld be filled, but the loss to his family was irreparable.—Mr. Deacon seconded the motion, and remarked that Mr. liaison was an active member of one of the most important committees ot the Board, and always did his work in a thoroughly capable manner. It was not reasonable to suppose that on a Board such as that that they could be unanimous upon all possible occasions ; it WAS not even possible that members of one particular party could he unanimous upon everything, and it had sometimes occurred that he had differed in opinion with his colleague Mr. Itnison, but he had always been impressed with the fact that Mr. Imison acted honestly, and he thoroughly appre- ciated his motives, and, be believed they all recognised hisearnest endeavours to do his best for the Board.— Dean Finegan supported the motion, which was carried unanimously, and the Clerk was instructed to communi- cate it to the family.

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing December there were 63 applications for the pay- ment of school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 59 cases. 147 persons appeared before the Clmmittee for contravention of the Education Act, and 24 were praecuted and convicted by the magistrates. lb THE EXPENDITURE OF TEE BOARD. The-Fhpince Committee reoorted that the receipts for the past month amounted to £llB 6s. 6d. and accounts amounting to £654 6s. Od. The estimate of the expendi- ture of thelloard was submitted. The School Management Committee estimated that the expenditure at Si turns Cress School would be £2,415 ; and the income: School fees, £850; Government grant £1,447 6s. 7d. ; other sources £4O; total income £2,337 63. 7d., leaving a deficiency of £77 13s. sd.—Warrington-road School; Expenditure £1,207 ; income school fees £365; Government grant £619 18s. 3d. ; other sources £10; total £994 18s. 3d., leaving a deficiency of £212 is. 9d. West Bank School: Estimated expenditure £1,905; income school fees £640; Government grant £1,016 4.4. Od. : other sources £2O ; total £1,676 4s. Od. ; leaving a deficiency of £228 16s. Od. District Education Committee, £445; Sites and Building Committee £650 ; Finance Committee £2,380 ; total £3,993 us. 2d.—The Committee recommended that a precept be served upon the overseers for the sum of £3,900, &ling the estimated amount of the deficiency in ' the School Fund up to 29th of September 1890; also that the precept be signed and sealed and made payable on or before the Ist day of March, 1890.—Dr. O'Keefe moved the adoption of the minutes, and in answer to Mr. Brown, stated that the precept was £lOO more than last year.—The minutes were passed:......

div.head: TH2 VACANT SEAT.
div.p: TH2 VACANT SEAT.

The Clerk read a letter from the Education Department authorising the Board to fill up the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Imison.—On the proposition of Dr. O'Keefe it v as decided that the rule observed since the establishment of the Board, be adhered to, and the vacancy filled by the members of the denomination to Which S 4 ClCccaSed gentleman belonged.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. That the honour of being president of Widnes Conservative Club, which has been thrice refused. has at last been accepted by Viscount Cross G.C.8., secretary of State for India, and the Tories ought to be happy now that they have secured a titled head. That the membership of the Club is now stated at 317. That Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the Runcorn Union, has received a communication from the Cheshire County Cooncil, which is not fraught with "tidings of comfort and joy" to the already overburdened ratepayer. That the comMunication is a contribution order amounting to £4,706 13s. 5d., which is More than twice the amount which was estimated for at • the commencement of the half year, and a supplemen- tary rate will be required ia the various townships of the Union to meet the Cell. That the Runcorn share will be about 16S0-1 nice little bill for the luxury of having two repre- 'sentatives on a County Council. ' That at the vestry meeting last March the over- seers hada considerable balance in hand and per- haps they will be enabled to meet the excessive demands of the C.C. Without issuing a supplemen- tary rate. By so doing they will earn the grateful thanks of a great army of taxpayers. ! That the order will, no doubt, be submitted to the ' Guardians at their meeting on Tuesday next, and . Mr. Speakman, who is a member of the Finance , Committee of the County Council, may enlighten the Board on the subject. That the salary of Mr. John Aston, the respected Clerk to the magistrates of the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division, Las been increased from £3OO to £3.50. May he live many years to enjoy it. That a inovem.mt is on foot amongst the church- Li of Whines to perpetuate the memory of the late Mr. J. 13. Itnison. Various suggestions have been made, but the one received with most favour is the provision of an organ for St. Paul's Church.
PENKETII. OFF TO EGYPT.

On Monday morning Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gar- nett, and Miss Garnett left Hall Nook, Penketh, en route for Egypt via the overland route. It is expected they will 'visit Paris, Naples, Venice, Rome, and other places of note. arriving in Egypt about,the 7th of February. The tour will probably extend over two months. AN ARRANT IMPOSTER. An occurrence which ought to be a warning took place yesterday week at Penketh. A respectably- dressed man appeared to be taken suddenly ill, and some good Samaritan went to his assistance and carried him into a house close by. A doctor happen- ing to be passing he was called in. He said the man was really ill and was not safe to be alone. The man said he was walking from Manchester to Liver- pool where he expected to get a boat for Glasgow for which he had enough money to pay the fare. But it was plain lie could not walk to Liverpool so the good people into whose hands he had fallen, managed to get his train tare from Warrington, and gave him 9s. the amount required to make it up. One friend harnessed his pony, and conveyed him to Bank Quay Station, and saw him comfort ably i.eatect in a train for the north. Afterwards it was found that, on some pretext, this arrant imposter got out ; of the train, loitered about the station for awhile, then went to the booking-office, and got the money back for his ticket and decamped. His description , is—rather above middle height, light complexion, dark hair with sandy beard and moustache; dressed respectably with gloves, collar and black tie, and wears a light coloured Inverness.

ANOTHER CHARGE AGAINST LORD GALLOWAY. At Glasgow Central Police Court on Thursday, Alan Plantagenet Stewart, Earl of Galloway, was charged with having, contrary to the Glasgow police act, 1886, on the 22nd day of January, 1.890,1 n the Trongate and Argyll-street, dlasgow, been riotous and disorderly, or. indecent in his behaviour, by accosting, following, and molesting Margaret Brawn. a 37, Well-st., Glasgow.", Lord 'Galloway, on being brought into the Central Police Office on Wednesday afternoon was, after the charge had been received, liberated on bait, of £lO. Mr. C. D. Donald,solicitor,appeand for the defence, and tendered a plea of not guilty.—Margaret Brown, aged sixteen years, and two policemen gave evidence, and Stiperidiarg Gemmell found the charge not proven. The accused then got his pledge of £lO and left the court. CBITCLILEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Adve.

div.head: ...' . „ – . , Is . .. . , ,
div.p: MR. STAN SFELD, M.P., AT FRODSRAM-
THE LIBERAL POLICY.

On Thursday night a crowded meeting was held in Frodsham Public Rail, under the auspices of the local Liberal Club Mr. T. A. Rigby preeided. A re- solution of welcome to the Right Ron. James Stans- feld, M.P., was passed, on the proposition of Mr. Shore, seconded by Mr. White, and supported bff.r. James Tomkinson.

Mr. Stansfeld, in replying, spoke at length on the - Irish question, and said the policy of the present Government was coercion, intended to crush out the • national spirit of the Irish people, and make them, obedient servants to their English and Scotch superiors. Their policy was to refuse to the vast majority of the Irish people that system. of national self-government which they felt to- be their doe; which they felt would enable them to concentrate their energies upon the advancement, the improvement, and the regenera- tion of their native land. It was part of their policy, as far as they could persuade the people, to find money to buy out the landlords at more than their interest—at the people's cost and the people's risk (hear, hear.) The Liberal policy, on the other hand, was Home Rule—(ap- plause)—national self-government; an Irish Parliament, with an Irish executive springing out of that Parliamen- tary government, legislating for Ireland within limits which the Imperial Parliament should decide, on purely Irish affairs, but alway subject to the absolute supre- macy of the Imperial Parliament itself (applause.) ltl was part of the Liberal policy that there shall be a ful reduction of unjust rents and of arrears (hear, hear). It was part of the policy of the Liberal party, when they got the chance, to repeal the Coercion Act. (Applause.) The last Coercion Act that should ever be passed in this country. (Applause.) In some senses it was the worst Coercion Act ever passed. because the Tory Government made it perpetual. Perpetual ! In three years hence it would be blotted out for ever. (Applause.) There was no such thing as a union which was not a willing Union. It was subjugation. (Ap- plause.) In the event of a gigantic European war— and the soil of Europe was at present trembling beneath the tread of hundreds of thousands of armed soldiers— where would be the paltry, miserable poky by which Ireland was now held in subjection by 30,000 soldiers. (Applause.) Those soldiers would have to be re-called ; terms would have to be made to Ireland, and they would have to be asked to defend our shores. (Applause.) There was no conceivable extravagant ex- penditure upon the Army or Navy which could sci much add to our strength as the satisfying of the Irish people would add to it in the face of the world. (Applause.) The time had come when the country must decide be- tween the two policies. They had thrashed out the subject before the public. There was not much more to be said on either side. The Tories did not believe the Liberal facts, and would not listen to their arguments, and the Liberals returned the compliment (laughter.) The Liberals happened to believe that the country was with them, and they ca.'led for and claimed a dissolution. t (Applause.)

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.

The annual meeting of the shareholders of Parr's lanking Company, Limited, was held at the Bank premises at Warrington, at noon on Friday. Mr. J. C. Parr, the chairman of the Board of Directors, presided, and there was an unusually large attend- ante of directors and shareholders. .rint REPORT.—THE CuatinnaN ON TaanE 131PROTEmaNT. The report of the directors was as follows :—" The Directors, in submitting to the shareholders the p annual balance sheet Certified by the auditor, have t that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satiefactory. Including £21,912. 6s. Ild, brought from previous account, the net balance of profits, after providing amply fter all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at six per cent, is is £136,602 3s. sd. The distribution of this sum recom- mended by the Directors, is as follows :—lnterim half- year's dividend of 7i per cent., declared 26th July £2,000; dividend to be now paid of lop per cent. .free ot income tax, making 18 per cent, for the year '£58,800; bonus of 4s. per share (one per cent.), free of income tax £5,600 ;to property account £5,000; balance to next account £25,202 3s. 5d.; total £136,602 3s. sd. The directors who retire at this time by rotation are Colonel McCorquodale,Mr. Edward Greenall, Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart., M.P.., Sir Thomas G. Frost, and Mr. John Thomp- son': Mr. Thompson does not offer himself for re-election. The other gentlemen named are eligible and are recom- mended for re-election. A sub-branch has been opened at Great Crosby?' The CIikIRVIN, in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, remarked that he was happy to feel that the figures were such as to recommend themselves, and he felt sure that they would receive a very favour- able reception at the hands of every shareholder. At the last annual meeting they ventured to hope that better and more prosperous' times were in store, but he did not think even the most sanguine anticipated the marked iinprovement that had taken place during the past twelve 'months in their commercial surroundings, and which, he was happy to feel, was not absent from the balance sheet Although they might fairly congratulate themselves on their improved prospects, it would net be wise to indulge in over-confidence as to their continuance, but they all hoped that the present revival might be permanent. They all knew that there were certain dis- turbing elements that might check the tide of prosperity, but the directors felt that the shareholders were entitled to participate, whilst at the Same time should be continued the wise policy of adding something to the property account and to the next account. The year just past had been marked by no prominent feature. beyond the successful completion of the grest Consol Conversion Scheme, which was accomplished in the spring of the year. Turning to the balance sheet, the first item that showed any change was the money lodged, there being an increase of £156,000. This might not be more than a normal fluctuation, but it was satis- factory to notice that it was on the right side. Turning to the assets, their Consols . and Government securities remained at the same figure, for although the conver- sion he had alluded to naturally reduced them, they had always been held in their boas so much below their market value that It practically made no difference. There was a decrease of £175,333 in the cash and surplus funds, which might .be taken as evidence that the funds of the bank were better and more profitably employed than in the last few years, but the proportion was still larger than the exigencies of the business required ; they could afford to see it still further reduced, with advantage to the banks Another satisfactory featute that did not appear in the balance slnait was the increase of 981 in the customers' accounts, of which 631 were deposit accounts, and 337 current accounts. This might be taken as a proof of the bank's steely progrese, and the success of the business. The current experwes showed an increase of £836, but that wonld not seem large when compared with the in—_ creased business done, and the increased profit earned. After deductine expenses, amounting to £52,029, andt after rebating the bills at 6 per cent., they were Left with £136,602 3s. 51. as a balance, which was apper, - tioned as stated in the balance sheet. TheFdistributien being somewhat large, he thought it right to explain ;he • reason that actuated the directors in making the prspo- - sal. It had hitherto been their practice to deatare 15 per cent. dividend each half year, .nakme a total of 17. i per cent. This had now been continued thitteen years, and it seemed to the directors that as the bonus was considered part and parcel of the annual distribution-. it would meet the convenience of shareholders better if the distribution was consolidated into one dividend, and paid half-yearly. The directers therefore proposed to make it 18 per cent., to simplify it, to be paid as long as tip position and profits of the bank allowed of it. The Mcreased profits seemed to point to a somewhat larger increase than a half per cent., arid it was therefore pro- posed to pay a bonus of 4s. per share, bringing up the entire distribution to 19 per cent, per annum. Mr. N. ECM:anti seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously. misCELIANEOus ECENEss. Mr. TllnNlia proposed that, as recommended by the directors, a dividend of 10. i per cent., and a bonus of 4s, per share, be declared.—fr. Roamer Davies, who seconded the motion, said the, directors were in his opinion justified in adding the increase to the dividend. He agreed with what the Chairman had said with regard to the improvement in trade, and thouelit that the im- provement was &ore likely to be a permanent <me than the sudden rise they saw in 1873 and 1374. At the same time, he re-echoed the sentiments of the Chairman in asking them not to rely too strongly On the continuance they saw every day.--The proposition was carried. On the proposition of Mr. It. POIRPOINT, seonded by Mr. FFARRINGTON BCE NSLEY, the directers Were thanked for their services during the past year. awl it was re- solved that their remuneration for the year begun bo £5,000. The retiring directors , were re-*elected on the Motion of Mr. STANTON. and on.the prepesition of Mr. W. SHARP, seconded lw Mr. TINSLEY, the inceLicg re-elected Mr. J. C. Stead. accountant. Liverpool, auditor.—Colonel McCerqundale, in inoving a vote of thanks to the general secretary, thesecretary, and other officers of the bank, spoke in high terms o, the abilities of Mr. Dun, who briefly acknowledged the conipliment.---The proceedines closed with the p.nising of a vote,of thanks to the Chair- man.
