div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ALLEGED THEFT OF FOWLS.

On Saturday-, at the Warrington Occasional Court, two men named Joseph Shawcross and John Jackson were remanded to the Warrington County Petty Sessions on a charge of having- stolen three fowls, value 95., the property of William Beswick, at Walton Inferior, on the previous night. Constable Dutton met the prisoners on the Warrington-road, Walton, early on Saturday morn- ing, with a bag containing three fowls in their possession, and apprehended them. Mr. Beswick said the fowls belonged to him, and were locked up on Friday night. •
AVOIDING DISTRAINT BY, A "MOONLIGHT FLIT."

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, John Austin, Chorley-st., was summoned for having, on the 11th inst., fraudulently removed his furniture to prevent ' distraint for arrears of rent. Mr. Ralph Norman, the landlord, said that the defandant had, occupied a house in Haydock-st., belonging to him. The rent being 345. is arrears a distress warrant was issued, and defendant Moen removed his goods at night time to avoid distraint, Defendant was ordered to pay the arrears, together with costs, amounting altogether to £2 Bs. 6d., within a fort- night. He said that he would do so. •

ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF PIGS FROM AN INFECTED AREA. On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, a respect- able-looking man named Peter Gartland. who lives in Edward-st.' was summond for having caused two pigs to be removed out of an infected area, on the 30th Dec. Inspector Norman stated that in consequence of an out- break of swine fever in Bewsey-road, on the ILth Dec., that district was declared an infected area. On the 30th ult, two pigs belonging to the defendant were removed from Edward-st. to a slaughter house. Defen- dant, who said he was working at Wigan at the time, and did not know that his wife had sold the pigs, pleaded guilty, and was ordered to pay the costs, 3s. 6d. -
A CLOCK THAT GOT ITS OWNER INTO TROUBLE.

The Warrington magistrates on Monday ordered John Roberts, of the Old Crow Inn, Fennel-st., to pay a fine of 10s. and costs for having opened his licensed premises during prohibited hours on the 12th January. Evidence was given by Constable Evhns to the effect that at 12.21 p.m. on Sunday, 12th inst., he was passing along Dial-st. when he noticed the defendant's public-house open. The house had entrances in Dial and Fennel-sts., • and both doors were open. Ile went into the tap-room and found there half-a-dozen men, several of whom were drinking beer. The clock in the house gave the time as 'being half-past twelve. Defendant pleaded guilty, say- ing thatithe clock as out of order, and that had misled them as to the correct time.

div.head: ACT FOIL THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN:
div.p: THE ACT FOIL THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN:

A ease under the new Act for the protection of children came before the magistrates sitting at Warrington on Moonday,when John Gandy, of Crepper's-bro w,was sum- moned for causing his daughter, six years and nine months old, to offer firewood for sale, in contravention of the terms of the Act. Inspector Cox said that on the 13th inst., he met the defendant's little girl in Scotland- roud, carrying a basket containing firewood. She had been to Academy .street with a bundle, and was on her way to Town's End with the remainder. She was bare- footed and thinly clad. As it transpired that the girl Was carrying Wood to householders who had ordered it, and was not offering it for sale, the magistrates, on the advice of the clerk, dismissed the case. STEALING A SUMMONS FROM A MAN'S POCICET.

The bench of magistrates who sat at Warrington, lin Monday, granted a summons under rather unusual cir- cumstances. Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, attended the Court, and said that on the Friday previous he applied for a summons against a man to show cause why a dangerous dog should not be destroyed. The sum- mons was granted, and was made returnable for that day. It was made out and given to the complainant, who, however, when on the way from the Magistrates' Clerk's Office to the Police Station, was induced to go to the defendant's house—the Golden Ball, Winwick-road- -and whilst there both the summons and information were stolen out of his pocket. Under the circumstances he asked the Bench to grant a fresh summons, a rcquest that was complied with. A " CHEAP" RIDE THAT PROVtD EXPENSITE._-

Mr. Preston, on behalf of the London and North- Western Railway Company, appeared at the Warrington Police Court on Monday to prosecute a Manchester man named David Burgbloom, on a charge of having tra- velled on the London and North-Western Railway 'between Daresbury and Warrington without haying paid his fare. Burgbloom pleaded guilty. Evidence was given to the effect that on the sth inst. the defendant came to Warrington by the 2.37 p.m. train from Dares- bury. On reaching Warrington he waited about on the platform for ten minutes and then went down to the booking-office. He was asked by the collector for , his ticket and replied that he had not come by train. He left the station for a short time and then returned and booked to Manchester by the 4.20 train. On arrival at the exchange station he was charged by Detective Kynaston, who had been following," him all the afternoon, with having travelled from Daresbury to Warrington without having paid his fare. At first he denied it, but afterwards admitted the offence and offered to pay his fare. The Bench imposed a fine of 203, and costs, _l2s. ed.

div.head: PICKING AND SI'DALING.
div.p: PICKING AND SI'DALING.

On Tuesday, ;i-ille-N‘i;:rin.gq;--;;^1;(;lice Court, Julia 136,VieS, wife of an engine driver, employed on the Ship Canal, and Elizabeth Williams, wife of a Ship Canal ganger, were charged with having stolen from the shop of Skelton Bros., Horsemarket-st., a kettle, box iron, cooking tin, and kettle lid, together value 9s. 3d. Evi- dence was given showing that, on Monday afternoon- the prisoners went to Messrs. Skelton's shop in Horse, market-st., and purchased a number of articles, the total value of which was 18s. 4d., only 2s. 6d. being paid on account. They took the goods to the shop of Mr. Kenyon, druggist. Horsemarket-st., and asked to be allowed to leave tkem there for a time. Suspicious conduct at an eating-house on the part of Davies caused the prisoners to be watched. Information was subseauently given to the police, and led to the arrest of the prisoners, when it was found that in addition to the articles bought from Messrs. Skelton the articles enumerated in the charge were found in their possession. Prisoners were fined 20s. and costs each, or in default one months' imprison- ment with hard labour—Thomas Troy and James Griffiu were charged with having stolen two tweed coats, value 16s. 6d., from the shap of Joseph Newman, Butter- market-st., on Saturday evening. Troy was charged, on Monday, with having been found in possession of the coats, hut as no owner had been found up to that time he was remanded. During the day it was discovered that the coats had been stolen from Mr. Newman's shop whilst an auction was in progress, on Saturday. There was no direct evidence to donnect Griffin with the theft, beyond the fact that he was seen in Troy's company, and he was accordingly discharged. Troy against whom previous convictions were recorded, was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions.
THE POLICEMAN'S LOT: THE WAY THEY GET KNOCKED ABOUT. _ - .

Evidence was given at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, that goes a long way towards confirming the saying that the policeman's lot is not a happy one Among the prisoners awaiting trial were a Ship Canal labourer, named Charles Fudge, his wife Mary Ann Fudge, and a young fellow, respectably dressed, named 1 James Backhouse. The Fudge's were charged with hav- ing been drunk and disorderly in Corporation•st , on Saturday night ; Charles Fudge was further charged 1 with having assaulted Constables Evans and Hardy; and James Backhouse was charged with having assaulted Constable Davies and attempted to rescue Mary Ann Fudge from custody. Evans apprehended the prisoners Charles and Mary Fudge in Corporation- at., for drunkenness. They behaved in a violent man- ner, and the assistance of another Constable had to be obtained. The male prisoner lay on his back in the road, kicked anyone who came near him, and the officers had great diffculty in bringing the two to the police station. On the way down Backhouse interfered and attempted to release the female prisoner from the custody of P.C. Davies. The magistrates committed Charles *Fudge to gaol for one month's hard labour, and his wife for 14 days Backhouse was bound over in one surety of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and was also ordered to pay the costs, 10s.—At the same sitting of the Court a youth of the name of Lawrence Mannion was fined ss. and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane on Sunday morning, and for having as- saulted Constable Dean at the same time and place. Prisoner, who was drunk and behaving in a disorderly manner in Dallam-lane, was ordered home by the Con- stable. He refused to go, and struck Dean a violent blow in the mouth.

div.head: • MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH _POLICE COURT.
div.p: • MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH _POLICE COURT.
SA.T.IIRDAY.--Raore Alderman Burgess (in the chair)
and Mr. R. Garnett.

DmrsitEnNEss.—Joseph Marratt, joiner, Foundry-st., drunk and disorderly, in Foundry-lane, on Friday night, and also charged with breaking five panes of glass at the house of Joseph Southern, Fo,mdry-lane. He was fined ss. and costs for the drunkenness, but no evidence was offered on the second charge, and it was dismissed.— Thomas Burke, drunk and disorderly, in Knutsford-road, on Friday evening, fined ss. and costs. MONDAL—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Aldermen Harrison, Davies, and Sutton. DRUNKENNESS.— The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Thomas Hares, in Mill-lane, on Saturday night, fined 2s. ed., including costs ; Sarah O'Brien, in on Sunday morning, sent to prison for a month ; Joseph Pemberton, in Bewsey-road, on the 9th inst., fined ss. including costs. LODGING HOUSE KEEPERS SUMMONED.—James Daley, Scotland-road, and John McCaffivy, Upper Bank-st., were each fined ss. and costs for not complying with the requirements of their licenses as lodging-house keepers. THE SHINTY NUISANCE.—TIIORIRS Hilteliffe, Robert Corless, Edward Berry, George Newton, John Thomas Carter. Joseph Dickinson' wm. Allcock, and Thomas Griffiths, boys, were each fined Is. for playing shinty in Crown-street, on the 9th January. ANOTHER CHANCE.—Mary Knockton, a young woman, living in Erwood-street, was summoned for having used bad language in Bridge-street, on the 11th inst. The Chief Constable spoke in her favour' and the Mayor, in discharging her, advised her to make a /um start in life,

SMOKY CHIMNEYS. - John Stokes (Powys-street), Lawrence Wade (Winwick-road), James Longworth (Prince-street), James Whittaker (Mersey-street), and Thomas Ithittaker (Naylor-street), were each ordered to pay a fine of is. for having allowed the chimneys of their houses to be on fire.

DmTumuli.% THE PEACE —James Crafford and Thomas Jury, summoned for having committed a breach of the peace byfighting in Bridge-street, on the 11th January, were disJharged on payment of reduced costs. TIIESDAT.—Before Mr. John Platt, Mr. E. J. Guest, and Mr. W. Owen. Owen.

DRUNKENNESS.—Herbert Lawrence was fined 2s. ed., including costs, for having been drunk and disorderly at Market Gate, on the evening previous. Smoot, ATTENDANCE CASES.—Several people were sum- moned at the instance of Mr. George Riley,School Atten- dance Officer, for having neglected to send their chil- dren to school, and were fined in varhus amounts. ,
, WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS.—James Coyne was fined ss. and costs for this offence.

TErdasnar.—Before Major Litton and Captain Ridgway. DRUNICENNESS.—FQr this offence Robert Evans was fined 2s. Bd. and costs, and a woman named Towey was sent to prison for a month. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Crornall. DRITNICENNESS.—CharIes Flynn, a soldier, was charged in custody, with having been drunk in Naylor-st., on the same morning.— He was remitted to the military authorities to be dealt with.

ALLEGED ILLEGAL Rciviover.„—An elderly woman, named Ellen Rogers, was summoned for having removed her goods in order to avoid a distraint, from a house in Longford-st., belonging to Sarah Hatton.—The case was dismissed.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COLIIT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Tinsley. SLEEPING OUT.—Thomas Ratcliffe, James Morris, and Albert Furness, labourers, were charged with sleeping in a brickshed, without any visible means of subsistence, at Golborne, early the same morning Ratcliffe and Morris were committed to prison for seven days, and Furness for 14 days.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. U. Gaskell, jun. DRUNKENNESS.--Edward Godfrey, Wm. Egan, Ernest , Bean, Patrick Fallon, Michael Gill Ann Johnson, Thos. 'Forney, and Mary Walsh, were each, fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.

A FlGllT.—Thomas Maher, of St. Helens, and Patrick Murphy, were charged with committing a breach of the peace. On the occasion of the football match, Warring- ton v. Widnes, the defendants had a. fight about a bet, in a field off Lowerhouse-lane, and P.S.Strickland came upon the scene. The defendants were bound over tobe of good behaviour for three months.—Wm. Holden, of 33, Bank-st., who was assisting in the fight was dealt with in a similar manner.

THEFT OF COAL.—Sarah Bate and Mary Connolley, girls, of Sankey-st.. pleaded guilty to stealing 601hs. of coal, from the works of Messrs. Gaskell Deacon and Co., on the 21st inst.—lnspector Keighley said the parents were worse than the children in sending them out.—The girls promised not to offend again and they were dis- charged with a warning. THE EusrcATuur Aur.—For breaches of this Act a num- ber of parents were fined ss. including costs, on the evidence of the officers of Widnes School Board.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. junr. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon. each of the following: Hugh Hoyland, Martin Kavanagh, Thomas Carr, James Brett, Thomas Donegan, and James Murphy ; Richard Roach was fined 7s. Oct. and costs.

ASSAULT ON THE Pormil.—Catherine Hines, aged 18 years, of Marsh-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly and also assaulting P.C. Beaton. About half- past one on Monday morning the prisoner was drunk and creating a disturbance in Waterloo-road. She was using most indecent language and breaking the windows of her sister's house. P.C. Heaton took her into custody, when she kicked him several times on the legs and stomach. The prisoner, who had been previously con- victed of assaulting the police, asked to be sent out of the place, and the Bench sentenced her to a month's imprisonment for the assault and fined her 10s. and costs for drunkenness.

THEFT OF A PIGEON .—William James Martin, 13 years of age, of Midwood-st., was sentenced to receive ,ix strokes with a birch rod for stealing a pigeon belonging to Moses Hammond of the same neighbourhood.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. G.L. Wigg and Mr. G. L. Davies.

DiturnmNEss.—For this offetice a- fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon each of the following :—John Preston, Ann Parkes, John Boardman, Mary Jane Doyle, George Dmiley, John Russell, and William Wynn ; Thomas John- son and Thomas Garner were fined 2s. ed. and costs.

DOGS AT LARGII.—John Dyson, Heath-road, and Thomas Buttery' Crown-st., were each fined 6d. and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled. A CARTER IN TROUBLE.—John Moores, carter, was summoned for leaving his cart in Church-st. an unneces- sary time, and he was fined ss. and costs, CHIMNEY ON Fm.—William Graham, Bridge-A. was fined 6d. and costs Bs. 6d.
ASSAULT —Elizabeth Oxley, of the Holloway, was surrirnoned for assaulting Ellen Roden, and she was fined 10s. and costs.—Mr. Burton appeared for the com- plainant.

Secretaries of Football Cluts are requested to note that reports of matches rlayed on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

FRODSHAM A V. rHATTO HEATH A.—These teams met 011 Saturday at Frodsham, and the visitors scored one goal two minors to one try and five minors. Play on both sides was very fine. THarro HEATH V. FRODSHAM. 2ND TEAMS —These second teams met at Frodsliam, on Saturday, the visit- ors being the winners by one goal and three minors to a try and three minors. WIDNES Sr. MARY'S V. MOSS BANK.—This match was played at Widnes, last Saturday, and resulted in a vic- tory for the cupholders by one goal, one try, and two minors to one minor. Thaw° HEATH V. FRODSH.AM. IST TEAMS.—This match was played at Orange Park, St. Helens, on Sat- urday. Thatto Heath running out winners by a goal and four minors to one minor. Moss BANK 2nd v. HALTON VIEW lst.—This return match took place at Moss Bank, and ended in a victory for the home team. Score : Moss Bank, 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors ; Halton View, 1 goal, 4 minors. =RUNCORN HORNETS V. MR. A. FRANCIS'S TRAlL—These teams met on the Hornets' ground. on Saturday, and a good and fast game ended in favour of the Wasps. The Hornets played a very grand passing game. The whistle sounded with the score—Hornets, one gcal, two tries, three minors ; France's team, five minors. WIDNES V. Si'. HELENS "A" TEAMS—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday afternoon. St. Helens kicked off, with a strong wind, but Widnes were the first to attack, and after being within an ace of scoring several times Peters got over. No goal resulted. The visitors could make no headway against the capital com- bination of the "Chemicals," and shortly afterwards Peters scored a second try, the place kick again failing. A minor now resulted to Widnes. At half time the score was Widnes two tries, two minors, to nil. In the second half Widnes continued to have the best of the game, and frequently crossed the visitors' line. The game ended in a win for Widnes by one goal, five tries, one minor, to St. Helens WARRINGTON 2ND V. WYCLIFFE. This match was played on the ground of the latter. The honaesters started against a strong wind, and at the commence- ment Warrington attacked, their passing tactics com- pletely baffling the Wycliffe. As a result of some good play between Williams and Knowles, Oxley ran in, but the place was a failure. This was followed by Heesom dropping a goal, and scarcely had the game been re- started than Oxley gained his second try, the same player failing at goal. From a try by Barnes Oxley placed a goal. and an effort by Williams resulted in a further addition to the visitors' score, the kick at goal being futile. In the second half, Beaman scored for Wycliffe, and Woodward scoring:for Warrington, a good game was brought to a conclusion, the final score read- ing—Warrington, two goals, four tries, four minors ; Wycliffe, one goal. The winners owe their substantial victory to good all-round play, Williams, Knowles, Hee- som, Wilkinson, and Barnes being the most prominent. For Wycliffe Beaman, Deakin, Noon,Fletcher, and Lowe were.tthe pick, RUNCORN "A" TEAM V. BIRKICNIIE.AD WANDERERS.— Played on the Irwell-lane enclosure on Saturday, before a good crowd of spectators. The previous meeting between these teams at Birkenhead resulted in a victory for the Wanderers, and this causxl a lot of interest to be centred in the return fixture. Woods started the game on behalf of the home team, and no return being made, play was located in the Wanderers' half, being confined there for some time, and good play by the home for- wards penned the visitors on their lines. Hurst eventu- ally relieved to centre by a good dribble. Houghton replied with a grand bit of dodgy play, and a few minutes later the latter player almost got over, which again forced the Wanderers to defend. Some exciting play was now witnessed, the Wanderers at length getting relief through smart work by Sutherland, which carried play to the home half. Some grand passing between Pendlebury, Cawley, and Woods ended in the latter cross- ing the visitors' lines. Woods took the place, but failed to add. Kicking out, Hurst passed to Nosworthy, who put in a fine run, but May proved equal to the occasion. The game still continued to be fought with great eager- ness, half-time being called with the score Runcorn one try, one minor; Wanderers nil. Resuming the play was ' very exciting, Woods, Pendlebury, and Hollingworth doing good service, until some* line passing between Hurst Kelly, and Nosworthy efiabled the latter to get over after a good run, the 'kick at goal failing. From

div.head: 'HE
div.p: 'HE

t • now to call of time nothing further was scored, a hard fought game ending in a draw, the score being—Run- corn, 1 try, 1 minor, Wanderers, 1 try. Teams : Runcorn :U. May: full back; Haughton, Cawley, and Woods, three-quarter backs; Pendlebury and Hollings- worth, halfbacks; Williams, Bowyers, Andrews, Dutton, Gittens, Lee, Stubbs, Clarke, and Hughes, forwards; Wanderers: S. Bowyer, full back ; F. Bowyer, Kelly, and Nosworthy, three-quarter backs; Hurst and Herbert, half backs ; May, Garner, Sutherland, Jones, Murray, Morgan, Atkinson, Harper, and Elliott, forwards. Owatis COLLEGE v. RUNCORN.—This match was played at Monchester, on Wednesday, before a small attendance of spectators. The College had got a good team together, including Cooper, late of Old Leysians, Hastings of the Rechdaleriornets, and Howes of Sale, the Pvisitors being only moderately represented. Before the game was very old Crompton got a try, the same player converting it into a goal. Then Riley scored for Run- corn and Crompton landed another goal. Just before half-time Hasting got a try for the College, Hall failing at goal. Next Hughes got a try for Runcorn, and from the place Crompton kicked another goal, so that at half time Runcorn led by three goals to one try. The second half was opened by Entwistle scoring for the College, but Howes failed at goal. Later Crompton again ran in for Runcorn, and as he kicked another goal Runcorn won by tour goals to two tries. RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.—Runcorn met Bradford on Saturday, in the presence of about 6,000 spectators, at Park Avenue, and the greatest interest was centred in the game. The teams were as follows :—Runcorn: .T. W. Brazendale (back), Rev. G. H. Kensington, J. H. Crompton, and T. H. Davies (three-quarter backs), H. Hughes and W. E. Evans (half backs), P.Riley, It. Dolan, W. F. Hancock, Hampson, W. H. Broady, W. Higley, W. Hughes, J. Gayter, and W. Faulkner, (forwards). Bradford: E. Doyle (back), A. Bairstow, Robertshaw, and J. Jenkinson (three-quarter balks), F. Bonsor, and J. Wright (half backs), J. L. Hickson, J. Toothill, J. Fisher, J. Richards, A. G. Nettleton, G. Oates, E. Dew- hurst, H. Moulding, and E. Forster (forwards). The ball was started by Hickson at a quarter to three, and as there was no return Broady rushed it to midfield, where a capital pass was made by Bons'or to Jenkinson. 1314 this means the latter was compelled to kick into touch. The forwards then played with great dash, and Brazen- dale returned magnificently ; but Hickson checked fur- ther progress for a time. Broady and Hughes were equal to the occasion, both saving in fine style. Then Cromp- ton succeeded in breaking away, passed the ball to Kingston, who made a grand run, and succeeded in gett- ing over, and Brazendale obtained a neat goal. Pia? was then confined to neutral ground, and the forwards of both teams showed that they were equally matched. their play being exceedingly fine. Runcorn, however, maintained their ground, and by a series of judicious passes they gained a good footing. Davies took the ball to the centre, and Doyle. who was conceded a chance, failed,to drop a goal. Then followed a series of scrim- mages on the Runcorn line, and the homesters showed a dogged determination to hold their own ; but, again Brazendale relieved, and got the ball away. Bonsor, Robertshaw, and Bairstow watched the opportunity, and the sphere was taken back again. Robertshaw, who appeared to be the most formidable of the trio, was, 'how- ever, tackled by Kingston and Brazendale close on the line, and the Runcorn forwards, who kept in close quarters, followed up, and put a stop to progress until Robertshaw, who had received a pass from Wright, secured a dropped goal. The second half was played in a down pour of rain. W. Hughes put the ball into,motion, and it was returned by Doyle'. Hampson obtained pos- session, broke away, but Robertshaw was quickly to the rescue. Davies put in some good play, ind the sphere was taken to the centre ; but Doyle, who was watching hisopportunity, took it back to neutral ground. Here Crompton distinguished himself by putting in a splendid run; but the collaring process adopted by Wright and Robertshaw had its effect. Brazendale and Evans did good work in saving. Crompton and Hugh Hughes materially aided the play for Runcorn, whilst Davies gave the spectators an example of his powers as a runner, and was only brought up in the nick of time to avert danger. Later on he again essayed a dashing run, only however, to be again brought to. The defen- sive tactics of Bradford were the secret of their success in preventing what would otherwise have been signal defeat. Thu passing of FL Hughes, Evans, Crompton, and Kingston was the admiration of the spectators, who frequently indulged in loud applause, and the home team were somewhat mystified with the judgment displayed. A good chance was given by Crompton to Davies, and Runcorn then experienced bard times, as they were in the quarters of Bradford. Bonsor, by a free kick, suc- ceeded in getting the ball to the Run;orn half, but it was again taken back. Brazendale, through a penalty kick, had a try at goal, but nothing came of it. The game throughout was well contested, and at the call of time the score stood: Runcorn, one goal ; Bradford, one goal, one minor._

WARRINGTON "A" v. TummooK.—The match between these two teams which was in the first instance aban- doned through the fog, took place on Saturday at T ue- brook. The Warringtonians mustered only a poor team, and to make matters worse, two of the players failed to put in an appearance and no substitutes being forth- coming Warrington had to play, what is looked upon as the best fixture on the card, with only 13 men through- out the game. Tuebrook losing the toss, Eccles started the ball, and no reply being made play was at once in the visitors', quarters, until Thorniley, by a strong e rush, transferred the game to midfield. A spell of pretty passing, however, between Bleasdall,Eccles, and Morris neutralized any advantage gained, but a determined rush headed by Thorniley, Davies, and Isherwood. carried play back to neutral territory, and a free kick falling to the visitors, took hostilities near the home line, and a minor was conceded directly afterwards from a long kick by Sampson. Following the drop out play was fiercely contested at centre,' and notwitstanding the' great odds Warrington had to contend against, they more than held their own, and a fine dribble, in which Berry, Beard, and Molyneux were notable, ended in Davies dropping at goal, the ball falling short of the bar. A strong dodgy run by Morris, who was finely floored by Thorniley, re- moved the threatened danger, but only momentarily, for a splendid bit of short passing by Berry and Thorniley, and a powerful kick by Jolley more than neutralized. Again Morris came to his side's relief, and aided by the wretched tackling ot the visiting team transferred the game to Warrington quarters. This was followed by Tuebrook dribbling up the field, and a kick by Ellams being miserably mulled, that player gained an easy try, which Eccles converted. In no way disheartened, the visiting forwards played with redoubled energy and had they been aided in any way by their backs a different result might possibly have been arrived at. Subsequently, Berry almost scored, and a rapid piece of passing between Howarth and Jolley should have resulted in a try, but Barnes failed to catch the ball and danger was averted. A grand screw scrim- mage followed, apd, led by Berry, Beard, and Davies, play was back under the posts, and Lawless was prominent by a grand tackle. Gradually Bleasdall and Eccles relieved, but Jolley getting a pass from Lawless punted finely to the home quarters. Here Beard, Isher- wood, and Berry shone prominently by good work, and a strong run by Morris, who was grandly tackled by Davies, brought half-time, with Tuebrook 1 goal to 1 minor. Re-starting, the home team soon attacked,. but Sampson stopped the rush at his 25 flag. A smart dribble by Berry, Davies, and Thorniley was spoiled by hard kicking, and Ellams kicked to touch at the. home quarter flag. Here Lally by a good piece of play further improved the position, an 4 Mather, intercepting a pass, was only stopped by Quine near the line. Ultimately Mather stayed a most determined rush by Fletcher, Pearson, and Kerr at midfield; but this was replied to by Jolley kicking back, and Quine mulling the hall, Mather was enabled to score a try near the touch flag, the place failing. From the drop-out a touchdown was immedi- ately conceded to the visitors. Berry afterwards fol- lowed up a free kick and took play to the line, but a strong rush, headed by Pearson,'Weston, and Bleasdall, was the means of the game being transferred to Warring- ton quarters, where Eccles effected a splendid run in, the same player converting. Still playing up manfully the visitors reached midfield, and a tremendous kick by Jollertent the ball to the Tuebrook line. The visitors were now evidently pumped by their exertions, and to make matters worse Beard twisted his knee, and was of no further use, leaving only six forwards. However, only one more try was obtained, by Ella,ms, after a splendid run, and Tuebrook were left winners by 2 goals, 1 try, to 1 try, 2 minors. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Sampson; three-quarter backs, Lally, Jolley. and Barnes; half-backs, Lawleis and Mather; forwards, Beard, Molyneaux, Isherwood, Davies, Thorniley, Berry, and Howarth. Tuebrook: Full back, Quine; three- quarter backs, Morris, Eccles, and Ellams ; half backs, Bleasdall and Fall; forwards, Weston, Fletcher, Jones, Pearson, Sloe, Kerr, Wootton, and Hewitt.

div.head: WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
div.p: WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.

WIDNES y. ST. lIIILENS.—The return match between Widnes and St. Helens, under the West Lancashire League, was played at St. Helens, on Saturday. The match excited considerable interest, as the previous engagement was only won by minors, Widnes being the victors by one try and three minors to St. Helens one try. The Saints, by their victories over Morecambe and Aspull, had raised the hopes of their supporters, who expected to have the former result reversed. Widnes started the ball against the wind, and neat passing by Little, Cross, and Fairclough to Foreman resulted in a dead ball by the latter attempting at goal with a drop kick. From a scrimmage at this point Brennan was conspicuous with some dodgy play, in the course of which he had his jersey torn from his back. Stscilow brought relief with a good run and kick, the ball going into touch in the visitors' quarters. Some very striking loose play followed, in which Widnes had slightly the host of it, and notwithstanding the strong wind which was blowing with the home team they found it no easy task to break through the visitors' front ranks. Laws got possession in the home quarter, and got away, but was collared a few yards from the line. Parkinson was then given a penalty kick, which with the strong wind against him was but a slight gain. The home team then gradually worked the ball to the visitors' line, where a scrimmage ensued. Hartles relieved grandly, but Sudlow receiving a free kick a little beyond the quarter flag raised the hopes of the Saints that with the few minutes that remained before half-time there was a chance of scoring a major point. The kick was left to Borthwick, but the ball striking the upright, Dearden followed up well and

div.head: :74311jnR,'SAT,U,RpAy, JANUARY 25, 1890
div.p: :74311jnR,'SAT,U,RpAy, JANUARY 25, 1890

fell upon it just behind the posts. Borthwick again took the kick, and sent the ball flying over the bar. This was received with enthusiastic cheering, which seemed to have produced a disheartening effect on some of the visiting team, for from this point the character of their play seemed to undergo a change compared with that of the first twenty-five minutes. 'A few minutes later Little got possession and grounded the leather, which Borth- wick failed te improve upon. When the whistle for half time sounded the score was: St Helens, one goal, and one try, to Widnes nil. Immediately after the kick off, and when from a long kick by the visitors the ball was allowed to go dead by the home full back, Laws following up dropped on the leather about a foot from the line, but was thrown over by the force of his fall., A try was claimed, but was disallowed. Thevisitors again crossed the line on two occasions, but the boll was kicked dead by the home team to save further disaster. The game endedfn a win for St. Helens by one goal and one try to two minors. Teams :—Widnes : Harties, back ; Morris, Parkinson, and Brennan, three-quarters backs ; Howard and Barber; half backs ; Hewitt, Smith, Robinscn, Kenyon, Gordon, Laws, Barber, Tickle, Holt, , forwards. St. Helens: Goulding, back; Sudlow, ,Fair- dough, and Foreman, three-quarters ; Cross and Little, half backs; Graham, Hardman, Flynn, J. Brownbill, John Brownbill, Dearden, Borthwick, Twist and Althant forwards. Referee, Mr. Simpson of Broughton Rangers.
WARRINGTON v. RUGBY.

Rugby brought a strong team to Warrington on Satur- day, but they still were lot able to cope with the legal players. Frank Turner haying kicked off, an invasion was early made into the Rugby quarters. The first te show up was Antrobus, who got away from a pack, and passing to Evans, the last-named passed to Lawless, but Stannard was on his man before he could get fairly into his running. By this means play was confined to mid- field for a long spell, and Warrington only kept their lines clear through the cleier saving tactics of Boscow. Antrobus ran the oval to the quarter flag, and this effort being supplemented by a neat kick on the part of Law- less, play once more rested at the Rugby quarter flag. Harrison here punted well, but Nevins neutralized the effort by a good return to Rugby quarters. A. neat Riles of passes was next witnessed between Bate, Antrobus, Evans, and Lawless, but a grand chance was not taken, and from a drop at goal by Massey, Hopewell conceded a minor. Immediately on the drop out a combined movement by the home forwards, the chief operator being Littlewood, rushed the leather past the Rugby defence, and Fair Turner scored a try, his brother, Frank Turner,plaeing a grand goal. Rugby now rallied, and play was taken in dangerous proximity to the War- rington goal. Both Harrison and Evans made strenuous efforts to score, and only the effective tackling of the Warrineton backs prevented them from accomplish- ing their desired nurpose. A tricky run by Harrison through the thick of the Warringtonians was deservedly applauded, but a lucky- kick by Lawless took play to neutral ground. Exchange kicks by Nevins and Hopewell were followed by another grand forward movement, in which Frank Turner' Povey, and Donohue were the leaders, and again the Rugby defence was harassed. Another brilliant run and pass by Antrobus was negatived by the tackling of Stannard, who was down on Lawless before he thoroughly gained posses- sion. A sharp piece of work by the half backs found Bate making a vigorous attempt to score, but unfortun- ately for the homesters he was held in play, and a scrim- mage was ordered. Another burst of passing by the Warrington baekseuded in nothing being scored ,and Law- less essayed a drop at goal,the ball travelling outside the posts. Warrington still forced the game at the Rugby end, for the drop out brought no relief, and from another scrimmage Bate threw to Antrobus, who ran and passed to Evans, the latter transferring to Lawless, a strong run being the result. By short rushes and judicious kicking Rugby relieved, only to find the War- rington hacks indulging in some transfers, Harrison finally intercepting, and the half way flag was reached. Boscow was called upon to defend his charge, which he did with credit, a grand screw kick placing his side on the aggressive. Bate threw wide to Massey, but the safetackling prevented him getting away. Fair Turner looked like scoring from a line out, and ancther drop at goal by Lawless forced the third minor. Immediately on there-start from some exchange kicking Harrison made his mark near half-way, and Stannard essayed the kick at goal, with the result that a grand goal, with the result that a grand goal was placed, a feat that was received with loud cheers. From the restart the " wire- pullers " went away, with commendable dash, and a good pass from Fair Turner to Evans saw Hall tackling the home centre before he could get away. From the pack which follower .Antrobus ran beautifully down the open, but failed to dodge his last man,. and *sinx wide to Lawless, Harrison intercepted, and relieved to the quarter flag. Another fine piece of passing 1)3, the Warrington backs was duly appreciated, and although Evans tried to get in the tackling of Stannard was too sure. Frank Turner and Holmes in conjunction drib- bled over the line in grand style, but Hopewell saved luckily and only a minor was scored. Soon after the drop out Evans 'kicked over the line from half way, and the fifth minor was registered, this point bringing half time, the score then reading—Warrington one goal, five minors, to Rugby one goal. With the aid of the wind the chances of Warrington this half were of the rosiest description, and from the kick of Boscow's return at once compelled Rugby to defend. From a run and pass by Antrobus, Massey and Evans, in turn ran the leather, over the line, and a minor was 'scored before a minute had elapsed. The drop out found play at half way, but a movement started by Nevins changed the venue to the visitors, quarters, when a splendid cross dribble was finally taken up by Littlewood and Holmes, the first-named kicking across to Lawless, who raced up and scored near the corner, Frank Turner making a good bid for premier honours. Still Warrington attacked, and Handles' reply to the drop out found Ivans and Woolf° making ittenuous endeavours to relieve their lines. It was of no avail, for another burst of passing by Bate, Antrobus, and Evans was taken up by the for- wards, and Fair. Turner and Handles outpacing Hope- well in the race over the line, Bandies was first up and scored near the corner flag. Again the kick at goal was a failure. The visitors were now a beaten team, and lacked that stamina which was so predominant in the Warrington ranks. The slightest attempt to relieve was easily repulsed, and after Nevins, Evans, Antrobus, and Donohue had displayed remarkable form, a fine piece of work by the following quartette, Bate, Antiobus, Evans, and Lawless, resulted in the last-named wriggling through the opposing, backs, and thus gaining his second try. Frank Turner kicking a grand goal from a difficult place. The game proceeded in the Rugby, quarters during the remaining portion of time, repeated bursts of passing being enlivened by smart dribbles, and about five minutes from the call of time Lawless negotiated his third try, Frank Turner failing at the place. A good game was brought to a close, the tele- graph board denoting the score as follows: Warring- ton, two goals, three tries, nine minors ; Rugby, one goal.

From a spectator's point of view, the game was a thoroughly enjoyable one, and the harmony which th•e- Veiled amongst spectators and players must in some measure be some consolation to the Rugby players for their heavy defeat. The Warringtonians all through played a far superior game, and excelled chiefly in pas- sing. This mode of play was at times brilliant, but many instances occurred when a player had the oval transferred to him, and it looked as if he had something too hot to bold, apparently thinking his business was to pass, no matter where the leather went, and this brought some looseness and carelessness into the play. Antrobus. Bate, Boscow, Nevins, Frank Turner, Littlewood, and Fair. Turner were the pick of Warrington. Teams :—Warrington Boscow, back •, Evans, Law- less, and Massey, three-quarters ; Antrobus and Bate, half hacks ; Fair. furner, Frank Turner, Nevins. Bandies, Povey, Littlewood, Donohue, Eyres, and flolmes, for- wards. Rugby: R. Hopewell, back; Harrison, F. Stan- nerd, and 0. E. Hopewell, three-quarters ; Mason and Harrison, half-backs ; Ivens, G. Stannard, Woolfe, Cow- ley, G. Hopewell, Hall, Sparks, Wise, and Barratt, for- wards.

SINGIMA_RZDISCOVERY OF A HOARD.

A singalar story comes from Macclesfield. At the police court, a hawker named Fryer has been com- mitted fortrial at the sessions charged with 'stealing £lB. The prosecntor was a lodging--house keeper named Foy, whobad been excused payment of rates on account of his poverty. 131 s wife dried on Saturday, brit just prSor to her death she'pulled a pair a stays from beneath a pillow and handed the apparef to her husband. Foy cut the stays open after his witfe's deatb, and found £l3O secreted in them. Re gave his wife "a splendid wake," and it was aßeged that while he was asleep afterwards the-prisoner took the money from his pocket.

FooTBALL—RuGBY.

To-day's matches Warrington v. Rangers at Warrrington; Runcorn v. Sale at Sake; Widnes V. Tyldesley at Widnes (League match); St. Helens v. Leigh at St. Helens (League match) ;St. Helens. Recs. v. Hoibeek at Holbeck.

Football enthusiasts in Warrington are looking for- ward with suppressed excitement. to the meeting of the "Lions "from Swinton and' the local " wirepullers," next Saturday. The Warringtoniansare on the winning track just now, but so are the Swintonians, so that it will be a case of "Greek meet Greek " when they face each other on the Wilderspool enclosure. Last Saturday both clubs did a big thing in compiling points, Swinton running away with the Liverpool Old Boys to the tune of five goats, three tries and two minors to one minor, and Warrington beating Rugby by two goals, three tries and nine minors to one goal. By the way the Rugby Club can claim to boa very "tall" organisation if its qualities are to be measured 'by the stature of its players. They seem to have a fairly developed race of giants dawn Rugby way. What is more the Rugbians play a fine open gentlemanly game ;in fact they play the Rugby game pretty much as it should be playee. They lacked, however, as the score indicates, the stamina and energy of the local team.

Here is what " Philistine " of the "Athletic News" says of the St. Helens Club and its Secretary r.—" The rather uncertain form shown by the St. Helens Club has not been conducive to providing a source of inspiration in the bosom of its followers that the Saints would be near the top, but still they have stiuggled on, helped by the unmeasumble supply of balmy hope which the irrepressible secretary of the club continues to pour on the wounded feelings of its defeated players. What the club would become without its present secretary is some- thing dreadful to think about. All clubs having fixtures with St. Helens must also make up their minds that they have to play the Secretary as well as the players. He is getting his fine work in all the time from the appoint- ment of the referee to the writing of the report, and when he bas finished there is not much left for the other Bide. He is a genius, and as a secretary can give points away to any other breathing the pure air of freedom and football. One can only hope that the club will, under such influence, thrive and be as successful as it ought to be."

"The play in the Runcorn v. Bradford match "says the "Athletic News," "was of the finest description,both teams having their full strength on the ground, thus making it a regular tug-of-war. The Re '.Mr. Marshall, who was present at the dinner after the game, at the Talbot Hotel,,paid a high compliment to the football which Runcorn had displayed, which stamped them as a club of the first water, the play having been of the finest description. Crompton's rust when he passed to the Reverend Kingston was a beauty,, and the sprint by the reverend, which put the finishing touch, was a treat."

Both Lancashire and Cheshirewill put county teams in the field to-day, the first-named against Durham, and Cheshire against Northumberland.. In the match at Hartlepool Lancashire will be represented by the follow- ing team :—Back, A. Hoyle (Broughton Rangers), ; three- quarter backs, J. Valentine (Swinton), J. Marsh (Swin- ton), and E. H. Flower (Broughton) ; hale backs, J. Mills (Swinton) and W. Bumby (Swinton);: forwards: C Anderton (Free Wanderers), H. Eagles (Salford), W. Atkinson (Wigan). E. Bullough (Wigan), G.. Holley (Swinton), T. Melledew (Rochdale Hornets), T. Kent (Salford), T. Whittaker (Manchester), H. Hasidism (Manchester Rangers). The Cheshire Committee have selected the following team to play Northumberland: J. W. Brazendale (Rancor:l), back ; .T. T. Haslain (Dukinfield). J H. Crompton (Runcorn), and F. P. Jones (New Brighton). three-quarter backs ;H. Hughes (Runcorn) and F. W. Spence (Birkenhead Park), half backs; A. G. Wood, P. Lockwood, H. T. Moodie (Birkenhead Park), W. Faulkner, W. Hughes, R. Dolan, P. Riley, W. F. Hancock (Runcorn), and W. A. Williams (New Brighton), forwards.

A 'sudden death took place on the football field at Hindley. Wigan,. on. Saturday. Edwin Ashton, a member of the Hindley AU Saints' was playing for his team against the members of the Flindley Brass Band Fifteen. The match had not been in progress more than ten minutes when the ball went in touch. Ashton got the ball to throw into play again, and as . it left his hands he fell. Noticing that he did not get up, the other players went to'seo what was the matter, and found that he was dead.

The St. Helens Rbcs'. supporters have hitherto con- sidered, and deservedly so, " Jimmy " Pikington as their pet and idol, but a rival claimant to popular favour has latterly been developing his ability to a remarkable extent. This is " Jacky " Seddon, vNiose chief point—if there is any superiority in any one direction—is that of "dropping" the oval over the bar almost from any posit;on in the field. On two successive matches Seddon has done the trick twice' and the calm and, seemingly easy manner in which he ha landed the leather over the bar has commanded the commendation of friends and foes alike.
The Kendal Hornets were simply never in the hunt with the Recs. The scorer a lone shows this—Recs. 3-1-7, Hornets 0-0-1. It is not often that the Hornets them- selves are stung with such a defeat.

The old rivals St. Helens and Widnes met once again, last Saturday, in the West Lancashire League. By way of a change the St. Helens men came out in the good old form and gratified their supportera by winning hand- somely. It is a pity St. Helens cannot keep up" the stride." its represeatiqives showed last Saturday, for if this were possible St. Helens would even yet show up fairly well in the League results.

FOOTBALL—ASSOCTATToN. The Haydock Collier lads accomplished a local record in Cup ties last Monday. This wa to achieve the dis- tinction of a defeat by Burnley in the county contest to the extent of IS goals to none. This, too, after Haydock had played the Burnley representatives to a draw on the Haydock ground r

Earlestown had some diffieulty in overcoming the Liverpool Pretis Guards in their tie 'fbr the Liverpool Senior Cup. The match was played on the Guards' ground, and how exciting the finish was can be imagined from the result—Earlestown 5, Press Guards 4.

/dxscELLANEoutit Two matches have been arranged by the Secretary of the Warrington Chess Club. One of these takes place this afternoon at the Farmer's Club, the headquarters of the Chess Club with ten members of the Liverpool North End Chess club, and the other a month hence at Liver- pool against a third team of the Liverpool Chess Club. The Warrington Club is only a young institution but it numbers some experienced players who may be expected to give a good account of themselves.

Warrington Gymnasium will be represented to-day in the first round for the National Challenge Shield by Messrs. J. E. Warren, Fair. Turner, J. Holmes, T. Locker, G. Vernon, A. Vernon, W. Podmore, and J. Pod- more. As I mentioned last week the Exeter Hall team whom the Warringtonians have to meet are a formidable lot, having already twice held the trophy.
MANCHESTER, LIVERPOnL, &c., AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The adjourned annual meeting of the members of the above Society was held,on Thursday morning,at the Lion Hotel, Warringtoh. when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr.J. C. Hale, of Present. The principal business before the meet- ing was to fix upon the division of the Society's dis- trict in which the show of 1891 shall be held. The Secretary (Mr. T. Rigby) read a letter that had been received from the Town-clerk of Bury, stating that he had the authority of the Mayor to repeat the Invitation to the Society to hold the annual show for 1891 in the borough. A letter had also been received from Bolton, intimating that a deputation, including the Mayor and Town-clerk of that town, would attend that meeting to invite the Society to hold the 1891 show in Bolton, instead of at Bury, as suggested at the last meeting. Mr. John Barrett, the 3fayor of Bolton, explained the request of the deputa- tion, and stated that at a large meeting, held at the Swan Hotel, Bolton, on Monday, a resolution was unani- mously passed that the society should be urged to hold the next sow at Bolton. It was now some eighteen years since the society held its show there„ and it would give great satistaction if the members could see their way to hold it at Bolton next year. An informal discus- sion followed, during which the Chairman asked the de- putation if some idea could be given as to the amount of assistance likely to be received from Bolton. The Secretary, asked for information, said that the usual practise was to ask for a guarantee towards the expenses of £250 ; for a suit- able site without charge, and for a supply of water, to the land. Rethought that altogether Bolton contri- buted about £l,OOO when the show was last held there. An opinion was expressed on behalf of the deputation that there would be no difficulty as regards contributing to the expenses, after which the deputation withdrew. A discussion followed, and it was resolved that the show be held in the Eastern Division, in which the two sites proposed are situate, but the question of finally selecting the site was, according to the rules, left over to a special meeting. The remainder of the business was of a routine character.

FUNERAL OF LORD NAPIER OF MAODALA. The remains of the late Lord Napier were on Tuesday laid to rest at St. Paul's Cathedral, with an accompani- ment of an imposing military ceremony. The body was removed at nine o'clock from the residence of the deceased -field marshal on a gun carriage, by a battery of the Royal Horse Artillery, escorted by a squadron of the 12th Lancers, and followed by coaches containing mourners, to the Tower of London, from whence the funeral procession proper started at 11.15. By ten o'clock immense crowds were wending their way, towards St. Paul's, the traffic at Blackfriars being partially blocked. At Tower Hill the concourse was enormous, and Tower- Was crowded with spectators, who stood behind the lines of soldie.rs The body of the deceased while at the Tower was deposited in the chapel of St. Peter tivincula, where a short service was held, officers cf , Ugh rank meanwhile bearing the deceased's coronet, his Eald marshal's baton, and his orders. The cortege left • the tower at 11.35, the bands of the Grenadiers and Scots Guards playing the" Funeral March." The procession 'was in the same order as from Eaton-square to the Tower. The Household Cavalry and Infantry lined the whole route, except the last portion, which was kept by the third London Rifle Volunteers. The greater portion of the Cathedral was reserved for officers and mourners, among the first arrivals being the First Lord of the Admiralty and the Secretary fee War, followed by the Lord Mayor and the civic officials. Among those who • !!.t, to the left of the bier were Lady Napier (widow), • Emilie Napier (daughter), Hon. Charles Cecil and '"hert Napier (sons), Miss Yule, and Mrs. More Nisbet; While representatives ot Royalty, the Army, Navy, and ,the diplomatic corps, were seated at the west door. The Prince of Wales and Prince George of Wales were in 'the front rank. The choir and clergy having emerged . from the vestry whilst the " Funeral March" was being `". the Roy ..,,Played, the great west door opened and a guard of honour p.ssion, Royal Engineers entered, preceding the funeral roce • which arrived to the strains of a melody from Chopin's " Funeral March." The vast congrega- tion rose t 9 their feet as the body was carried in by tight non-commissioned officers of Engineers. The in nee of Wales and other distinguished mourners fol- °Wed, the Prince placing a laurel wreath on the coffin, Which was slowly lowered into the crypt during the ~singing of the hymn "Peace, perfect peace." Tremen- '4Mm crowds waited along the line of' route to witness titi,e return of the military procession, and the Prince of Wales was loudly cheered as he drove back to Marl- borough House. After the conclusion of the debate on the Newfound- land fisheries in the French Chamber of Deputies on Monday, M. la (Wee questioned the Government regard- ing the cancelling of the credits voted by the Paris Municipal Council for the benefit of the strikers in the Rhone district. MI Constans, Minister of the Interior, in reply, declared that they had been cancelled because the Municipal Council in voting them had exceeded its powers. M. Joffrin, the member for Montmartre, who was declared elected in place of General Boulanger; then ascended the tribune, amid violent protests fronsthe Right and the Boulangists. MM. Cuneo d'Ornano and the Due de la Fauconnerie were called to order .and M. D6roul4de was publicly censured by the President, the Chamber deciding upon his temporary exclusion froinkthe sitting. FUNERAL OF LORD CAIRNS.

The funeral of the late Earl Cairns took place on Satz-- day afternoon in Bournemouth Cemetery. in a grave immediately at the foot of that ofahis father, who died at Bournemouth in April, 1885. On the coffin lid were the earl's coronet and a breast plate bearing the inscrip- tion," The Right Honourable Arthur William, second EaCairns. Horn 21st December, 1851: Died 15th Jan- uary, 1890." The chief mourners were Lady Kathleen Cairns, Mr. Ronald M'Neild, Mr. Jam WNeild, Bowers, Mr. Henry Graham, Mi. Stopford, Captain and Mrs. Dawson. Countess Cairns, the Dowager Countess, and Earl Cairns (the next-of-kin) were prevented from attending owing to indispOsition. The service was con- ducted by the Rev. C. L. Burrows. Numerous wreaths were placed on the coffin, among the send6rs being the. widow and mother of the deeeased 'earl, Lady Greville,• LordCarew, the lion. Helen Henniker, and the Hen. Alistair Hay.

div.p: THE GOVERNMENT AND4NATIONAL;
EDUCATION:

The Executive Committee of the Liberation Society have published a minute in which they review the edu., cational proceedings of last year, and anticipate the probable course of events in the approaching session Id their opinion the abandonment of' the revised code and the character of the Technical Instructien Act justify the conclusion that the Government have made a sur- render to the supporters of the denominational system by which the advancement of the national system has been retarded, if not seriously threatened. Although it is not within the Committee's province to, express an opinion on the expediency of free education; they hold that, if the principle be adopted, a broad distinction must be drawn between unsectartan schools under pub- lic control, and sectarian schools in the management of which the inhabitants have no voice. There are more than 10,000 parishes in England and Wales in which the children of Nonconformists are by law corn, polled to attend Church of England schools,: and that monopoly will be extended if they receive further grants of public money, without any guarantee that the rights of conscience will be respected. The Committee are of opinion that one of the greatest hindrances to national education is the claim for exceptional treatment on the part of the schools which, while designated "voluntary;" are mainly supported by the State ; it being proved that they are inferior to Board Schools, of the benefits of which more than half the population aredeprived. They therefore earnestly advise the friends of religious equal- ity to prepare for such resolute action as may be called for by educational proposals made in the, coming session.
SHIPWRECKED ON A DESERT ISLAND*:

EXTRAORDINARY ADVENTURES. The owners of the Liverpool ship Holt Hill have received full' particulars of the wreck of that vessel and the narrow escape of the crew. The Holt Hill, a four masted iron sailinc, ship of 2,387 tons, when going, from Rio to Calcutta in ballast met with very thick weather,. so thick that observations could not be taken, and at nine o'clock on the night of the 13th November she struck some rocks, which subsequently turned out to be St. Paul Island. The night was very dark and a terrible sea was breaking on the island and over the ship. The island consists mainly of precipitous rocks, but fortu- nately the Holt Hill ran into a gorge, and to this fact no doubt the crew owe their lives. The immense waves soon smashed up the after part of the, ship, leaving the fore part inside the cove. The crew had no time to deli- berate, so in the darkness of the night they one by one dropped from the how of the ship into the shallow water. James Williams, the mate; lost his life. It was assumed that he had been carried overboard by the waves that were sweeping over the vessel. When the day dawned the men clambered up the almost perpendicular rocks, and.thent their posi- tion was at once revealed to them. The island was. barren, and as not a particle of food was saved from the. wreck, noryet any water, the men had not much hope. Fortunately there were plenty of penguins on the island; and these' together with some lobsters and other sLelled fish that the men were able to catch,, served to satisfy their hunger. This kind of existence went on from day to day, burns the shipwrecked men were on the wrong side of the island to sight passing vessels, they moved to the northern part. On the eighth.day- they were glad- dened by the sight of a sail. This was the barque ' Coorang, of Port Adelaide. The signals from the island were seen on board the barque. and eventually the ship- wrecked men—numbering 31—were taken off and landed at Port Adelaide, where the Mayor of the town opened a subscription at the-Town-Hall far their benefit. The mate, James Williams, who lost his life, belonged to St. Agnes, in Cornwall. The Holt Hill belonged to the Holt Hill Company, Limited, and Messrs. W. Price and Company, of Liverpool, were the managing owners. She was built at Liverpool in 1884, and was one of the largest sailing ships.

Everything that tends to weaken our constitution and ren- der it liable to diseases is an enemy of mankind, and every- thing that tends to withstand the attacks of these enemies and to restore health and strength to the human system is a true friend. Among the most prominent and most dreadful, like so many generals in the attacking forces of the great enemy of mankind—death—may be mentioned the following: —lndigestion, liver complaint, nervous disorders, and chest affections, while the different symptoms by which these dis- eases manifest themselves may be regarded, as so many sub. officers in the ranks of the enemy. When anyone of these attacks us we may be-certain, that some of the others are close at hand. The stomach; 'flier, lungs, nerves and blood, are portions of the body that the-enemy is very prone to assail, and if he succeeds in maintaining:his position for any length of time in any one of them, and is not quickly expelled, he soon extends his pernicious dominions to other parts of the body. When the stomach is (Disordered we may be certain that the enemy in some form. or other has gained a foothold there, and if the- fothl be not properly digested the blood does not receive a sufficiency of the vital particles necessary to diffuse through all parts of the system In order to afford proper nourishment to- the belly. Hence- other parts of the body suffer from the derangent of the stomach. The same may be said of the fiver. It is the great filter of the body to purify the: blood. If the enemy assails it and hinders it in the performance of its proper functions, the- formation of life will be retarded,. con •itipation will result I from Insufficient bile, and impure blood will be conveyed towll parts of the body. On the other hand, if too much bile-is formed it proves hurtful to, the bowels, musing diarrheas,. dysentery. Any disorder in either at these organs—the stomach, or the liver, acts injuriously upon the nervous sys- : tem, and makes the sufferer over sensitive and irritable. causing sleeplessness, loss of memory, palpitation, and other painful forms of disease.. In our climate, affections of the chest are very prevalent in the form .of colds, coughs. bronchitis, asthma, etc. By the insidiouS attacks of these various enemies of man, thousands are annually laid low and brought to a premature grave. ADVANCING ROM gWABDS.

Sir,—ln our Parish Magazine "Banner of Faith," cir- culated with the knowledge of Bishop Juyne, last month appears, under a lesson for Sunday school teachers, page 284, "Where is the body of Christ? Answer, His Sacramental body is in the Holy Eucharist." " Now my senses tells me there is nothing only bread and wine; the Bible tells one that after the Apostles had eaten the last supper, Christ went out with them for a walk, and they sung a hymn, and Jesus spoke to them, (Matt. 28c. 30-31 vs.) At once this clearly disproves this absurd teaching of making God with a bit of bread or water. The Bible is full of figurative language, and was so thoroughly understood by the Jews, and it is by compar- ing passages that we arrived at the truth, or why not translate literally—" I am the door, the vine, ye are the branches, Judah is lion's whelp, Issacher is an ass, the seven cows are seven years, Caperneum is exalted into heaven, surely the people is grass." Augustine says— " Let us hear what saith the Bible," and he also said "No man who opposes reason is in- his senses; no man who opposes the Scripture is a Christian." "Tracts for the Times" says "We are to seek Christ on the • sacraments not through the word ; " no similar remark made here in a sermon lately. Now Christ Himself preached in the synagogues throughout all Galilee, and for this purpose he came. Bishop Wil- berforce, four days before his death, declared his con- - viction that the changes being introduced into the Church were of a Romanizing tendency, and the ' thorough hatred with which he regarded it :—" I hate and abhor the attempt to Romanize the Church of Eng- land." Bishops Magee, Thirwall. Pelham, Jackson, Ellicott, Hervey, 011ivant, Waldegrave, Dr. Tait, Dr. • Langley, all addmit there are Romanizers in the Church. We may well apply Mr. Gladstone's words to them (see Vaticanism, page 16). "I am confident that if a sys- tem so radically bad is to be made innocuous, the first condition for attaining such a result is that its move- ments should be carefully watched, and, above all, the -basis on which they work should be faithfully and Un- flinchingly exposed." If the bishops will not put down Ritualism, then the laity must use their power, and put down the bishops. Electors have this choice at the • ballot box by returning right, sound Protestants. . ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, January 13th, 1890.

THE NEW TON DIVISION. Sir,—lt is not my intention to enter upon a news- -paper controversy as to what is or is not being, done in the Newton Division. Your correspondent, "Liberal Elector," is so satisfied that nothing is being done that he says we are dead, and yet in the very same breath he says, at the eleventh hour, such and such things will be done. I confess that I am at a loss to reconcile these expressions of opinion. To begin with, I will suppose that from his want of knowledge of the facts of his case, that he cannot havesubscribed a penny towards maintaining an organisation in the Division, but in this he is only on a par with the men in Earlestown and Haydock whom he singles out for distinction. And why does he repine so much at the implied loss of or want of leaders? I thought it was one of the points of man- -hood upon which Englishmen, and especially Lancashire men, prided themselves, that, having a voice— that is a vote, in the affairs cf the country, he knew how to uqe it without being patronized by anybody. Bad our friend called himself by the other name I could shave understood the matter. Another thing surprises 'me, namely, that he should have been a constant reader .of your paper, and yet not have seen that year by year the revision of the lists of voters has been seen to by the Liberal party, for which again I say he can take no credit. I strongly advise him to step out and make his influence felt, for evidently the hour and the man have come. lam just a little curious to know in what corner of the division this ardent spirit dwells. lam quite sure the information he gives would he very acceptable to our Conservative friends who met in solemn conclave, on Saturday, to consider their position in view of the im- pending dissolution of Parliament so freely spoken of last week, but suddenly hushed up, although they have been so boastful as to their advantages on the new register. I believe it is a pure myth, and that the common sense of the community will assert itself at the polls whenever they are taken. lam glad to learn that Bt. Helens, and I was going to say Warrington, are doing so well, for between them they saddle the Newton Division with a dual vote almost equal in number to that ' by which the Newton Division was lost, and if your cor- respondent will but sharpen his pen for Warrington, he may rest content that, if they:can win, we are almost certain to follow suit, for the day will come when we shall, as before,get the upper hand,and this is not merely a pious hope but a well considered calculation ,based upon good data of which your correspondent seems utterly oblivious. As a last piece of advice I would recommend him to take a more cheerful view of political life, and give up whining, which only lowers the temperature of 'feeble folk.—Yours truly, ANOTHER OF THE 11,022 ELECTORS.

KILLED WITH A TOY REVOLVER. On Thursday, at Shoreditch, a coroner's jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against, Richard Bridgmore, aced 18, who on Monday at Hoxton shot dead Jessie Worland, aged 12. The youth and the little girl were playing along with other companions, and Bridgmore chased the girl with a toy revolver. She took refuge in a cupboard, but the door did not shut. The youth fired, hitting the girl in the head, and she fell lifeless almost immediately.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

THE BILLS IN PARLIAMENT. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (TIDAL OPHNINGS, kc.) This Bill came on Saturday before Mr. Campion, one of the examiners of the House of Commons, for proof of compliance with Standing Orders. There was no oppo- sition at this preliminary stage,and,the necessary formal proofs having been given, the examiner decided that the Standing Orders had been .duly complied with. The object of the measure, which will in due course be sub- mitted to the House for consideration, is to alter certain works authorized by the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (VARIOUS POWERS). This Bill came on Saturday before Mr. Campion, one of the examiners of the House of Commons, for proof of compliance with the Standing Orders. There was no opposition at this preliminary stage, and, the necessary formal proofs having been given' the examiner decided that the Standing Orders had been duly complied with. The object of the Bill is to enable the Canal Company to abandon certain works and to substitute others in their place, to raise additional capital, kc. THE FATALITY AT WARBURTON. _

Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an irniiie-a—;.i•the Thel- wall hospital, on Saturday, on the body of Samuel Knight, aged 2, a native of Hollins Green,who met with his death under circlimstances already reported. The brother of deceased gave evidence of identity. It was stated by a witness named Long that Knight, whilst following his employment on the Warburton section of the Ship Canal on Thursday, was in the act of picking up a bar of iron,which lay between a steam navvy and a wagon. Whilst doing so a second wagon ran down the line parallel to the first. In passing the stationary wagon, however, there was a collision, and on Knight getting up his head was crushed between the buffers of the steam navvy and the wagon, death beinginstantane- ous. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: DISPUTE AT THELWALL.
div.p: DISPUTE AT THELWALL.

About 30 fitters, labourers, and boiler smiths engaged on the No. 6 (Thelwall) section of the Ship Canal, struck work early on Monday morning, but have since returned to work. The action of the men was owing to the following notice, which was posted on Monday :—" From this day henceforward no fitter will be allowed extra time for overtime made, but will be paid for the bare time they work only." It is stated that prior to this notio6 being issued the men employed on night work received for five hours' actual labour pay equal to el hours, and for 10 hours' received remuner- ation equal to 15 hours' ordinary toil. It was the discon- tinuance of this practice which was thecause of complaint on the part of the men. It is asserted that this mode of payment has been established on the Cadishead section, and that it is proposed to introduce this system into several other sections. STOCKTON HEATH SHIP CANAL MISSION.

A Band of Hope meeting was held in the above mission room on Wednesday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. Waddington, missisonary on this section, who gave a very earnest address on the subject of temperance, in which he invited those present to take the pledge, which several did at the close of the meeting. After singing and prayer the following sustained a programme which was thoroughly enjoyed by a large and appreciative audience :—Miss S. Briggs, E. Lambert, David Briggs, Miss Hobin, R. Hughes, Percy Carpenter, Miss E. Hughes, E. Milner, Mr. Henshaw, Miss M. Travis Miss V. 13eswick, D. Hughes, Mr. Hallows, Miss D. lames, Miss Ada Gregory, Miss Reid, and George Hobin. The meeting was concluded in the usual way. The Rev. R. Grimston has kindly promised to give a limelight exhibi- tion of Ship Canal and other views in the mission room, on Wednesday next. THE MORRIS BROOK MECHANICS' INSTITUTE. This Institute, particulars regarding which have pre- viously been published in the • Examiner," was form- ally opened by Mr. John Price, the president, on Tuesday evening. Already about 80 members have joined the institute, the officers of which are as follows :—President, Mr. Price; vice-president, Mr. J. Lewis; treasurer, Mr. A. Robbins ; secretary and librarian, Mr. George Mann- ing; Committee, Messrs. J. A. Ewart, G. Harlock, W. Browning, J. Lythe, G. W. Raby, E. Collins, and Harold Dix. Games of various kinds comprising indoor quoits (made of indiarubber) dominoes, draughts, chess, &c., are provided for the members, as well as daily and weekly papers. In addition, there is also a useful library, containing about 250 books. It is also intended to provido a bagatelle table. The expenses of the Institute will be defrayed by the members' sub- scriptions, which amount to 2d. a week each. The room was well warmed and lighted, and presented a cheerful appearance. The weather on the night of the opening was of a very unfavourable character, and the attendance was small. Mr. Manning conducted the President through the rooms and explained the various arrangements for the comfort and amusement of the members. He said he had, on the previous day, received from a Warrington gentleman an addition to the library of 12 volumes, and the gentleman in question)had pro- mised to increase the number to 25 ; he hoped that the whole of the space in the library would be soon occupied by suitable books. Many persons had promised to give their assistance. Mr. Manning explained how the game of quoits was played indoors,and added that the Institute would be open every day from 10 a..m. to 10 p.m., Sundays excepted.—The President then threw the first quoit, after which he declared the Institute open for the workingmen of No. 6 section. Mr. Manning then presented Mr. Price,on behalf of the council and members, with a quoit bearing a silver plate, on which was the inscription : " Presented toJohn Price, Esq., on opening the Mechanics' Institute, Morris Brook, January 21, 1890." Mr. Price suitably returned thanks, and promised to do all in his power to make the Institute a success. They had, he said, some very good quoit players at Warrington, Lvium, and at other places. Quoit playing outside was sometimes rather a rough game, but inside it was much quieter, and he hoped the games which wnuld be played in that room would be conducted in a good spirit, and that the players who lost would manifest as good a temper as those who won. (Hear, hear.) He was grate- ful to them for the present which had been made to him, and could assure them that he was willing to do what he could to make the Institute a success. A vote of thanks to Mr. Price for his attendance and services was passed, on the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Browning, and the formal proceedings terminated.

div.head: TERRIBLE VOYAGE OF A CUNARD
div.p: TERRIBLE VOYAGE OF A CUNARD
STEAMER.

The Cunard Royal mail steamer Catalonia arrived at Queenstovin on Tuesday night, from Boston, after a fearful passage. during which she encountered a succession of hurricanes and snowstorms, attended with mountainous seas. A steam pipe burst and scalded to death three firemen ; who were asleep in the forecastle. A fourth man is in a precarious state. The steamer shipped immense seas, which smashed to pieces three lifeboats, carried away the bridge and ventilators, and large quantities of water got below and minguished seven of the fires. Several seamen were knocked down on deck, and one of them was swept off the bridge and dashed ngainst an iron stanchion. He was picked up insensible, and carried below. Two steerage passengers —a man and a woman—were also injured, and the inter- mediate cabin was flooded.

EATIL OF MR. H. ,BLECKLY.

After a ratter prolonged illness, Mr. Bleckly died yesterday atbhis resicience in Altnncham. By the death of Mr. Bleckly, Warrington loses another of those gentlemen who have taken a prominent and active part in its municipal affairs and who have promoted the growth of its industries. Mr. Bleckly, we believe, originally came from the south of England to Warrington, and became connected with the old Dallam Iron Company, of which he was evidently the managing chief. It was by an amalgamation of this Dallam Company with the Bewsey Company and the Pearson and Knowles Colliery Company, that the great firm of the Pear- son and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, which gives employment to a large section of the work- people of Warringtorixame to exist. From the time of this amalgamation till his death, Mr. Bleckly had supreme control of the large operations of the iron manufacturing branch of the Company's affairs, and upon the death of Mr. Pearson three or four years ago he was made chairman of the Board of Directors.

For a considerable number of years, Mr. Bleckly had not takea any official part in the municipal government of Warrington, but, something like a quarter of a century ago, he was an influential member of the Town Council, and he was Mayor of the borough in the years 1868-7-8. It is worthy of remembrance just now, that, when Mr. Bleekly was Mayor, he was a strong advocate of the purchase of the Waterworks, a scheme which, however, at that time, as so often since, fell through. He was also at one titne a member of the Warrington Board of Guardians and for some time was chairman of that body. After retiring from the Board of Guardians he still. retained a strong interest in all questions relating to Poor-law government, upon which indeed he was always regarded as a reliable authority. Of late years Mr.lBeckly'spublic activities have been mainly devoted to magisterial work. He 'mason the Commission of the Peace for both Lancashire and Cheshire as well as for the-borough of Warrington, and for two or three years past he held the import- ant office of Chairman of the West Derby Hundred Quarter Sessions. He was generally admitted to be both an able and an impartial administerer of the law, and for the discharge of the important duties •of a magistrate he was indeed _peculiarly well-fitted alike by his legal acquirements and his intellectual di4crimination. Mr. Bleckly was also amen of fine culture, and his extensive reading and powers of original thought were displayed on several occasions by papers which he read before the members of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society of which he was- a member. He was a pronounced Conservative in politics. Mr. Bleckly had reached the ripe age of 78 years at the time of his death. He leaves a widow, five sons, and one daughter. Two of his sons, Mr. W. H. Bleckly and Mr. J. J. Bleckly, are managing direc- tors of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. CONSERVATIVE REFEFiENCE.
