div.head: CONSERVATIVE DINNER AT WARRINQTON.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE DINNER AT WARRINQTON.

On Thursday evening a dinner was given in the assembly-room at the Conservative Club to the council of the association, the members of the club committee and the directors of the club buildings committee. Mr. R. Pierpoint, chairman of the asso- ciation, presided, and there were about 120 persons present. After dinner the chairman proposed the loyal and patriotic toasts.—Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones, in proposing "The Bishops and Clergy," said when the question of the disestablishment of the Church came within the region of practical politics, Conserva- tives, Nonconformists, and Churchmen alike, would stand shoulder to shouldet to support the Grand Old National Church, which was the dowry of every free- born Briton. (Applause).—The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton in acknowledging the toast said all the religious bodies throughout the country were being more and more drawn together, and he thought in the future they were more likely to be drawn together than they had been. He thought it was because they were seeing more and more every day that the common enemy with which they had to oontend was the anarchy and immdrtlity which usually arose in a state of rebellion, when that rebellion was altogether without any justification whatever.—Mr. John Fairclough pro- posed the toast of "The Army and Navy and the Reserve Forces," and it was responded to by Captain Nicholson, Mr. William Bloomfield, a Crimean veteran, Mr. Thomas Peacock, who .wa.s present at the relief of Lucknow. also responded, and Mr. Thos. Hutchinson, as representing the reserve forces.—The Chairman read a number of letters of apology for absence, including one from Lady Greenall, on behalf of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., who was daily improving in heatth.—The Chairman afterwards proposed "The Conservative Cause." They iiad, he said, a great cause, but a deter- mined enemy to fight. They belonged to a party which did not set class against class, or one part of the country against another; but to a party which believed they were all one and indivisible. (Applause.) The toast having been heartily drunk, Mr. ROBERT DAvrrA proposed "The Conservative Asso- ciation and Club." He contrasted a Liberal Govern- ment with the Conservative Government. The Liberals. he said, werevery fond of saying what they would do in office, but when they were elected every man had his own hare to follow, and it was a wonder to him that the country had not learnt to distrust them. (Hear, hear.) The late Mr. Bright was right in saying he did not believe twenty members of House of Commons would have taken up Home Rule if it had not been for the principle of following Mr. Gladstone. (Hear, hear.) Their word as Conservatives, was unity, and unity with strength. They believed that cry had been sufficient to attract to their side some of the most powerful intellects in the Liberal party. On no other ground would Mr. Bright have joined the Conservative ranks. (Applause.)—The !Chairman and the Mayor (Alderman R. w. Francomb)

div.head: AN ALLEGED FEROCIOUS DOG.
div.p: AN ALLEGED FEROCIOUS DOG.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- I day morning, before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall, James Welsby, landlord of the Golden Ball, Pinners-brow, appeared to answer a summons charging him with, on the 2nd January, being the owner of a dangerous dog not then under proper control. Mr. A. Browne appeared in support of a complaint made by a man named Leach, a tailor, of Nicholson-at. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defend- ant, and took a technical objection, but the magistrates decided to proceed with the case Mr.. Browne said that the section he pro- ceeded under said a court of summary jurisdiction. might take cognisance of any complaint that a dog was dangerous, and not unaer proper control, and if such appeared ta be the case might make an order fer it to be destroyed or kept under proper control. in this case he applied for an order for the dog to be deStroyed, and should call evidence to prove that it was dangerous. It did not matter where the dog was kept, as proceedings were not taken under the Rabies" Act but under the Dogs' Act of 1871. People who had been bitten had an idea that so leng as the animal was living there was danger of hydrophobia, and the complainant Leach whonaturally was so afraid, asked that the dog might be destroyed. On the day in question Leach was at the Golden Ball, ' and had occasion to go to the back-yard, where he was collared by the defendant's dog and almost worried, being bitten several times in various parts of the. body. He was taken to the Infirmary, and was afterwards , attended by Drs. Adams and Melville.—Complainant said i that hewas at the Golden Ball on the afternoon of the day in 'question, and had occasion to go to the back- yard. He did not know that there was a dog there. When about four or five yards from the door the dog attacked him, and bit him, and he was taken to the Infirmary. Defendant went for a doctor.—Dr. Melville, assistant to Dr. Adams, described the injuries received by the complainant.—For the defence Mr. Jenkins con- tended that the dog was not in a public place, and also that the defendantoriterr in the yard;tiad no need to go near where the animal—s, retriever—was chained to its kennel. Evidence was then called for the defence to the effect that complainant persisted in going to the dog in spite of warning, and that after the occurrence he said that it was his owe fault that he had been bitten, and not the fault of the defendant.—Alderman Harrison said the Bench thought that the dog was a dangerous one, and ought to be destroyed, but on the other hand it would seem that the complainant was at fault, and courted the misfortune that befell him. They, having regard to the numerous cases of hydrophobia that were heard of, thought it would be better that the dog should be destroyed.—After a little discussion Mrnenkins, for the defendant, agreed to have the dog destroyed, and Mr. Browne, for the complainant, agreed to withdraw the summons, and consequently no order was made.

THE TOWN CLERK'S RESIGNATION.
MR. WHITTLE'S APPOINTMENT RECOMMENDED.

At a special meeting of the General Purposes Committee, held on Monday, the Mayor (Alderman Prancomb) submitted the letter he had received from Mr. Brook resigning his position as Town Clerk of Warrington. The contents of the letter are given below. After the letter had been read, the... Town Clerk further explained that owing to the greatly increased duties, and tho salaries he had had to pay for assistance rendered, the office was unremunerative, and, in fact, he was considerably out of pocket by holding the appointment. He was of opinion that he could not ask for an increase of salary, because if lie did so he would have to do the work of the office personally, which his private practice would not admit of. A feeling of regret at the resignation was expressed by all the members of the Committee present, and Alderman HARRISON moved the following resolii- tion—" That this Committee, in receiving and accepting the resignation of the Town Clerk of Warrington, W. H. Brook, Esq., cannot refrain from expressing its deep regret that he cannot see his way to continue in the office he has so ably filled Ifor the past ten years with such conspicuous ability and integrity." The DEPUTY MAYOR. (AU. Sutton) seconded this proposal, and it was agreed to unanimously. In the course of the meeting the TOWN CLERK spoke highly of the qualifications for the office oh is deputy, Mr. J. L. Whittle, and pointed out that he Was thoroughly familiar with every detail of the work. The Committee seemed #n be entirely in favour of the appointment of Mr. Whittle to the office, and a sub-committee was ap- pointed to consider the conditions under which the appointment should be made. The sub-committee, we understand, met on Thursday afternoon and the conditions upon which the new Town Clerk shall be appointed were thoroughly considered for presentation to the General Purposes Committee, and' through them to the Town Council: The main provision of the new arrangements will be that the Town Cterk devote his whole time to the duties of the office, no private practice being allowed. The salary recommended to be paid is £5OO a year, which is to corer all charges exam' ing moneys paid out of pocket. The sub-committee fqrther recommended that the Town Clerk be provided with offices. at the Town ,HaTT. and with the ervices of an assistant. Another re- commendation is that Mr. Whittle receive the appointnient. • ' THE TOWN CLERK'S LETTER. The following is a copy of the letter of resigna- tion of, Mr Brook t--Warrington, 17th January, 1890. Dear Mr. Mayor.-1 have for several years contemplatted giving up the town-clerkship of this borough. 'The duties attached to the office.haiie so greatly increased as to necessitate the employment of the whole time of a thoroughly competent solici- tor, which Mr. Whittle, whilst with me, rose to be a few years azo this, in addition to clerks and office expenses, has made the post practically unre- munerative for several years. I, however, retained it, having an object in view which I think is now attained. I have, tberifore, decided now to resign- the office, and shall be obliged if you will communicate this to the General Parposes Committee, and request them to take the neoessahr steps for the appointment of my success:tr. If the Bill now 6eing promoted in Parliament is proceeded with, I shall be quite will- ing to give any assistance or advice that may be re- quired in connection with it. In resigning, I think it may not be out of place to refer to one or two achievemonta during my town-clerkship; first, the i

div.head: DARING BURGLARY AT A COUNTRY SEAT.
div.p: DARING BURGLARY AT A COUNTRY SEAT.

Brannstone Hall, near Leicester, the residence of Captain Pochin, was entered by burglars on Wednesday, night before the occupants had retired to rest, and jewellery worth £l,OOO was carried off. The door of the room from which it was taken was secured inside by wire and string, and the front door of the hall fastened in a similar way. The thieves got clear off, leaving no clue.

div.head: COLLIERY EXPLOSION.-,FIVE LIVES LOST.
div.p: COLLIERY EXPLOSION.-,FIVE LIVES LOST.

An explosion resulting in dialogs of ftvelives occurred, on Thursday morning, at the. Glynn pits, Pontypool, owned by the Ebbw Vale Company. About four hundred miners are employed there„ but 'many of these were not at work at the time of theexplosion. A number of awn were engaged in repairing the roadways soon after mid. , night when some timber ignited. Ventilation was checked, and a quantity of gas gathered and exploded. The men hurried towards the Otbottom, and all escaped except five, who were, it is believed, either buried beneath falls of roof or overcome with after-damp. Later it was discovered that the coal in the workings had also caught lires and that little could be done at present in the way of rgackle... FOR PLAcmtcS,, euq we or colour, try the Examiner Office. div.head: FATAL FALL ATV WARRINGTON.
div.p: A FATAL FALL ATV WARRINGTON.

A. fatal accident happened on Tuesday afternoon. to a boy named Edwin Fogg (aged 122), vtrho lived with his stepfather, Thomas lla.tes =ilk dealer, 152, Winwick-road. The deceased.l.vas last week engaged by W. Buxton, foreman for;lstr.. Morris Owen, con- tractor,of Manchester, to wist in handing rivets up to the men wb '3 are engaged in fitting np a new iron bridge for the Cheshire Lines Railway Company, in Battersby-lane. The lad llnisbed his work at four o'clock, but after that time was seen walking about on a plank .on the top of, the bridge. Immediately after, one of the workmen, hearing a fall, looked round, and saw deceased Iving on the footpath. Tie was unconscious, and bleeding very much from the . head. The lad was at, once conveyed to the Infir- mary, but on, his arrival-rthere life was pronounced !to be extinct. _ _ _

Mr. S.:Brighouse, Coroner, held an inquiry relative to the matter, on Thursday, at the Bridewell. Formal evidence having been given William Buxton said he lived at 85, George-st., Wigan. He. was in the employment of Mr. Morris Owen, contractor for the erection cif iron bridges, of Manchester. He was at present engaged in erectibg a new iron bridge for the Cheshire Lines Rail- way in Battersby-lane,, Warrington, where they were widening the railway. As.the ironwork for the bridge was being manufactured at Datlam Forge, Mr. Owen had beraowed a young man, named Fogg, brother to the deceased, frcm that: firm.,to work at the bridge. Witness :engaged the boy Edwin to work with his brother, and he commenced on the 15th inst. His duties were ;yen, simple—to % bore, soles and heat the pokers, -and Witness promised to pay him a shilling a day. :The lad told witness, that he had ptssed hi s stan- dards, and be accordingly took him on trial for a. time. The bey went to his work as usual on Tuesday. :It was found, however,,that one of the other boys was I absent, and the rivettere asked witness if they, could ha.va.: Fogg to assist them as,a substitute. Witness assented,. and Fogg accordingly commenced this new work at one o'clock'in the afternoon. As it came on, to rain !Ate rivetters, at the request of witness ceased work at four. p.m.—By the Coroner The scaffold upon which de- ceased vras working was 15 feet from tlie ground. It was conapoSeclotpOitte, chains, and font...planks, each, of which wag nine incites wide and 18 feet long. The acci- dent occurred as near as he could say no 4.15. Deceased left oftwork with, the other men, but, for some unac- countable reason was seen to go on the scaffold again. j The scaffold was, approached by a single planks eleven inches. wide and two yard long. No one actu- ally witnessed the accident, but au the time stated he (witness) heard a man shout ant that cne of the lads had fallen to the road. He ran fmra the bridge and picked the deceased tsp. He war!. taken to the hospital,. but on arrival then> life was pronounced to Itoextinot. 141 Juror.—The boN•was ratherryoung to be so employed', was he not ?—lhfitness.---'Yes,, but as he I was an intelligent lad, and wculd have to work with his !brother, I thought there waano harm M engaging him. The scaffeld was firmly secued to the wall, so that it 'could not shake.—Peter Cetton, Winavick,...st.. said that the lad must have fallen t.otn the plank, judging from the position of the body in the groand.- consulting in private, raturned a verdict death." ANT IDNES LOCAL BOARD. V V IN PASLIAMENT,—SESSION 1890. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (TIDAL OPENINGS, .t 0 AND WIDNES HEINE SUPPLY. • Pursuant to the Act 35 and 36 Vic.. cap. 21, and in com- pliance with a requisition duly Imade to me, I. as the Chairman uf the Local Board for the District of Widnes, in the County of Lancaster, DO HEREBY SUMMON A MEETING of the Owners and Ratepayers of the said District to be held in the Town Hall, Widnes, in the said district, on Tuesday, the 4th day of February, 1890, at half-past Eleven o'clock in the forenoon, for the purpose, if thought desirable, of approving and giving consent to the opposing by the said Local Board a the undermentioned Bills, or either of them, now pending in Parliament, namely : " A Bill to alter certain Works mithorized by the Man- chester Ship Canal Act, 1885 ; and for other purposes." also "A. Bill for incorporating and conferring Powers upon the Widnes Brine Supply Company ; and for other purposes," and also to sanction the application of the General District Rate, or other the Public Funds or Rates under the control of the said Local Board, to the payment of the costs and expenses attending such opposition. Given under my hand this 20th day of January, 1890. • FRED. H. GOSSAGE, Chairman and Summoning Officer.

WIDN.ES LOCAL' BOARD. • IN PARLIAMENT.-SESSION 1890. : MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (TIDAL OPENINGS, Ac.) • AND WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY. Pursuant to the Act of the 35th and 36th Victoria, chap. 91. intituled "An Act to authorize the 'application of Funds of Municipal Corpovatiou and other .governing bodies in certain cases." NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a MEETING of the Local Board for the district of Widnes. in the county of Lancaster, will be held in the Town Hall. In Widnes aforesaid, on Tuesday; the Fourth day of February, 1890, at Eleven o'clock in the forenoon, for the purpose of considering certain Bills now pending in Porno- ment,'and intituled " A Bill to alter certain Works authorized by the Man- chester Ship Canal Act, 1886; and for other purposes." also "A Bill for incorporating and confirring powers upon the Widnes Brine Supply Company;' and for other purposes," and. if considered expedient, of passing a resolution or resolutions to oppose the said Bills or either of them in Parliament, and to apply the General District Rate, or other the public funds or rates under the control of the said Local Board, to the payment of the costs and expenses attending such opposition. Dated this Twentieth day of January, 1890. JAS. T. ALLEN. Clerk to the said Local Board.

THE CONDITION OF CRETE. The following important news was: telegraphed on Sunday from Crete :—All the Christian Judges of the 'Court of Appeal in Crete sent in their resignations to Shakir Pasha yesterday. This step has been taken by these men as a protest against the Imperial Firman, and it is the latest interpretation of feeling. It is also stated that on account of the new, condition of affairs in Crete the position of the Christian Administrative Councillors is becoming very difficult, ancL iL is feared that they too will resign. •
